Receive buffer — bytes the remote sent that your program hasn't Read yet. State machine — the TCP state (LISTEN, SYN RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, TIME WAIT, etc.). When Go calls conn.Read() and there's no data yet, instead of blocking the OS thread, the Go runtime registers the socket fd with the netpoller — a thin wrapper around epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS/BSD), or IOCP (Windows). The goroutine is parked (marked non-runnable) and the OS thread is released back to the Go scheduler to run other goroutines. When the kernel signals "data ready," the netpoller wakes the gorout

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2
text: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer protocol browsers and servers use to exchange requests and responses over TCP. HTTP/1.1 (1999/2014) is text-based: each request is an ASCII header block followed by a body, and responses must be returned in the order requests were sent on a given connection — one slow response blocks every request behind it ( head-of-line blocking ). HTTP/2 (2015) rewires the transport: it uses binary frames and multiplexed streams , so many requests fly concurrently over a single TCP connection without any ordering constraint. Go's net/http speaks HTTP/2 automatically when TLS is configured — zero code change. Why it matters: HOL blocking is a real latency killer for Meridian's dashboard pages; HTTP/2 eliminates it without changing a line of handler code. Your checkout service doesn't speak raw TCP to browsers — it speaks HTTP . But HTTP has evolved dramatically, and understanding the difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 explains real performance characteristics you'll observe and tune in production.

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: HTTP/1.1: the text-based workhorse
text: HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9110/9112, 2022 — the current restatement of the protocol first standardised as RFC 2616 in 1999, still dominant) is a text protocol : every request and response is human-readable ASCII headers followed by an optional body. Here's a minimal checkout request and its response, crossing the wire: Keep-alive (persistent connections, on by default in HTTP/1.1) means one TCP connection can serve multiple requests sequentially, avoiding repeated 3-way handshakes. But "sequentially" is the operative word.

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: Head-of-line blocking: HTTP/1.1's fatal flaw
text: Requests on one HTTP/1.1 connection must be answered in order . If request 1 is a slow database query and requests 2–5 are tiny image fetches, requests 2–5 are stuck waiting even though they could complete instantly. This is head-of-line blocking (HOL blocking). Because HTTP/1.1 mandates in-order responses, the two fast requests can do nothing but wait — and then the responses drain strictly in the order they were sent:

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: HTTP/2: multiplexing and binary framing
text: HTTP/2 (RFC 7540, 2015) keeps the same semantics — methods, headers, status codes — but rewrites the transport layer completely: HTTP/2 encodes everything in binary frames, not text. Frames have a type, flags, a stream ID, and a payload. Parsing is faster and less error-prone than ASCII parsing. Each request/response pair is a numbered stream within one TCP connection. Streams are independent and interleaved — no ordering constraint between them. Multiple streams coexist concurrently on one connection. Stream 1 can be a slow DB query; streams 3, 5, 7 return instantly without waiting. HOL blocking is eliminated at the HTTP layer. HTTP headers repeat massively across requests (User-Agent, Cookie, Host). HPACK compresses them with a shared dictionary, slashing wire overhead. Server can proactively send resources the client will need (e.g., CSS/JS) before the client asks. Rarely used well in practice; largely superseded by HTTP/3 and preload hints. HTTP/2 eliminates HTTP-layer HOL blocking but NOT TCP-layer HOL blocking. If a single TCP packet is lost, ALL streams on that connection stall until retransmission. HTTP/3 fixes this by running over QUIC (UDP), where each stream has independ

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: DNS
text: DNS is the internet's distributed phone book: it translates human-readable hostnames (payments.example.com) into the IP addresses that routers actually forward packets to. DNS is a hierarchy — recursive resolver → root name servers → TLD server → authoritative name server — with every answer cached by a TTL (time-to-live) measured in seconds. DNS queries use UDP (fast, no handshake) and fall back to TCP for large responses. Why it matters: a cold DNS lookup adds 50–200ms before your TCP connection even starts. A misconfigured TTL (too short) hammers resolvers on every request; a stale TTL (too long) means traffic still hits the old server after a failover. Both kill Meridian's uptime SLA. Your browser knows it wants payments.example.com — but routers only understand IP addresses. DNS (Domain Name System) is the distributed phone book that translates names to addresses. Every HTTP request you've ever made starts with a DNS lookup.

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: The DNS resolution hierarchy
text: DNS is not one server — it's a hierarchy of servers, each responsible for a slice of the namespace: The first stop — usually your ISP's or a public resolver like 8.8.8.8 (Google) or 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare). It does the work of walking the hierarchy on your behalf, then caches the result. 13 clusters of root servers (a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net) that know which TLD server (.com, .io, .net) to ask. They don't know IP addresses — only referrals. The authoritative server for a top-level domain. The .com TLD server knows which name server is authoritative for example.com. The definitive source for a domain's records. Your DNS provider (Cloudflare, Route53, etc.) runs this. It returns the actual IP address. Every DNS record carries a TTL in seconds. Resolvers cache the answer for that duration. Short TTL = fast propagation of changes; long TTL = fewer queries, more cache hits. DNS is UDP by default (port 53). Responses over 512 bytes fall back to TCP. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) are modern encrypted alternatives. Unencrypted DNS exposes every domain you visit to your network path.

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: Common DNS record types
text: Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address. payments.example.com → 93.184.216.34 Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address. payments.example.com → 2606:2800:21f:cb07::1 An alias — points one hostname to another. www.example.com → example.com. The resolver then looks up the target. CNAMEs cannot coexist with other records at the zone apex. Mail exchanger — where email for a domain should go. Not directly relevant to HTTP but on every DNS exam. Arbitrary text. Used for SPF/DKIM email validation, domain ownership proofs (for TLS certificate issuance), and service discovery. Identifies the authoritative name servers for a domain. This is the answer the TLD server returns, pointing you to the authoritative server.

heading: Animating a DNS lookup
text: Watch how payments.example.com gets resolved, hop by hop: The TLD server is still only a signpost, not the destination. The resolver follows its referral to the authoritative name server, gets the real answer, and caches it before handing the IP back: Go's standard library resolves DNS with either the pure Go resolver (preferred, uses net syscalls and Go's netpoller) or the cgo resolver (delegates to libc's getaddrinfo). Control it with GODEBUG=netdns=go or GODEBUG=netdns=cgo. The pure Go resolver integrates with Go's netpoller — DNS lookups don't block OS threads.

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: TLS & HTTPS
text: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is a cryptographic protocol that runs on top of TCP and wraps all bytes in encryption. HTTPS is simply HTTP carried over TLS. Before any HTTP data flows, the two sides run the TLS handshake — an exchange that: (1) negotiates cipher suites, (2) proves the server's identity via a certificate signed by a trusted CA, and (3) derives a shared symmetric session key using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (so the secret is never transmitted). TLS 1.3 completes this in 1 round-trip . After the handshake, every byte — URL path, headers, body — is AES-GCM encrypted and integrity-checked. Why it matters: Meridian's payment endpoints carry card numbers and account balances. Without TLS, any router between the browser and your server can read or modify them. With TLS, eavesdroppers see only ciphertext. DNS gave you the IP. TCP gave you a connection. But everything so far is in the clear — anyone on the network path (your ISP, a coffee-shop router, a nation-state) can read every byte. TLS (Transport Layer Security) fixes that. It runs on top of TCP and wraps all subsequent bytes in encryption.

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: What TLS actually secures (and what it doesn't)
text: An eavesdropper on the wire sees only ciphertext. Your HTTP headers, body, and even the URL path are encrypted. Only the IP address and port are visible. A message authentication code (MAC) on every record means an attacker can't silently modify bytes in transit. Tampering is detected and the connection is terminated. The server's certificate proves it's actually payments.example.com and not an impostor. A certificate authority (CA) vouches for the binding of domain name to public key. Server Name Indication (SNI) is sent in the ClientHello in plaintext so the server knows which certificate to present. Your ISP (and anyone on the path) sees the hostname you're connecting to — just not the URL path or body. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is the evolving fix. The current standard (2018). Cuts the handshake to 1 round-trip (vs. 2 in TLS 1.2), removes weak cipher suites, mandates perfect forward secrecy. Go's crypto/tls introduced TLS 1.3 support in Go 1.12 and made it the default in Go 1.13. HTTPS authenticates the SERVER to you — not you to the server. The padlock means "this server is who it claims to be and the traffic is encrypted." It does NOT mean the server is trustworthy, safe,

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: Go's HTTPS server — zero extra effort
text: Go's net/http package handles TLS transparently. Provide a certificate and key, call ListenAndServeTLS: TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral Diffie-Hellman for all key exchanges (ECDHE — Elliptic Curve DH). Here's the magic: the client generates a temporary DH key pair per connection. The server does the same. They exchange public keys, and both sides independently compute the same shared secret using their own private key and the other side's public key — the shared secret is never transmitted . Because the private keys are ephemeral (discarded after the handshake), an attacker who records today's traffic and later steals the server's long-term private key cannot decrypt old sessions. The ephemeral keys are gone. This is perfect forward secrecy (PFS) . TLS 1.2 made PFS optional; TLS 1.3 made it mandatory, which is why TLS 1.2 RSA key exchange (where the pre-master secret is encrypted with the server's long-term key) is now considered legacy. Go's crypto/tls implements all of this in pure Go, audited, with hardware acceleration for AES-GCM where available. You do not touch any of this directly — ListenAndServeTLS does it correctly by default, including ALPN negotiation for HTTP/2. Post-quant

chTitle: Networking & How the Web Actually Works
heading: The Full Request Journey
text: A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of your application servers and forwards incoming requests to one of them on the client's behalf. Clients talk to the proxy (they may not even know your Go server exists); the proxy talks to your backends. A load balancer is a reverse proxy whose primary job is distributing traffic across a pool of backend instances — choosing one via round-robin, least-connections, or consistent hashing. It also performs health checks (removing unhealthy instances from rotation) and typically TLS termination (decrypting HTTPS so backends receive plain HTTP internally). Why it matters: without a load balancer, one Go instance handles all of Meridian's traffic — one deploy kills the service. With a load balancer, you deploy a new instance, verify it's healthy, drain the old one, and users never see a blip. Now we put it all together. You're a user hitting the checkout button on an e-commerce site. Here is every single thing that happens between that click and the JSON response your JavaScript reads. Every hop. Every protocol. Every layer. This is the centerpiece — the thing that separates engineers who understand the system from engineers who just write

desc: net/http clients done right: timeouts, transports and connection pooling, retries, context, and decoding responses safely.
text: Let me paint you a picture, sport. Your checkout service calls a payment processor. No timeout set. The processor is having a rough Tuesday. Your goroutine sits there. Waiting. Holding a connection. Then another request comes in. Same story. Then another. You've just discovered that http.DefaultClient has no timeout — and now you have a goroutine pile-up that'll bring your entire service to its knees at 2 a.m. I've seen engineers ship that exact mistake to production. Brilliant engineers, by their own estimation. They were wrong. By the end of this chapter you'll build HTTP clients that are worthy of my reputation: with timeouts at every layer, a properly tuned transport, context propagation, idiomatic response decoding, and a retry strategy that won't hammer a struggling payment API into oblivion. Let's get to work.

heading: The Default Client Is a Trap
text: Here's the scene. Your checkout service is calling an exchange-rate API to convert USD to EUR before charging a card. You reach for the obvious thing: What's wrong with it? Everything you can't see. The call to http.Get uses the package-level http.DefaultClient, which is defined as: http.Client is the struct you use to make HTTP requests. Its zero value (&http.Client ) has no timeout — if the server never responds, the call blocks forever. In a server handling concurrent requests, one hung downstream call becomes one blocked goroutine per in-flight request, draining file descriptors until the process dies. Always set Timeout on any client that calls an external API. http.DefaultClient is exactly this zero value — it is safe only for one-off scripts, never for production services. An empty &http.Client . Zero fields set. No timeout. If the exchange-rate server stops responding, your goroutine blocks forever — or rather, until the OS eventually gives up (which could be minutes). In a request handler, that's a leaked goroutine. Under traffic, it's a leaked goroutine for every concurrent checkout. The fix is exactly one change: build your own client. http.Client.Timeout is the end-to-e

heading: Timeouts at Every Layer
text: One request, four phases, each with its own clock — and the one umbrella that covers them all: The Client.Timeout is a blunt instrument. It covers the entire round trip. Sometimes you need surgical precision: what if the dial takes ages but the response streams fine? What if TLS negotiation stalls? What if headers arrive but the body never finishes? http.Transport exposes those knobs. Here's the full picture: These timeouts layer on top of each other. Here's a request through all of them: Which one to set when? Situation Reach for --- --- Simple script or tool Client.Timeout alone is usually enough Service calling external APIs Client.Timeout + ResponseHeaderTimeout at minimum High-stakes financial calls All four transport timeouts + Client.Timeout Per-request dynamic deadline context with WithTimeout or WithDeadline (see Section 4) Client.Timeout is a static ceiling on the whole client for every request it makes. A context.WithTimeout deadline is per-request and propagates cancellation to everything downstream that receives the context — database calls, sub-requests, log flushes. In a real service handler, you typically carry both: the client's static Timeout as the outer safety n

heading: Transport and Connection Pooling
text: http.Transport is the layer beneath http.Client that actually manages TCP connections. It maintains a connection pool keyed by host — when a request finishes, the connection goes back into the pool and the next request to the same host reuses it, skipping the TCP handshake and TLS negotiation entirely. The pool is the reason you must create one http.Client at startup and reuse it: a brand-new client has a brand-new, empty pool, so every request pays the full dial + TLS cost. On the job: at 100 requests per second to a payment API, a per-request client means 100 new TLS handshakes per second — 5–10x slower than a pooled client and far more load on the remote service. Here is the mistake I see constantly, and it makes me genuinely, personally sad: Every request creates a fresh http.Client with a fresh http.Transport. The transport has a connection pool — but a brand-new pool. Every request opens a brand-new TCP connection, does a fresh TLS handshake, sends the request, then discards the connection. At 100 requests per second that's 100 new TCP + TLS round trips per second to your payment API. You've implemented the slowest possible billing system. One client. Reused everywhere. The t

heading: Context-Aware Requests
text: A context deadline (set via context.WithTimeout or context.WithDeadline) is an absolute timestamp attached to a context.Context. When the deadline expires, ctx.Done() is closed and every operation carrying that context — HTTP calls, database queries, downstream sub-requests — is signalled to cancel. Unlike http.Client.Timeout (which is a static per-client ceiling), a context deadline is per-request and propagates automatically through the entire call tree. On the job: in a payment service handler, the gateway gives you a 3-second context; threading it into every downstream call ensures that when the customer times out, all the work for that request stops — no zombie goroutines charging cards after the customer already got a 504. Your checkout service receives an HTTP request with a context. That context has a deadline: if the customer waits more than 3 seconds, the gateway cancels the whole thing. Your downstream payment call should be cancelled at the same moment — not left running like a zombie goroutine after the customer already got a timeout page. The answer is http.NewRequestWithContext: http.NewRequest attaches context.Background() — a context that is never cancelled. Use it

heading: Retries
text: A retry re-sends a failed request, hoping a transient error (network hiccup, momentary overload) has cleared. Exponential backoff makes each successive retry wait longer (100ms → 200ms → 400ms…) so you don't hammer a struggling server. Jitter adds randomness to that wait so thousands of retrying clients don't all fire at the same millisecond — the "thundering herd" that turns a brief overload into a sustained outage. On the job: retrying without backoff+jitter at scale is actively harmful — it amplifies the load at exactly the moment the server is already struggling. The payment API is flaky. Your exchange-rate provider returns 500s every few minutes. You need to retry — but not blindly, and not in a way that makes a struggling server worse. Two rules before you write a single line of retry logic: 1. Only retry idempotent requests. A GET is always safe to retry. A POST /charge is not — retrying might double-charge the customer. For non-idempotent writes, use an idempotency key (Part 3 covers this in depth). For now, limit retries to GET and HEAD, or to writes that explicitly fail at the network level (connection refused, timeout) where you can be sure the server never saw the reque

text: Here's the thing, sport. You've absorbed the concepts. You know how HTTP clients work, you know Go's type system, and you've watched me explain goroutines like the world's most patient genius. Now you build something real. We're making a Pokedex CLI — a REPL-style tool that talks to a paginated REST API, caches responses in-memory with a TTL reaper, and ships a full test suite that I personally will not be embarrassed by. By the time you're done, you'll have a working program you actually earned . Not bad. It's no me , but — well, let's see, shall we? Every project chapter follows the same law: build in stages, test each stage, never ship a function without understanding what it does. Onward.

heading: REPL Scaffold
text: A REPL is an interactive shell: it R eads a line of user input, E valuates it (looks the command up and runs it), P rints the result, and L oops back. Every interactive CLI — from the Python shell to psql to this Pokedex — is a REPL. Without it you'd have to restart the process for every command. The Pokedex REPL is a single for loop around a bufio.Scanner. Before you touch a network, you need a shell. A REPL — Read, Eval, Print, Loop — is the heartbeat of any interactive CLI: read a line of input, figure out which command it maps to, run it, print the result, and loop. The Pokedex CLI lives entirely inside one of these. Here's the real-world framing: a developer-tools team is building an internal catalog browser. The catalog is a paginated API. The team wants a local CLI so engineers can page through locations, look up entries, and poke around without firing up a browser or crafting curl commands. That's your Pokedex. Same shape, different domain skin.

heading: The command registry
text: Every command gets an entry in a map[string]cliCommand. This is the idiomatic Go approach — no giant switch on strings, no reflection magic. A map of function values, keyed by name. Let me animate exactly how the REPL dispatches a command — from raw input through the parser and into the callback: ' and block on the next Scan(). Notice config is injected into every callback — not stored in a package-level variable. This isn't ceremony. It means every command handler is a pure function of its inputs, which means every command handler is testable without any global setup . The testing section will thank you for this.

heading: API Client
text: An API client is a thin wrapper around http.Client that knows one server's URL scheme and turns its raw JSON bodies into typed Go structs. "Typed JSON decode" means you define a Go struct whose fields mirror the JSON keys exactly, then call json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result) — the decoder fills the struct from the stream. If a field is missing in JSON you get its zero value; if the JSON has an extra field, Go ignores it. The payoff: callers get strongly typed data with compile-time safety instead of map[string]any soup. The catalog lives behind a real REST API. We need typed structs to hold the responses, an http.Client with a timeout, and a JSON decoder. This is the HTTP-clients chapter made concrete — if any of this feels new, flip back to HTTP Clients.

heading: The API client
text: A thin wrapper around http.Client. It owns the base URL, the HTTP client (with timeout), and the cache. Every method takes a context.Context first — the standard rule for anything that does I/O. When you decode JSON null into a string, Go sets the pointer to nil. When you decode a real string, Go allocates a new string and points to it. A plain string field has no way to distinguish null from "" — they both become the empty string. The pointer carries the distinction. This has worked this way since Go 1.0; it is not version-specific behaviour. You can also use any or a custom type implementing json.Unmarshaler, but string is the zero-ceremony idiom the standard library itself uses. The cost is one heap allocation per non-null field, which for rare pagination cursors is completely inconsequential. json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result) streams the HTTP response body through the decoder without buffering the whole body into a []byte first. For large responses this means lower peak memory. json.Unmarshal requires the full bytes in memory — fine for cached data, but prefer the streaming decoder for live network responses. (As of Go 1.26, io.ReadAll is faster than earlier releases w

heading: Pagination
text: Pagination is how an API returns a large dataset in small, sequential pages instead of one huge response. Cursor-style pagination gives you an opaque next URL in each response — you follow that URL to get the next page, instead of computing ?offset=40 yourself. The server controls what "next" means: it can encode a database cursor, a timestamp, or a sort key inside the URL. You can't skip to page 10; you can only walk forward. The trade-off is predictable latency and stability under concurrent writes (no row-skip/duplicate problem that offset pagination has). If next is null, you're on the last page. The catalog API is cursor-style: every page tells you the next page's URL. Your config tracks two cursors — nextURL and prevURL — updated every time you call map or mapb. By this section config also holds client PokeClient; make sure it's wired up in main.

heading: Cursor-style pagination vs. offset pagination
text: Offset pagination (?offset=20&limit=20) is simple but breaks under concurrent writes: if a row is inserted before your next fetch, you get a duplicate or skip an entry. Cursor-based pagination follows opaque URLs the server mints — you can't compute them yourself, which means you can't skip pages, but every page is stable. These REPL commands run in the main goroutine with no parent deadline. context.Background() is correct. In a server handler you'd propagate the request's context — the handler's ctx carries the client's timeout. In a REPL, the user set no deadline, so Background is honest. Always ask: who should cancel this? If nobody, use Background.

heading: The Cache
text: An in-memory cache stores the results of expensive operations (here: HTTP round-trips) in a map inside the process, so the same request can be answered from RAM in microseconds instead of going to the network. A TTL (time-to-live) is a maximum age for each entry — after interval has passed the entry is stale and must be re-fetched. Without a TTL the cache grows unbounded and serves forever-old data; without the cache every explore hammers the same API endpoint, burning your rate-limit budget and adding hundreds of milliseconds of latency per REPL command. The combination — fast reads, bounded staleness — is why caches exist at all. Here's where this project earns its concurrency stripes. You don't want to hammer the catalog API for the same location every time the user types explore. You want a cache: fast, in-memory, with a TTL so entries don't live forever. This is a preview of the Caching & Redis chapter (coming later in Part 1), but we're building a real one right now because the Pokedex needs it today, not in five chapters.

heading: The Cache struct
text: The reaper is a background goroutine started once by NewCache. It sleeps on a time.Ticker, wakes up every interval, acquires the mutex, scans every entry, and deletes those whose createdAt timestamp is older than interval. Without it, a TTL is just a policy on paper — entries never actually leave. The reaper is the enforcement mechanism. It runs for the process lifetime in this CLI; in a server that creates and destroys caches you'd add a stop channel so the goroutine can exit cleanly and not leak (see Exercise 4). Now watch the cache's lifecycle — from a new entry being added, through a hit, to the reaper firing and cleaning up: sync.Mutex is a two-word struct: a state int32 and a sema uint32. The state word packs several bit fields: whether the mutex is locked, whether it's in starvation mode, and the count of goroutines waiting. When Lock() is called on an unlocked mutex, it's a single atomic CAS on state — no syscall, no kernel involvement. Fast. When a goroutine calls Lock() on an already-locked mutex, it first spins briefly (calling runtime doSpin) hoping the holder releases before the spin budget runs out. If it doesn't, the goroutine is parked on a semaphore (runtime Semacq

desc: database/sql and pool tuning, the pgx driver, context-aware parameterized queries and transactions, migrations (golang-migrate/goose), the sqlc vs sqlx vs ORM choice, indexing and EXPLAIN, killing N+1, and zero-downtime expand-contract migrations.
text: You built an HTTP client. You built a Pokedex. Very cute. Now we're doing something that actually matters in production: talking to a database without destroying it, without leaking connections, without getting your accounts table emptied by a nine-year-old with a URL and a ' key. Every ledger service, every payments API, every financial system that's ever handled real money runs on a relational database somewhere in the stack. That's what we're building today — an accounts and transactions ledger — because it covers every database concern worth caring about. By the time I'm done with you, you'll read an EXPLAIN plan without flinching, you'll know why database/sql has a pool baked in, and you'll be able to ship a schema migration while traffic is live without so much as a 503. Pay attention. This chapter is a lot. But so is production.

heading: database/sql & the Pool
text: database/sql is Go's standard library package for talking to relational databases. It provides a driver-agnostic API — sql.DB, sql.Rows, sql.Tx — that works with any database driver (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite) registered at startup. Critically, sql.DB is not a single connection; it is a connection pool that manages multiple live connections under the hood. Without database/sql (or a pool-aware equivalent like pgxpool), each concurrent request in your service would either open and close its own TCP connection — paying full handshake cost every time — or you'd have to write the pooling logic yourself. A connection pool is a cache of open database connections that are borrowed for the duration of a query and then returned, rather than closed. Opening a TCP connection to Postgres takes time (DNS, TCP handshake, TLS, auth). A pool amortizes that cost: the connection is opened once, used for many queries, and kept warm between requests. sql.DB is Go's built-in pool. The three knobs that matter are SetMaxOpenConns (ceiling on simultaneous live connections), SetMaxIdleConns (how many to keep warm when idle), and SetConnMaxLifetime (retire connections before they go stale). Get any one wrong

heading: The three knobs and why each one matters
text: There are exactly three tuning calls on sql.DB. Every production service needs all three. Here is what each one does and what happens when you get it wrong. The ceiling on simultaneous live connections. Default is 0 — unlimited . Without this, a burst of 10,000 concurrent requests hammers Postgres with 10,000 connections; Postgres dies. Rule of thumb: match your Postgres max connections / number of app replicas, minus headroom. How many idle connections to keep warm in the pool after a request returns one. Default is 2. Too low: every request pays a TCP + TLS handshake to Postgres. Too high: you hold open connections Postgres counts but nobody is using. Set to roughly half of maxOpen. How old a connection can get before the pool retires it and opens a fresh one. Without this, connections that were opened during a maintenance window or a network blip silently stay broken in the pool forever. Set it shorter than Postgres's idle in transaction session timeout or any upstream load balancer idle timeout. Never call sql.Open and skip SetMaxOpenConns. The default is unlimited . A load spike will open one connection per goroutine until Postgres refuses them all — and then every request in

heading: The pgx Driver
text: A database driver is a package that implements the database/sql/driver interface — the bridge between Go's standard API and a specific database's wire protocol. When you call sql.Open("pgx", connStr), you're telling database/sql to use the pgx driver, which speaks Postgres's binary wire protocol directly. The driver handles connection handshakes, query serialization, type mapping, and protocol-level features like prepared statements. Without a driver, database/sql has no way to reach any actual database. For Postgres, pgx (github.com/jackc/pgx/v5) is the de facto choice — faster and more complete than the older lib/pq, which is now in maintenance mode. Here's the thing, sport: database/sql is the standard interface, but the driver under it decides everything about performance and features. For Postgres, there is one right answer: pgx . pgx is the de facto Postgres driver for Go. It is not a thin database/sql adapter — it is a complete Postgres wire-protocol implementation with its own, richer API. You can use it two ways: 1. Behind database/sql — register pgx as the database/sql driver. You use the standard sql.DB / sql.Rows API. Good for portability; you lose some pgx-only feature

heading: Querying Safely
text: We have a pool. We have a driver. Now let's actually talk to Postgres. Our ledger service has two tables. They'll be our spine for this entire chapter.

heading: QueryContext and ExecContext
text: Every database call in production code takes a context.Context. No exceptions. Context carries deadlines and cancellations — if the HTTP request that triggered this query is cancelled (client hung up, load balancer timed out), the context fires and the DB driver cancels the in-flight query. Without context, a slow query runs forever even when nobody is listening. The three methods you'll use constantly: db.QueryContext(ctx, sql, args...) — returns sql.Rows; use for SELECTs. db.QueryRowContext(ctx, sql, args...) — returns sql.Row; use when you expect exactly one row. db.ExecContext(ctx, sql, args...) — returns (sql.Result, error); use for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

heading: Parameterized queries — the only acceptable kind
text: A parameterized query (also called a prepared statement or placeholder query) is one where the SQL text and the user-supplied values are sent to the database as separate payloads — the SQL has a placeholder ($1, $2, …) and the driver sends the actual value in a separate Bind message. Because the value never gets concatenated into the SQL string, Postgres always treats it as data, never as SQL syntax. This makes SQL injection structurally impossible: a malicious string like '; DROP TABLE accounts; -- lands as a text value to compare against a column, not as additional SQL to execute. Parameterized queries are not optional. They are the only acceptable way to include user input in a query. Here is the most important rule in this section, and I want it burned into your neurons: always use parameterized queries . Not string formatting. Not fmt.Sprintf into SQL. Parameterized queries where the driver sends the SQL and the values as separate payloads to Postgres, and Postgres treats the values as data, never as SQL. The bad version with a malicious owner value of '; DROP TABLE accounts; -- executes as: Your accounts table is gone. The parameterized version can't do that — the value '; DR

heading: Scanning rows
text: After QueryContext, you must iterate and scan. Here is what that loop is actually doing — the driver returns a result set, and rows.Scan reads each row's columns, in order , into your struct fields: The pattern is always the same, and there are three rules to follow every single time: Miss rows.Close() and the connection is never returned to the pool — you leak connections until the pool is exhausted. Miss rows.Err() and a mid-stream error is silently dropped. Miss the scan-order match and you'll be debugging corrupted data at 2 a.m. All three. Every time.

heading: Nullable columns and sql.Null
text: Postgres NULL is a value that means "no value." In Go, there's no universal null. The database/sql package provides sql.NullString, sql.NullInt64, sql.NullBool, sql.NullTime, and friends — wrapper structs that carry both the value and a Valid bool. Go 1.26 added errors.AsType[T] as a generic shorthand for the errors.As pattern. When pgx wraps a Postgres error, you used to write: With Go 1.26 you can write: Same semantics, no separate declaration. The generic version is cleaner in inline checks. Use it when you're on Go 1.26 and working with pgconn.PgError, mysql.MySQLError, or any other typed driver error.

heading: Transactions
text: A database transaction is a unit of work that is treated as a single, indivisible operation. Either all the steps inside it succeed and commit, or none of them do (rollback). The guarantees a transaction provides are summarized by the acronym ACID : Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (the database goes from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's in-progress changes), and Durability (a committed transaction survives a crash). In Go, you open a transaction with db.BeginTx, run queries against it via tx.ExecContext, and end it with tx.Commit() or tx.Rollback(). For Meridian: a funds transfer between two accounts is the textbook example — you must debit the source and credit the destination atomically, or the ledger goes out of balance. The full ACID story, isolation levels, and SELECT FOR UPDATE are covered in Transactions, Consistency & Sagas (Part 3). A transfer between two accounts is the canonical database transaction: you must debit one account and credit another. Either both happen, or neither does. If your process crashes between the two, the ledger must be consistent when it comes back up. That atomicity guarantee is exactly

heading: The Tx API
text: The pattern to memorize: BeginTx, explicit rollback on each error path, panic-safety defer, Commit at the end. Rolling back a committed transaction is a no-op in Postgres — ROLLBACK after COMMIT returns sql.ErrTxDone, which the caller discards with =. We used LevelReadCommitted above, which is Postgres's default. There are higher levels — RepeatableRead, Serializable — that provide stronger guarantees at the cost of more contention. The full ACID and isolation story, SELECT FOR UPDATE, optimistic vs. pessimistic locking, and concurrent transfer safety belongs in Part 3, Chapter 3 (Transactions & Consistency). What you have here is the mechanical API. Keep reading — the financial-correctness story comes later, and it's worth it.

heading: Migrations
text: A migration is a versioned, numbered SQL file that describes a single schema change — adding a column, creating a table, adding an index. A migration tool (like golang-migrate or goose) applies them in order and tracks which have run in a schema migrations table. The payoff: every environment (dev, staging, prod) runs exactly the same schema changes in exactly the same order, from a fresh database up to the current version, reproducibly. Without migrations, schema changes live only in someone's head or a Slack message, and your next environment starts from scratch with no way to replay what was done. The critical rule: migrations only go forward in production — never run a down migration on a live service. Your schema will change. The question is whether those changes happen in a disciplined, versioned, repeatable way — or as a psql command someone ran at 11pm that nobody else knows about and that doesn't exist in the next environment. We are not doing the second thing. Migrations are versioned SQL files that describe schema changes. A migration tool applies them in order, tracks which have run, and ensures every environment (dev, staging, prod) has an identical schema.

heading: golang-migrate
text: golang-migrate is the most common choice. You write numbered .up.sql and .down.sql files: Run them from your Go code at startup (or via CI): golang-migrate tracks applied migrations in a schema migrations table it manages itself.

heading: goose — an alternative worth knowing
text: goose uses the same numbered-file convention but lets you embed Go migrations (pure Go functions that run as part of the migration) alongside SQL ones — useful when a data transformation is hard to express in SQL alone. SQL-only migrations, widely used, clean CLI, good Docker support. Default for most services. SQL + Go migrations. Useful when you need to run Go code mid-migration (e.g. backfill computed values). Simpler embed story. Never run m.Down() in application startup code. Down migrations are for development rollbacks only. In production you go forward — write a new up migration that undoes the change. Automating Down in prod will ruin someone's week.

heading: Data-Access Choice
text: You've got a pool, a driver, and a migration story. Now decide how you'll write queries. This is the question that causes the most religious debates in Go communities, and I'm going to settle it for you right now. Three options. Let me be honest about each.

heading: Option 1: sqlc (recommended)
text: sqlc reads your SQL queries and your schema, and generates type-safe Go functions — no reflection, no any escape hatches, no runtime surprises. You write SQL; sqlc turns it into Go code you can read. After sqlc generate, you get: Column types in the generated code are derived from your Postgres schema — BIGINT becomes int64, UUID becomes uuid.UUID, TEXT becomes string. Mistype a column name in SQL? sqlc generate fails at build time , not at runtime with a Scan error at 3 a.m.

heading: Option 2: sqlx
text: sqlx extends database/sql with struct scanning via reflection — you write raw SQL and sqlx scans rows into structs by column name: Less boilerplate than vanilla database/sql, but no compile-time safety — a typo in a column name silently scans zero values.

heading: Option 3: ORM (GORM, ent)
text: ORMs let you write Go structs and call methods that generate SQL. Quick to get started; painful at scale. Compile-time type safety. You read and own the SQL. Generated code is readable Go. Migration + schema + queries all cohere. My recommendation for new services. Less ceremony than raw database/sql. Reflection-based scanning. No generated code. Good for small services or teams already comfortable writing SQL. ORMs hide SQL until they don't — and when you need to tune a slow query or fix an N+1, you're fighting both your code and the ORM's query generation. EXPLAIN becomes much harder when you didn't write the SQL. Use an ORM if your team genuinely needs rapid prototyping and will rewrite hot paths later.

heading: Performance & EXPLAIN
text: Your schema exists. Your queries run. Now they need to run fast enough under load — and when they don't, you need to know why.

heading: Indexes
text: A database index is a sorted auxiliary data structure — typically a B-tree — that Postgres maintains alongside a table. It maps column values to the physical location (TID) of the matching rows, so a query that filters on an indexed column can jump straight to the relevant rows instead of reading every row in the table. An index trades write overhead (Postgres updates the B-tree on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) for dramatically faster reads on that column. Without an index on accounts.owner, every WHERE owner = $1 query is a sequential scan — at 10 million rows, that's 10 million row reads to find a handful of matches. With the index, it's three or four B-tree page reads plus a heap fetch for the matching rows. The rule: add an index on any column you filter or join on in a hot query path. A database index is a sorted data structure (typically a B-tree) over one or more columns, maintained by Postgres alongside the table. Without an index, a query that filters on a column does a sequential scan — it reads every row, one by one, until it finds matches. With an index on that column, Postgres jumps directly to the matching rows. For our ledger service: we'll query accounts by owner freq

heading: Reading EXPLAIN
text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you what Postgres actually did to execute a query — which indexes it used, how many rows it scanned, and where the time went. Without the index (sequential scan): With the index (index scan): The first line tells you the scan method . Seq Scan = every row touched. Index Scan = only matching rows touched. The cost numbers are Postgres's internal estimates (not ms). actual rows tells you what really came back.

heading: Killing N+1
text: The N+1 query problem happens when you fetch a list of N items in one query and then fire a separate query for each item — 1 query for the list plus N queries for the details, making N+1 round-trips total. At N=100 accounts that's 101 database round-trips; at N=10,000 it's 10,001. Each round-trip crosses the network, waits for Postgres to plan and execute, and returns data. N+1 is not a subtle bug — it is a throughput killer that becomes a production outage at scale. The fix is always the same: replace the loop + inner query with a single JOIN or IN clause that fetches everything in one round-trip. ORMs are notorious for generating N+1 silently; raw SQL and sqlc force you to see the query, making N+1 a deliberate choice rather than an accidental one. On the job: any loop in your service that calls the database inside is a red flag. In Meridian's ledger, loading 100 transfers and then fetching the sender account for each one is 101 queries. Under load it's the difference between a 20ms response and a 2-second timeout. The rule: if you find yourself querying inside a loop, stop and write a JOIN or an IN clause instead. When database/sql executes a query, it can go through three wire-

heading: Zero-Downtime Migrations
text: This is the section that turns a good engineer into a senior engineer. Listen carefully. You have a production service. It has 10 replicas running. You need to add a metadata JSONB column to accounts. If you run ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN metadata JSONB and your app code tries to INSERT without that column, you get errors. If the column is added and old code tries to INSERT with the column, same problem. The answer is the expand-contract pattern — a disciplined sequence of migrations and code changes that lets old code and new code both run safely during a rolling deploy.

heading: The four phases
text: Phase 1 — Expand (backward-compatible addition): Add the new column as nullable with a default. Old code doesn't know about it; Postgres fills it with NULL or the default. New column exists; nothing breaks. Phase 2 — Backfill: Populate the new column for existing rows. Do this in batches to avoid a long-running transaction that holds locks. Phase 3 — Switch: Deploy the new code that reads and writes metadata. By now the column exists and all rows have a value. Old replicas are still running but being replaced by the rolling deploy. Both old (ignore metadata) and new (read/write metadata) code work simultaneously. Phase 4 — Contract: Once all replicas run the new code, add the NOT NULL constraint (if desired) or drop the old column you replaced. Renaming balance cents to amount cents in a single migration will break every running replica that references the old name — which is all of them during a rolling deploy. Use expand-contract: add amount cents, migrate data, switch code, then drop balance cents in a later migration once all replicas are updated.

heading: Read Replicas & Read-After-Write Consistency
text: You've got a pool tuned, queries parameterized, migrations running zero-downtime, and schema changes rolling out without a 503 in sight. Your ledger service is humming along. Then traffic doubles. Then it doubles again. A single Postgres primary can handle more than most people think — but at some point, read load becomes the bottleneck. The answer the industry reaches for is read replicas : additional Postgres instances that stream a copy of the primary's data via streaming replication and serve SELECT queries. The idea is simple. WRITES go to the primary, which is the single source of truth. READS go to one of N replicas, which carry an identical (or nearly identical) copy of the data. You can scale reads horizontally by adding replicas without touching the primary. Most ledger reads — account balance lookups, transaction history, reporting queries — are reads. Routing them to replicas takes load off the primary and makes the whole system faster. Route read queries through ReadPool(), write queries through WritePool(). That's the happy path.

heading: Replication lag and the read-after-write anomaly
text: Here is where it gets interesting, and where a lot of services have a subtle, maddening bug. Postgres streaming replication is asynchronous by default . The primary commits a write and immediately acknowledges it to your Go code. Postgres then streams that WAL (Write-Ahead Log) record to replicas, which apply it. This usually takes milliseconds — but it is not zero. That gap is replication lag . Now consider this sequence: 1. Alice submits a funds transfer. Your service writes it to the primary. Commit() returns nil. 2. Alice's browser immediately refreshes the transaction list. 3. Her GET request routes to a replica — which hasn't caught up yet. 4. Alice sees her transaction missing. She hits refresh again, angrily. 5. Two seconds later the replica applies the WAL entry. It appears. This is the read-after-write anomaly : a user who just wrote data doesn't see their own change because their subsequent read landed on a lagging replica. From Alice's perspective, the write was lost. The data is fine — the replica just hasn't caught up yet — but the user experience is broken, and in a financial context it breeds distrust.

heading: Mitigations
text: There are two practical mitigations. Neither is perfect; pick the one that fits your consistency requirements. Option A — Post-write primary routing (recommended for ledger services) Track the user's last-write timestamp in a short-lived store (an in-process sync.Map keyed by user ID, or a Redis key). For a configurable window after a write (typically 1–5 seconds), route that user's reads to the primary instead of a replica. After the window closes, reads return to the replica. The primary handles only the brief window of post-write traffic from that user, so the replica still absorbs the bulk of read load. Option B — Session/sticky routing Some connection proxies (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) or service meshes support session affinity: once a user sends a write, all their connections are pinned to the primary for the session. Simpler to implement if your infrastructure supports it; harder to tune the stickiness window. Postgres supports synchronous commit = on (or remote apply), which blocks the primary's COMMIT until at least one replica has applied the WAL record. This eliminates replication lag — and therefore eliminates the read-after-write anomaly — but it increases write latency by

heading: Document Databases
text: You now know relational Go cold. Time for the discipline most courses skip entirely: knowing when not to reach for SQL. The ride-share and catalog crowd default to MongoDB , and sometimes they're right — so you're going to learn exactly when a document database wins, when it's cargo-culting, and why Meridian's ledger will never live in one. A document database — MongoDB is the headliner — stores data as self-contained documents: JSON-like records with nested fields and arrays, grouped into collections instead of tables. There's no fixed schema; two documents in the same collection can carry different fields. Related data is usually embedded inside one document rather than split across tables and reassembled with a JOIN. Why it matters: when your data is naturally a self-contained tree — a product with its variants, a CMS page, an event payload — one document read beats a five-table join. BSON (Binary JSON) is MongoDB's on-disk and on-the-wire encoding: JSON's data model plus richer types (ObjectId, dates, binary, int64). In Go you tag struct fields with bson:"..." exactly the way you tag them json:"...", and the official driver marshals between your structs and BSON for you.

heading: The same data, two philosophies
text: An order with line items is the cleanest way to feel the difference. Relational normalizes it across two tables and rebuilds it with a JOIN. A document database embeds the items and hands you the whole thing in one read: Same information. The document is one fetch with zero joins — but the items are now trapped inside the order. The relational version is two tables you can query independently ("every order containing SKU-A") and update in one place. Data has real relationships, you need cross-row invariants and ACID transactions, queries slice the data many ways, and correctness matters more than raw write throughput. Foreign keys, JOINs, and strong consistency are the defaults. Each record is a self-contained tree read and written as a unit, the schema varies or evolves fast, and you want easy horizontal scale-out. Catalogs, CMS content, user profiles, event/audit payloads, per-tenant blobs. Embedding duplicates data. A value copied into a million documents takes a million writes to change; the same value in a relational column is one UPDATE. Model for your write pattern, not just the pretty one-read. "It's one fetch" is a trap if that data changes constantly.

heading: Talking to MongoDB from Go
text: The shape mirrors database/sql: get a handle to a collection, then insert and query with bson-tagged structs. This needs a running MongoDB and the official driver, so it doesn't run in the sandbox: bson.M is just map[string]any — an ad-hoc query document. Note the structs are the same idea as your SQL row structs, only the tag changed from db/json to bson. This is not "Mongo can't do transactions." It has supported multi-document ACID transactions since 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters). It's about fit . Mongo's design center is the single document as the atomic unit ; multi-document transactions are the exception, with extra cost and operational caveats. A double-entry ledger violates that on every single write — a transfer debits one account and credits another, and the books must balance globally with strict consistency and a permanent audit trail. That invariant is the relational model's home turf: foreign keys, SERIALIZABLE/repeatable-read isolation, and decades of tooling. Choose the database whose defaults match your invariant. For money that's SQL; for a product catalog it might well be Mongo. On the job: the most expensive database mistake isn't picking "the sl

desc: Routing, middleware and handlers; advanced JSON (custom marshalers, RawMessage, omitempty, safe decoding); streaming with json.Encoder and NDJSON; and real-time with server-sent events and WebSockets.
text: Listen up, sport. You've got the database humming, the queries are parameterized, and the schema is clean. Now you need to expose all of that to the world — and the world is unforgiving, malicious, and will send you garbage JSON at 3 a.m. In this chapter I'm going to show you exactly how Go's HTTP server works, from the moment a TCP connection lands all the way to the moment you flush the last byte of a WebSocket frame. Routing, middleware, advanced JSON, streaming so your memory stays flat even as your dataset grows, server-sent events, and full-duplex WebSockets. Our running scenario is Meridian's payments API : the POST /transfers endpoint, a streaming account-statement export, and a live transfer-event feed for the operations dashboard. By the end you'll know every layer of the stack, and you'll know how the dangerous one operates. You're welcome. --

heading: Handlers, Routing & Middleware
text: The scenario: Meridian's payments service needs a REST API — account lookups, POST /transfers, and a live statement stream. Let's stand it up correctly — no guessing, no cowboy wiring — starting from the one interface that governs everything in net/http. On the job: Every production Go HTTP service you'll encounter is built on exactly this interface. Get the wiring wrong and you end up with a global mux, no method matching, and zero middleware — and you discover that at code review, not at 3 a.m.

heading: The http.Handler interface
text: A handler is any value that knows how to respond to an HTTP request. In Go, the http.Handler interface has one method — ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, Request) — and everything in net/http speaks it: a function, a struct, a middleware chain, the mux itself. You need it because every incoming request needs something that takes the request, does the work, and writes the response — and the single interface lets all these shapes be composed and wrapped uniformly. Every HTTP handler in Go satisfies a single interface: That's it. One method. ResponseWriter is where you write the response; Request carries the incoming request. Anything that has ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, Request) is a valid HTTP handler — a struct, a closure, a middleware chain — all the same interface. http.HandlerFunc is a function type that satisfies Handler: So you can write a plain function and adapt it with http.HandlerFunc(myFunc). In practice, http.HandleFunc does this for you on the default mux. We'll use our own mux below, which is the correct production approach.

heading: ServeMux and Go 1.22+ routing
text: A ServeMux is a request multiplexer — a table that maps URL patterns to handlers. When a request arrives, the mux finds the longest matching pattern and calls that handler's ServeHTTP. You need one because a real API has tens of routes, and wiring them by hand into a single ServeHTTP is a maintenance disaster. Go 1.22's ServeMux also matches on HTTP method (GET /api/accounts/ ) and extracts named wildcards via r.PathValue. http.ServeMux is Go's built-in router. Before Go 1.22, it was minimal: exact paths and trailing-slash prefix matches. Go 1.22 gave it a major upgrade — method + path patterns, named wildcards, and precedence rules . Go 1.26 changes one existing behavior: ServeMux's automatic subtree-root redirects now use 307 Temporary Redirect instead of 301. The redirect applies when you register a subtree pattern with a trailing slash (or ... wildcard) and a client requests the subtree root without the slash. For example, registering /assets/ redirects /assets to /assets/ unless /assets is registered separately. Before Go 1.22, ServeMux had no method matching and no named wildcards — you needed a third-party router like chi or gorilla/mux. Go 1.22 closed the gap for most use-c

heading: Middleware — func(http.Handler) http.Handler
text: Middleware is a function that wraps a handler, runs code before and/or after it, and returns a new handler. The canonical Go signature is func(http.Handler) http.Handler. You need it because cross-cutting concerns — authentication, logging, rate limiting, request IDs — belong outside your business logic, applied uniformly at the routing layer. Middleware composes like Russian dolls: stack them with a chain helper, and they execute in order on every matching request. Middleware is a function that wraps a handler, runs code before and/or after it, and returns the wrapped handler. The canonical signature is func(http.Handler) http.Handler.

heading: Graceful shutdown
text: A production HTTP server must drain in-flight requests before dying. Server.Shutdown does it: The 15-second timeout means: give in-flight requests up to 15 seconds to finish, then hard-close anything that's still open. Wire it to os.Interrupt (Ctrl-C) and Kubernetes SIGTERM so rolling deploys drain cleanly. When a new TCP connection is accepted, net/http spawns one goroutine to own it for its lifetime — the conn.serve goroutine. That goroutine reads requests off the connection in a loop, calls your handler's ServeHTTP synchronously, and writes the response. For HTTP/1.1, the goroutine handles one request at a time (pipelining is the exception). For HTTP/2, net/http runs a multiplexing layer so multiple streams share one connection; each stream gets its own goroutine calling your handler. ResponseWriter is backed by a bufio.Writer — writes are buffered until the handler returns or you call Flush(). The first call to Write or WriteHeader freezes the response status; calling WriteHeader after Write is a no-op (and logs a warning). This is why you must set headers before writing the body. The Shutdown method calls Close on the underlying net.Listener (stops accepting new connections),

heading: Advanced JSON
text: Meridian's API speaks JSON. But the naive json.Marshal / json.Unmarshal approach will get you into trouble the moment a field is optional, a payload is polymorphic, or a client sends hostile input. Let's go deeper. On the job: The POST /transfers handler is hit by both internal services and third-party integrations. Every one of them is a potential attacker or a misconfigured client. Safe JSON decoding is not optional — it is the first gate.

heading: Custom MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON
text: Implement json.Marshaler and json.Unmarshaler on your types for full control:

heading: json.RawMessage for deferred and polymorphic decoding
text: Sometimes you don't know the shape of a field until you've read another field. json.RawMessage lets you defer decoding — capture the raw JSON bytes first, then decode into the right type once you know what it is.

heading: omitempty gotchas and struct embedding
text: omitempty skips a field when it holds the zero value — but the zero value depends on the type: omitempty omits 0, false, and "". This is usually what you want. Use a pointer field ( string, int64) when you need to distinguish zero from absent. omitempty does NOT omit a non-pointer struct even if all its fields are zero. Use MyStruct if you need true omission. A time.Time zero value (0001-01-01) is NOT omitted by omitempty because time.Time is a struct, not a primitive. Use time.Time or implement MarshalJSON to emit null for the zero value. Struct embedding flattens fields into the parent's JSON, but can produce surprises with custom marshalers:

heading: Decoding untrusted input safely
text: A client sending you JSON is a client you cannot trust. Three rules for every handler that decodes a request body: Rule 1: limit the body size. Without a size limit, a client sends a 1 GB body and your server allocates 1 GB of memory. Use http.MaxBytesReader on the request body before decoding. Rule 2: reject unknown fields. By default, json.Decoder silently ignores JSON keys it doesn't recognize. A typo in a field name sends the data into a black hole. Use d.DisallowUnknownFields() to return an error instead. Rule 3: decode once, into a strict shape. Never decode into map[string]interface . Decode into a typed struct with exactly the fields you expect. Go 1.25 added net/http.CrossOriginProtection — a middleware that blocks cross-origin requests that aren't legitimately CORS-preflight'd. It rejects POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests that carry a Content-Type and originate from a different origin without a matching preflight, catching a class of CSRF attacks that SameSite=Lax cookies alone don't prevent. Wrap your state-mutating routes with it: This is separate from CORS headers (which you still set for legitimate cross-origin callers). Auth & API Design (Part 1, Chapter 17) cove

heading: Streaming & NDJSON
text: A streaming response writes data to the client incrementally as it is produced, rather than buffering the full payload in memory first. NDJSON (Newline-Delimited JSON) is the wire format: one complete JSON object per line, separated by \n, with no enclosing array. You need it whenever the result set is unbounded or large — Meridian's statement export, a reconciliation dump, a live event feed — because allocating 400 MB per request to build a single JSON array is a month-end outage waiting to happen. Here's the scenario: Meridian's account-statement endpoint needs to stream up to 100,000 transfers for a monthly report. Naively, you fetch all rows from the database, marshal them into a JSON array, and write the whole thing at once. Your server allocates hundreds of megabytes per request, and the client waits for the entire response before it can show a single row. That's a crime against memory and a crime against UX. The fix is streaming : write rows to the client as they come out of the database. json.Encoder lets you marshal one object at a time. NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON) is the format — one JSON object per line, no enclosing array. On the job: Statement export endpoints are

heading: Streaming with json.Encoder and NDJSON
text: The moment you call w.Write(...) or w.WriteHeader(...), the HTTP headers are frozen and sent. If an error occurs mid-stream, you cannot change the 200 status to 500 — the client has already seen the 200. Log the error and close the connection. This is why you must handle any setup errors (like the DB query failing) before starting to write rows. http.ResponseWriter in net/http is backed by a bufio.Writer (typically 4 KB). Writes go into the buffer and are flushed to the network automatically when the buffer fills or the handler returns. For streaming you need to flush manually: w.(http.Flusher).Flush() calls through to bufio.Writer.Flush() which calls the underlying TCP Write syscall. Go 1.8+ guarantees that the concrete ResponseWriter implements http.Flusher for HTTP/1.1. For HTTP/2 it also flushes the frame to the network. The type assertion flusher, ok := w.(http.Flusher) is the safe way — some testing ResponseWriter implementations (like httptest.Recorder) implement Flusher but don't actually push bytes anywhere, which is fine for tests. Prefer http.ResponseController (Go 1.20+): Rather than type-asserting to http.Flusher directly, wrap the ResponseWriter in an http.ResponseCon

heading: Server-Sent Events
text: Server-sent events are a browser-native protocol for one-way, server-to-client streaming over a plain HTTP connection. The server sets Content-Type: text/event-stream and keeps the connection open, writing text frames (id:, event:, data:, blank line) as events happen. The client's EventSource API reconnects automatically using the last id: it saw. You need SSE when the server pushes data the client only reads — live dashboards, notifications, audit feeds — and you want the simplicity of HTTP (works through proxies and CDNs) without the complexity of WebSockets. Server-sent events (SSE) give you a one-way live stream from server to client. Think: Meridian's operations dashboard showing live transfer events without the client polling every second — new POST /transfers completions appear the moment they're processed. The client opens one HTTP connection and keeps reading; the server pushes updates as they happen. SSE uses plain HTTP with Content-Type: text/event-stream. Each event is a few lines of text terminated by a blank line. The browser (or any SSE client) reconnects automatically if the connection drops, using the last id: it received. On the job: SSE is the right tool for Meri

heading: WebSockets
text: A WebSocket is a full-duplex, persistent connection between client and server. After an HTTP upgrade handshake, both ends can send frames at any time over a single TCP connection — no request/response cycle, no polling. You need it when the client and server both send in real time: Meridian's trading desk dealers send filter updates back to the server while the server pushes rate ticks to them. SSE only goes one way; WebSockets go both. Full-duplex. Bidirectional. One persistent connection, both ends sending whenever they want. For Meridian's trading desk — where dealers send filter updates (which currency pairs to watch) and the server pushes matching rate ticks in real time — this is your tool. WebSockets start as an HTTP request and upgrade to the WebSocket protocol. After the upgrade, the connection bypasses the normal HTTP request/response cycle entirely. On the job: WebSocket connections linger for hours. A server that doesn't enforce write deadlines will accumulate goroutines blocked on a single slow client. In a payments system, that slow client can be a mobile app on a flaky cellular connection — and it will block your goroutine until the TCP stack times out, which can tak

heading: The HTTP Upgrade handshake
text: The HTTP upgrade handshake is how a plain HTTP connection becomes a WebSocket. The client sends GET /ws with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, and a Sec-WebSocket-Key header. The server validates the key and responds 101 Switching Protocols — after which HTTP is over. The TCP connection is hijacked from net/http and handed directly to the WebSocket layer; frames (not HTTP packets) now flow in both directions. You need to understand this because after the 101, net/http's WriteTimeout no longer applies — the connection is outside its control, and you must enforce deadlines yourself. After the 101, HTTP is over. The TCP connection is hijacked from net/http and handed to the WebSocket layer. Frames (not HTTP packets) flow in both directions.

heading: Using coder/websocket
text: The coder/websocket package (module path github.com/coder/websocket) is context-aware, doesn't require goroutines for lifecycle management, and handles the upgrade cleanly. We'll use it here. It was formerly published as nhooyr.io/websocket — the same library, renamed when it moved under the Coder org, so older code and tutorials you find will still import the nhooyr.io path. (gorilla/websocket is the older alternative — battle-tested but not context-aware.) The handlers above work perfectly under httptest for unit tests (shown in the exercises below). The playground sandbox terminates long-lived connections — label SSE and WebSocket code clearly in your tests and run them locally or in a containerized environment.

heading: Read/write goroutine model and ping/pong
text: WebSocket connections need keepalives: ping frames from the server, pong frames from the client. coder/websocket handles ping/pong automatically when you use its built-in CloseRead mechanism or set a read deadline. Always set a write deadline before writing to prevent a slow client from blocking your goroutine forever:

heading: When to choose SSE vs WebSockets vs polling
text: Simple. Client asks every N seconds. Works everywhere. Best for low-frequency, low-latency-requirement data (daily reports). Wastes bandwidth at high frequency. Server pushes one-way over HTTP. Works through proxies and CDNs. Best for live dashboards, notifications, audit feeds where the client only watches. Auto-reconnect built in. Full duplex. Client and server both send freely. Best for interactive real-time features: trading, collaborative editing, chat, multi-player. Proxy-hostile (needs upgrade support). WebSockets are overkill for dashboards that only receive data. SSE is simpler, proxy-friendly, and reconnects automatically. Reach for WebSockets only when the client genuinely needs to send messages back to the server in real time. When websocket.Accept (or gorilla/websocket's Upgrader.Upgrade) is called, it uses http.Hijacker — an interface that net/http's concrete ResponseWriter implements. Hijack() returns the raw net.Conn and a bufio.ReadWriter, removing the connection from net/http's management entirely. From that moment on, net/http forgets about that connection: no more buffering, no more request/response framing, no timeout from WriteTimeout. The WebSocket library ow

heading: Server Hardening
text: You've built the handler. You've wired the middleware. Now you're going to skip the part that every junior engineer skips — and that every security postmortem traces back. The default http.Server has no timeouts . None. A client that sends one byte per minute will hold a goroutine and a TCP connection open indefinitely. A thousand of them will stop your server from accepting legitimate traffic. This attack has a name: Slowloris. And it works on unprotected Go servers out of the box. On the job: You won't spot this in local dev or in a load test with well-behaved clients. It shows up in a production incident when someone opens 10,000 slow connections and your server stops accepting real traffic. Operations pages you. The postmortem says "no timeouts configured." Senior engineers set these reflexively.

heading: The timeout knobs
text: http.Server exposes five timeout fields. None of them have a default: Field What it covers Recommended starting value --- --- --- ReadHeaderTimeout Time to receive the complete request headers 5 s — set this first, always ReadTimeout Time to receive headers + full request body 10–30 s depending on expected payloads WriteTimeout Time to write the full response 30–60 s; for streaming/SSE, set to 0 and control per-write with context.WithTimeout IdleTimeout How long a keep-alive connection may sit idle between requests 60–120 s (body cap) http.MaxBytesReader on the request body 1 MiB for API handlers; 0 for streaming ReadHeaderTimeout is the cheap, must-set Slowloris mitigation: Go reads headers in a tight loop from the TCP buffer, so this timeout fires before any user-land handler code runs. It costs almost nothing but closes the attack surface. ReadTimeout covers the entire read phase including the body. For handlers that stream large uploads, set ReadTimeout to 0 and use http.MaxBytesReader to cap individual request bodies instead. WriteTimeout covers the write phase. Set it to 0 for SSE and WebSocket handlers — those connections intentionally live beyond a normal write window, and

heading: Capping request bodies with http.MaxBytesReader
text: Even with ReadTimeout set, an attacker can send a 2 GB request body inside the timeout window if your upstream connection is fast. http.MaxBytesReader wraps the body's Read method and returns an error the moment the byte count exceeds your limit: For multipart uploads (file ingestion, NACHA batch files), do not load the entire multipart into memory. Use r.ParseMultipartForm(maxMemory) — it spills to a temp file on disk when the in-memory threshold is exceeded — and validate each part's size before reading: A client that omits Content-Length and streams slowly can still OOM a server that reads multipart naively. Cap every part before reading.

heading: Secure response headers as middleware
text: Timeouts and body caps protect the server . The next layer protects the client — specifically, the browser that renders responses from Meridian's API and its admin console. A handful of response headers tell the browser to refuse a list of attacks it would otherwise happily perform on your users' behalf. They cost nothing to set and they belong in one middleware applied to every route — not sprinkled per-handler where someone will forget half of them. Secure response headers are HTTP response headers that instruct the browser to enforce a security policy on the content you return — which scripts may run (Content-Security-Policy), whether to second-guess your declared content type (X-Content-Type-Options), how much referrer information to leak (Referrer-Policy), and who may embed your pages in a frame (X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors). You need them because the browser's defaults are permissive for backwards compatibility, and a single missing header is the difference between an XSS payload that fizzles and one that drains an account. The four that matter most for a JSON/admin surface like Meridian's: Forbids MIME sniffing — the browser guessing a response's type by peeking at

heading: Hardened server: before and after
text: If you set WriteTimeout to 30 s on a server that also handles SSE or WebSocket connections, those handlers will be forcibly closed after 30 seconds — regardless of whether they're still actively pushing data. The fix: use a single http.Server for short-lived API routes with a WriteTimeout, and a separate http.Server on a different port (or route prefix) for streaming/WebSocket routes with WriteTimeout: 0. The streaming handlers control their own write deadlines per-message via context.WithTimeout. Timeouts in http.Server are implemented via net.Conn.SetDeadline on the underlying TCP connection. When ReadHeaderTimeout is set, the conn.serve goroutine calls SetReadDeadline before entering the header-read loop, then resets it to zero (or applies ReadTimeout) after headers are read. When WriteTimeout is set, it calls SetWriteDeadline before calling ServeHTTP. Because these are set on the net.Conn directly, they fire at the OS level — blocked Read and Write calls return net.Error with Timeout() == true. This is why a WriteTimeout fires even if your handler is in a json.Encode call — the underlying Write syscall times out. For WebSocket connections, Hijack() hands you the raw net.Conn, a

heading: The Lab
text: Right. Exercises were your warmup, sport. This is my test. I designed it myself, and I'm personally invested in your failure rate. Don't disappoint me. The buffered version is a memory time bomb. The safe-decode version is the door you close before the attacker walks through. Make both changes. When all four checks print PASS and the final line reads ALL CHECKS PASS, the flag is yours. No partial credit. -- You now own the full HTTP server stack — and the hardening layer that seniors set without being asked: http.Handler / HandlerFunc — the one interface; every handler, middleware, and mux satisfies it. Go 1.22's ServeMux adds method + path patterns and r.PathValue wildcards. Go 1.26 changes automatic subtree-root slash redirects from 301 to 307. Middleware as func(http.Handler) http.Handler — wraps handlers, runs code before/after, short-circuits with return. Chain with a helper; order matters (outermost runs first in, last out). Graceful shutdown via Server.Shutdown(ctx) — drains in-flight requests, stops accepting new ones; wire to os.Interrupt and SIGTERM.
