desc: go vet, golangci-lint, go generate, build tags, Go workspaces (go work), race/coverage in CI, module versioning, private modules and the proxy (GOPRIVATE, GOAUTH, vendoring), reproducible builds, and supply-chain security (govulncheck, SBOM scanning).
text: Let me paint you a picture, sport. You've written flawless logic. The algorithm is tight. The data model is beautiful. And then a known-vulnerable dependency ships to production, a lint error that the CI pipeline didn't check causes a silent bug at midnight, and your builds aren't reproducible because someone forgot to pin the toolchain. That is not a technical failure. That is a discipline failure. And I won't have it. This chapter is the forge where sloppy repos get hardened. By the time we're done, your pipeline will lint, vet, race-check, vulnerability-scan, and produce bit-for-bit reproducible binaries — and a known-vulnerable module will fail the build before it ever sees a production server. I set that bar personally. Let's see if you can clear it.

heading: Static Analysis
text: Your compiler catches type errors. But there's a whole category of bugs — shadowed errors, misused sync primitives, reachable SQL injection vectors — that compile fine and blow up at 3 a.m. That's what static analysis is for. The scenario: the ledger service's repo just onboarded three new engineers. Each one has their own linting opinions and no shared config. Bugs are shipping. We're going to fix that.

heading: go vet
text: go vet is a static analyser that ships with the Go toolchain. It examines your source for a curated set of high-confidence bugs that the compiler lets through — mismatched fmt verbs, copied mutexes, unreachable code. Zero config, no install, runs in milliseconds. If go vet ./... is not in your CI pipeline, you're flying blind. go vet is the tool you get for free — zero configuration, ships with the Go toolchain, catches a curated set of high-confidence bugs that the compiler deliberately doesn't stop: What it catches: fmt.Sprintf("%d", "not an int") — wrong format verb for the argument type. A return before the end of a function, code after it that can never run. sync.Mutex and sync.WaitGroup must never be copied after first use. Passing by value is a bug. Goroutines capturing a loop variable by address instead of value (still flagged for older patterns). Malformed json:"name" tags that silently cause serialization failures. Running go vet on its own is not enough. It catches only the highest-confidence bugs. For anything resembling a real CI pipeline, you want golangci-lint running vet as one linter among many. Here's a snippet go vet will refuse to pass — a printf mismatch and a

heading: golangci-lint — the meta-linter
text: golangci-lint is a meta-linter — a single binary that runs dozens of Go linters in parallel and merges their output into one report. It includes go vet internally, so you replace both with one CI step. The critical detail: pin its version in CI. A floating linter version means a linter upgrade can break your build on someone else's schedule. golangci-lint is the industry standard: a single binary that runs dozens of linters in parallel and collapses them into one clean report. It runs go vet internally, so you only need one tool in CI. Install (use the official binary; don't go install it — version pinning matters): The linters you actually want wired in for the ledger service: Flags every place you silently discarded an error with . If you wrote rows.Close() without checking the error, this finds it. The deepest static analyser in the Go ecosystem — catches deprecated API uses, impossible conditions, redundant code, and much more. Think of it as go vet at graduate level. Catches assignments to variables whose value is never read afterwards — often a sign of a logic error or a forgotten return. Security-focused: flags things like integer overflows in crypto, use of math/rand instea

heading: Code Generation
text: Go has no macros and no template metaprogramming. What it has is go generate — a convention for running arbitrary tools on your source that produce Go source files before the compiler sees them. The scenario: the ledger service has a TransferStatus type with five states. Every time a developer adds a new state, they forget to update the String() method, and log lines start printing TransferStatus(4) instead of "settled". We fix that with generation.

heading: go generate directives
text: go generate is a code-generation convention built into the Go toolchain. You annotate a source file with a //go:generate comment; running go generate ./... executes those commands and produces new .go files before the compiler ever runs. The generated files carry a // Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT. header. Why it matters: generated code is correct by construction — no hand-written String() methods that silently fall behind a growing iota enum at 2 a.m. A //go:generate comment is a directive — not a compiler directive, just a convention. When you run go generate ./..., the tool reads every //go:generate line in every .go file in scope and executes the command verbatim: The directive lives right next to the type it describes. When someone adds a new constant, they run go generate ./... and the String() method is regenerated. The generated file gets a // Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT. header so tools (and humans) know not to touch it.

heading: stringer
text: stringer is the canonical first go:generate tool. Install it: Define the type and its constants: After go generate ./..., stringer emits transferstatus string.go — a String() string method that satisfies fmt.Stringer. Now fmt.Println(StatusSettled) prints "settled", forever, no matter how many states you add — as long as you remember to re-run the generator.

heading: Mocks and sqlc
text: Two more generators you'll wire into a real service: mockery or moq : generate interface mocks from your own service interfaces. Keep mocks out of the repo by regenerating them in CI rather than committing them. sqlc : compile SQL queries into type-safe Go. You write -- name: GetTransfer :one in a .sql file; sqlc generate produces a GetTransfer(ctx, id) method with the exact return type the query produces. No string soup, no runtime reflection. (Covered in depth in the SQL & Databases chapter.) Reflection is dynamic — it pays a runtime cost every call and loses static type safety. Generation is static — the code is checked at compile time and has zero runtime overhead. Use generation when: (1) you have a finite, enumerable set of variants (statuses, command types, error codes), (2) the generated code would be tedious but mechanical to write by hand, or (3) you're generating from a schema (SQL, proto, OpenAPI) that is the source of truth. Use reflection when the set is open and unknown at compile time.

heading: Build Tags
text: Go has a clean, explicit mechanism for conditional compilation: build constraints (also called build tags). They tell the Go toolchain to include or exclude a file based on the target platform, Go version, or a custom label you define. The scenario: the ledger service has slow integration tests that spin up a real Postgres container. You don't want them running on every go test ./... — only in CI or when a developer explicitly opts in. A build tag is a //go:build comment on the first line of a .go file that tells the compiler whether to include or exclude that file from a given build. The expression uses &&, , and ! over tag names, OS identifiers (linux, darwin), architecture names (amd64), and Go version identifiers. Files excluded by a constraint are never compiled — zero runtime overhead. Why it matters: the right tool for gating slow integration tests, platform-specific code, and debug-only instrumentation. The old // +build form was removed in Go 1.25; write only //go:build.

heading: The //go:build syntax
text: As of Go 1.17 (and required as of Go 1.17 alongside the old // +build form, which was removed in 1.25), the constraint is a comment on the very first line of the file, before the package declaration, with a blank line separating them: Build that file only when you pass -tags integration: Without the tag, the file is invisible to the compiler. With it, it's included. Dead simple, and no runtime overhead — excluded files are never compiled at all.

heading: Platform-specific files
text: The Go toolchain also reads constraints from filenames. A file named db linux.go is included only on Linux; db darwin.go only on macOS; db windows.go only on Windows. The naming convention is name GOOS.go or name GOOS GOARCH.go. You can combine file naming with explicit //go:build constraints for fine-grained control: This file is compiled only on Linux/amd64. Anything not matching is silently skipped.

heading: Integration test tags in CI
text: Here's the pattern for the ledger service. Regular tests run on every PR, integration tests run in a dedicated CI job: Before Go 1.17, constraints used // +build linux,amd64 with comma for AND and space for OR — a truly forgettable syntax. Go 1.17 introduced //go:build with proper boolean expressions (&&, , !). Go 1.17 through 1.24 accepts both; the gofmt tool rewrites old-style tags to the new form. Write only //go:build in new code.

heading: Go Workspaces
text: Here's a scenario that bites every team eventually: you're developing the ledger service and its logging library — ledger-slog-handler — in tandem. You're making breaking changes to the library's interface. You need to test them together before tagging a release. The old answer was replace directives in go.mod: That works, but you have to remember to remove the replace before you commit. Miss it once and you've shipped a module that points at a local path — it breaks every build that doesn't have that path. Not acceptable. Go workspaces (go work), introduced in Go 1.18, are the right answer. A Go workspace is a go.work file that tells the toolchain: "resolve these module import paths from local directories instead of the module registry." Created with go work init ./module-a ./module-b. Why it matters: it lets you develop two interdependent modules in tandem — changing a library and testing it in a consuming service — without replace directives in go.mod . Add go.work to .gitignore; it's a local developer override, not something that should affect CI or other developers' machines. Introduced in Go 1.18.

heading: How go.work works
text: A go.work file sits at the root of a directory that contains multiple modules. It tells the Go toolchain: "when resolving these module paths, prefer the local directory over the registry." Create it: Now, inside ./ledger-service, any import of github.com/myorg/ledger-slog-handler resolves to ./ledger-slog-handler — no replace directive, no manual cleanup. The individual go.mod files are untouched. go.work.sum is the checksum database for workspace-mode downloads. Commit it. go.work itself is a local developer override — add it to .gitignore so CI always resolves modules from the registry and nobody gets a surprise replace-equivalent on their machine. Go's module resolution normally runs MVS (Minimal Version Selection) — a pure function over your go.sum and the dependency graph that always picks the minimum version satisfying all constraints. (More on MVS in the next section.) Workspace mode inserts a step before MVS: the toolchain builds a workspace module map from the use directives. When the dependency graph walker asks "where is github.com/myorg/ledger-slog-handler@v0.3.1?", the workspace map short-circuits: "I have that module locally at ./ledger-slog-handler; use that." The ve

heading: Module Versioning
text: Modules are how Go manages dependencies. Understanding the machinery — not just the commands — is what separates engineers who ship reproducible builds from engineers who ship surprises.

heading: go.mod and go.sum
text: Every module starts with go.mod: module : the import path for this module. Everything in this repo is imported under this prefix. go : the minimum Go version the module requires. toolchain : (Go 1.21+) the specific toolchain to use, enabling reproducible builds. More in the CI section. require : the minimum version of each dependency. go.sum records the cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of every module zip the build has ever downloaded. The Go toolchain verifies these hashes against the checksum database (sum.golang.org) before using a module. A tampered module that matches the declared version but not the hash fails the build — immediately and loudly. Never edit go.sum by hand. Run go mod tidy and let the toolchain manage it.

heading: MVS — Minimal Version Selection
text: MVS is Go's dependency algorithm. The rule is deliberately simple: given a set of require statements across all modules in the build, always pick the minimum version that satisfies all constraints. This is radically different from npm's ^ ranges or Python's pip. In Go, require foo v1.2.0 means "at minimum v1.2.0" — but nothing picks a higher version without an explicit go get command or another dependency pulling it up. The result is reproducible by construction .

heading: Semantic import versioning (v2+)
text: Go modules encode major version bumps in the import path itself. If a module makes a breaking change, it bumps to v2 — and the import path changes to reflect it: This is not optional. A module at v2 and a module at v1 can coexist in the same build — they're different import paths, and thus different packages. This is the semantic import versioning rule: if you break the API, change the path. The go.mod for a v2 module: go mod tidy does two things: (1) adds any require entries that your code imports but go.mod doesn't list, and (2) removes any require entries for packages your code no longer imports. Run it before every commit. Add a CI step that runs go mod tidy and asserts no diff — a tidy check catches the "someone added a dependency without updating go.mod" failure mode.

heading: Private Modules & the Proxy
text: Everything above assumed one thing without saying it: that proxy.golang.org can see your code. The day Meridian extracts its shared money types into github.com/meridian/ledger-types — a private repo — that assumption detonates on the very first fetch: On the job: this is a day-one failure at every company with private repos, and the error actively misleads — it reads like the module doesn't exist , not like you lack credentials, because neither GitHub nor the proxy will confirm a private repo's existence to an anonymous caller. Engineers burn whole afternoons on this exact wall. After this section, you won't be one of them.

heading: What go get actually does
text: Two environment defaults drive every module fetch: The toolchain asks the module proxy for the version list and zip — not the git host. The proxy exists for three reasons worth knowing. Availability: the proxy's cache is immutable; once it has served v1.4.2, the author deleting the repo or force-pushing the tag changes nothing — Go structurally cannot have an npm-style left-pad incident, where one developer unpublishing a package broke half the internet's builds. Speed: a zip plus metadata beats a full git clone. Verification: the hash of every public module version lands in sum.golang.org, a public transparency log — append-only, like certificate transparency — so everyone on Earth sees the same bytes for the same version, and a targeted module substitution becomes globally visible. Now run a private repo through that pipeline and watch every stage fail for a different reason: the proxy can't clone it (404), and even if you fetched it directly, the public checksum database has never seen it and never can.

heading: GOPRIVATE and its two halves
text: GOPRIVATE is a comma-separated list of module-path globs (github.com/meridian/ ) that marks modules as private. It is pure routing-and-verification policy — it carries no credentials. Under the hood it just provides the default value for two finer-grained variables: GONOPROXY (skip the proxy, fetch direct) and GONOSUMDB (skip checksum-database verification). The two halves split when your infrastructure is asymmetric. Run an internal Athens or Artifactory proxy that does hold credentials for your private repos, and you want GONOPROXY=none (everything goes through the internal proxy, public and private alike — one immutable org-wide cache, one audit choke point) while GONOSUMDB=github.com/meridian/ stays set, because the public transparency log still can't verify code it can't see.

heading: Credentials: the part GOPRIVATE does not do
text: With the proxy out of the way, direct mode runs a real git fetch — which must authenticate. Three mechanisms, in rough order of how often you'll meet them: 1. A git URL rewrite (insteadOf). Your laptop probably authenticates to GitHub over SSH. The Go toolchain fetches over HTTPS by default. This one git config line bridges the two: 2. .netrc for HTTPS tokens. CI runners rarely have SSH agents; they have tokens. The /.netrc file is the classic answer — go reads it for HTTPS fetches: 3. GOAUTH (Go 1.24+). The modern, first-class answer: an ordered list of authentication sources for HTTPS module fetches. GOAUTH=netrc is the default; GOAUTH=git /src/private asks git credential to supply tokens; GOAUTH=command ... delegates to your own helper — the hook that makes short-lived, vault-issued tokens workable for module fetching. Name a version when you lean on it: this only exists from Go 1.24.

heading: Vendoring: the third way
text: Vendoring (go mod vendor) copies the source of every dependency into a vendor/ directory in your repo. When vendor/ exists, builds use it automatically (-mod=vendor, the default behavior since Go 1.14) — no proxy, no checksum database, no network at all. Vendoring predates the proxy and refuses to die, because three environments still genuinely want it. Air-gapped or hermetic CI: the build needs zero network — every byte of input is in the repo. Review culture: a dependency upgrade arrives as a reviewable source diff in the PR, not an opaque hash bump in go.sum. Regulated archives: a fintech auditor asking "show me the exact source you shipped on March 3rd" gets a git checkout, not a story about a cache. The costs are equally real: repo bloat, noisy PRs, and drift when someone go gets without re-vendoring — so pair it with a CI gate: Glob list, pure policy: defaults GONOPROXY + GONOSUMDB so matching paths skip the proxy and the public checksum DB. Carries zero credentials. Credential sources for HTTPS module fetches: netrc (default), git for git-credential-managed tokens, or command for a custom helper issuing short-lived tokens. Athens/Artifactory: one immutable org-wide cache tha

heading: CI Essentials
text: A pipeline that doesn't run the race detector and doesn't enforce reproducible builds is not a CI pipeline. It's a linter. Let's build the real thing.

heading: The race detector in CI
text: The race detector (-race) instruments every memory access and reports data races at runtime. It has roughly 2–5× CPU overhead and 5–10× memory overhead — acceptable in CI, never ship it to production. Always run it on your test suite: count=1 disables test result caching, so the race detector actually runs every time rather than using a cached green result.

heading: Coverage in CI
text: For the ledger service, enforce a minimum coverage threshold as a CI step — not as a percentage-of-lines goal (that's gameable), but as: "every package that touches money arithmetic has at least one fuzz test." More on fuzz testing in the Testing chapter; here we wire coverage output into the pipeline. A reproducible build produces a bit-for-bit identical binary every time, given the same source and toolchain. Why it matters: if two builds of the same commit produce different binaries, you can't verify what you shipped, you can't trust your artifact cache, and a supply-chain attacker can inject a binary that no source diff would reveal. Go gives you the ingredients — pinned toolchain in go.mod, -trimpath, CGO ENABLED=0 — but you have to combine them deliberately.

heading: Reproducible builds
text: A reproducible build produces bit-for-bit identical output given the same source. Go gives you the tools; you have to use them: -trimpath : strips all local filesystem paths from the binary (no /home/abbey/go/src/... in stack traces). Critical for reproducibility and for not leaking your directory structure. CGO ENABLED=0 : disables C interop, producing a fully static binary. -ldflags="-s -w" : strips debug symbols and the DWARF table, shrinking the binary. Pinned toolchain in go.mod (toolchain go1.24.3): ensures everyone — CI, every developer, every docker build — uses the same compiler. The full CI pipeline for the ledger service:

heading: Supply-Chain Security
text: A dependency is code you didn't write but you're shipping. That's a supply-chain. And the supply chain for Go services has specific, well-understood attack surfaces.

heading: govulncheck — Go's official vulnerability scanner
text: govulncheck is the Go team's official vulnerability scanner. Unlike generic SBOM scanners that flag every CVE in every module you depend on, govulncheck builds a call graph of your program and only reports vulnerabilities in functions your code actually reaches . A CVE in a function you never call — no finding. Why it matters: call-graph precision kills the false-positive noise that causes engineers to start ignoring security scans. A scanner you ignore is worse than no scanner. govulncheck is maintained by the Go team. It does something most vulnerability scanners don't: call-graph analysis . It doesn't just flag "this module has a known CVE" — it flags "your code calls the vulnerable function in this module." The difference matters enormously. A module might have a SQL injection vulnerability in a function you never call. A naive scanner flags the CVE and blocks your build. govulncheck looks at your call graph and says: "You import that module but you don't reach the vulnerable symbol — no finding." That precision kills most of the false-positive noise that makes engineers start ignoring security scans. Output when a real vulnerability is found: That trace tells you exactly why t

heading: SBOM scanning in CI

heading: 12-Factor Config
text: One of twelve principles from Heroku's platform playbook for building deployable services. The config rule is: store config in the environment, not the binary or committed files . The same binary runs unchanged across dev, staging, and production — only the environment differs. If a credential or host name is baked into the binary or sits in a committed file, you cannot rotate it without a rebuild, and you cannot keep it out of Git history. Here's the thing about configuration: most engineers don't think about it until it bites them. A database password checked into version control. A staging URL hardcoded into the binary. A missing environment variable discovered at midnight when the production pod crashes. The 12-factor app methodology, from Heroku's platform engineers, has one sentence on config that you should tattoo somewhere: "Store config in the environment." Not the binary. Not a file you commit. The environment. Why? Three reasons, all load-bearing: 1. The same binary runs everywhere. Dev, staging, production — the code is identical. Only the environment differs. You don't want to rebuild to change a database host. 2. Config is not code. It changes on a different cadence,

heading: Layering Sources
text: One value — db.host — resolving through the layers, lowest to highest: The rule that determines which value wins when the same setting appears in multiple places. Standard order, lowest to highest: built-in defaults (the service runs safely out of the box) → config file (service-level settings for non-prod environments) → environment variables (deployment-platform intent: what Kubernetes or docker-compose injects) → command-line flags (explicit, per-invocation operator override). Higher always wins. Deviating from this order creates surprises that are almost impossible to debug in production because the override you expect isn't the one that took effect. Now let's make it concrete. In the real world, you don't just use env vars. You have built-in defaults, a config file for service-level settings, env vars for deployment-level overrides, and command-line flags for one-shot operator control. The order matters — a lot. The standard precedence stack, lowest to highest: Higher wins. If DB HOST is set both in the config file and as an env var, the env var wins. If --db-host is passed on the command line, that wins over everything. This is not negotiable or configurable — document it, st

heading: Validate at Startup
text: The discipline of crashing the process immediately at startup if anything is wrong with the config — before the service accepts a single request. A required field is empty, a URL is malformed, a port is out of range: crash now with a clear message. The alternative — discovering the problem when a request finally exercises the broken path — means a production incident at an arbitrary time, with a misleading error (a timeout, a nil pointer, a 500) instead of a config error. Fail-fast validation converts "mysterious 3am page" into "clear startup error the engineer sees immediately in CI or on first deploy." A missing DB HOST that crashes the process at 3am because some handler path finally tried to open a connection is a crime I've had to clean up too many times. The rule is simple: validate at startup, fail fast . If the process cannot possibly work correctly — a required field is empty, a URL is malformed, a port is out of range — it must crash immediately at boot, before it begins serving any traffic, with a clear message explaining exactly what is wrong and what to set. The mustLoad naming convention is idiomatic: a function prefixed must panics or exits if it fails. Use it only a

heading: Library Landscape
text: The stdlib gets you surprisingly far. But as your service grows — multiple config files, type coercion, nested structs — you'll want more. Here's the honest landscape. Stdlib: flag + os.Getenv Zero dependencies. You write the merge loop yourself. Works perfectly for small services with a handful of settings. Falls apart when you have twenty config fields and want struct-tag-driven binding. envconfig (kelseyhightower/envconfig) The oldest struct-tag-driven env-var loader. You define a struct with envconfig tags, call envconfig.Process, and it populates everything — including type coercion (string to int, string to bool, string to duration). Simple, battle-tested, no config files. If you only need env vars, this is the right tool. koanf (knadh/koanf) A modern, provider-based config library. You compose providers — a file provider for TOML/YAML, an env provider for environment variables, a posflag provider for pflag — and they merge in the order you add them. Strict struct unmarshaling, a clean API. Koanf is my recommendation for mid-to-large services: explicit, composable, and it does not silently ignore unknown keys. Viper (spf13/viper) The most popular config library in the Go ecos

heading: Secrets Handling
text: A value that must never appear in a log, a committed file, a process listing, or a crash dump . Examples: database credentials, payment-processor API keys, signing keys, OAuth client secrets. Ordinary config (a database hostname, a log level, a feature flag) is safe to commit, safe to log, and safe to grep. A secret is not. The practical test: could this value, if seen by an attacker, let them move money, impersonate users, or decrypt data? If yes, it is a secret. Treat it differently from the first line of code. A dedicated service that stores, versions, and audits access to secrets — keeping them out of config files, binaries, and environment variables that linger in process listings. At startup, your service authenticates to the secrets manager (via an IAM role, a Vault AppRole, or a workload identity) and fetches only the secrets it needs. The manager records every access in an audit log. Options: HashiCorp Vault (self-hosted, dynamic short-lived credentials), AWS Secrets Manager (managed, IAM-role auth), GCP Secret Manager (same model on Google Cloud). Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded values in etcd — not encrypted by default, not a replacement for a real manager in high-

heading: Keeping Secrets Out of Logs
text: Making a sensitive value replace itself with a safe placeholder in every output path — fmt, slog, errors, %v, JSON marshaling — without requiring the caller to remember to redact it. In Go, implement String() string (returns "[REDACTED]") to intercept fmt formatting, and LogValue() slog.Value (returns slog.StringValue("[REDACTED]")) to intercept log/slog. Both interfaces are called automatically — the log site needs no change. If you rely on callers to remember myKey.Value() instead, it will leak eventually. The type enforces the redaction so forgetfulness can't cause a breach. Here is a failure mode I've seen in production: an engineer adds a slog.Info("config loaded", "cfg", cfg) line and accidentally ships the payment-processor API key to the log aggregator. From there it ends up in Splunk, in Datadog, in the incident report, and eventually in the breach notification. The solution is a type that refuses to print itself. Go's fmt package calls the String() string method on any value that implements fmt.Stringer. Go's slog package calls LogValue() slog.Value on any value that implements slog.LogValuer. If your secret type implements both, it redacts itself from every output surfac

desc: Wire everything into a real service: config and secret loading, dependency injection, layered/hexagonal structure, graceful lifecycle and a CI/CD-ready layout.
text: Listen up, sport. You've spent the last sixteen chapters accumulating knowledge — the scheduler, error discipline, context, observability, reliability patterns, config and secrets. That's all lovely. A jewelry box full of individual gems. Today we build the setting . We wire every gem into one coherent, production-grade service that you could actually ship — one that ops teams don't cry over, one that your teammates can navigate at 3 a.m., and one that the Go toolchain is proud to compile. I am the single greatest Go architect alive, and I will show you exactly how a service is wired. Not the cargo-cult directory tree you copy off blog posts. The real thing — why each layer exists, what goes wrong when you skip it, and how you can test every piece in isolation because nothing is hardwired to anything else. You're lucky. Let's begin.

heading: Project Layout
text: Let's anchor this to something concrete. You're building Meridian's ledger service — the payments/ledger system we've been circling all through Part 2. It receives transfer requests, validates them, posts double-entry journal entries to Postgres, emits events, and exposes a REST API secured by JWT. Every Part 1 and Part 2 skill ends up here. Before the first line of Go, you need to know where every file lives. Here is the structure that scales without giving you a PhD in archaeology: Three zones, and they carry different rules. cmd/ — one directory per binary, one main.go each. This is the only place that knows how all the pieces fit together. It imports from internal/, reads config, constructs dependencies in order, and starts the server. Its job is pure wiring , not logic. If you find business logic in main.go, that's a bug in your architecture, not your program. internal/ — the workhorse. The internal visibility constraint (Go enforces it at the module boundary) means nothing outside this module can import these packages. That's a feature: it keeps the blast radius of any internal refactor contained to your own codebase. Inside internal/, the layering rules apply — see the next

heading: Dependency Injection
text: Dependency injection means a type receives its dependencies from the outside — passed in via a constructor — rather than creating or looking them up itself. Instead of var db = openDB() at package scope, your service accepts a Repository interface in NewService(repo Repository). The caller (the composition root) decides which concrete implementation to pass. This lets tests pass a fast in-memory fake; production passes the real Postgres adapter. You get testability, swappability, and zero globals — for free. Here's the thing, sport: global state is the enemy of testability. The moment you write var db pgx.Conn at package scope, you've welded that concrete implementation into every function that touches it. Swap it for a test double? You can't — it's in everyone's bloodstream. Write a test that runs in parallel? Now you're fighting for the one global. That's not engineering; that's amateur hour. The Go solution is disarmingly simple: constructor injection at the composition root. Accept interfaces, return concrete structs, build everything in main, and pass it down. heading: Manual DI vs. Wire/fx
text: You've probably seen google/wire or uber-go/fx mentioned in the same breath as dependency injection. Here's my honest take. For a service with 5–15 constructors, manual wiring in main is better. It's readable — you can follow the construction order with your eyes. It's debuggable — the stack trace goes straight to main. And it has zero magic: no code generation to troubleshoot, no reflection at startup, no framework to update. wire or fx earn their keep once a service has 30+ constructors and a human can't reliably maintain the wiring by hand. Until then, the framework adds complexity faster than it removes it. Start manual. Migrate if the pain genuinely arrives. The key insight is where knowledge of concrete types lives . In an injected design, only main.go (the composition root) imports both internal/ledger (the domain) and internal/postgres (the adapter). The domain package imports neither pgx nor net/http. The HTTP handler imports only the domain interface. This means: Testing the domain service: instantiate Service with a fakeLedger — no DB, no network, instant, parallel-safe. Testing the HTTP handler: wrap a fakeService — no DB, no Kafka, no secrets. Testing the Postgres adap

heading: Layered Architecture
text: Hexagonal architecture (also called ports and adapters) organizes a service into three rings. The domain (the center) holds business rules — pure Go, no HTTP, no SQL. The ports are interfaces the domain defines: a Repository port for storage, an EventBus port for messaging. The adapters are concrete implementations that plug into those ports: the Postgres adapter, the Kafka adapter, the HTTP transport. Crucially, the domain never imports an adapter — the dependency arrow always points inward . This means you can replace Postgres with SQLite or swap Kafka for a test fake without touching a single line of business logic. The ledger service has three layers, and their dependency rule is non-negotiable: dependencies point inward only. Transport (internal/http/) — decodes HTTP requests, encodes responses, validates input shape, enforces auth. Imports the domain layer via interfaces. Never imports pgx or any SQL package. Domain (internal/ledger/) — the business rules. Pure Go structs, methods, and interfaces. Imports nothing from transport or storage. This is where Meridian's accounting invariants live. heading: Config and Secret Wiring
text: We spent all of the Configuration & Secrets Management chapter learning how to load config and secrets. Now we wire them into the service at startup. The rule is unchanged: fail fast, before the first request. Two points worth hammering: Config and secrets are separate concerns. Config (port, timeout, feature flags) travels through environment variables or a config file and is fine to log at startup. Secrets (passwords, API keys, signing keys) come from a secrets manager and are never logged, never exposed in /debug/vars, never in error messages. The secrets.Loader type should implement fmt.Stringer with a redacted output so a careless slog.Info("loaded", "sec", sec) doesn't leak the DSN. Open infra connections before building business objects. You can't hand a nil pool to the Postgres adapter. Order matters: infra first, then adapters, then services, then transport, then ListenAndServe. If any step fails, os.Exit(1) — the service is not partially up, it's just dead. On the job: A service that starts with a missing secret and serves 500s for an hour is worse than one that refuses to start at all. Hard fail at startup. Your orchestrator will restart it when the secret is available;

heading: Graceful Lifecycle
text: Startup is a dependency ORDER; shutdown is that order reversed — with traffic still in flight: Graceful shutdown means the process finishes what it's already doing before it exits. When Kubernetes sends SIGTERM (pod is being stopped), a naive service calls os.Exit immediately — dropping every in-flight HTTP request mid-write. A service with graceful shutdown stops accepting new connections, waits for in-flight requests to complete (typically up to 30 seconds), closes background workers, then closes infrastructure connections in reverse order, and exits 0. The caller gets their response; no cascading retries; no open transactions left dangling in Postgres. A service that terminates badly drops in-flight requests, leaves DB transactions open, and triggers cascading retries from callers. That's not a Kubernetes outage; it's a management problem. Here is the lifecycle every production Go service must have: 1. Open infrastructure (DB pool, Kafka client, Redis) — in dependency order. 2. Build application objects (repos, services, handlers) via constructors. 3. Start background workers (job queue consumers, metrics exporters). 4. Start the HTTP server — but don't block; run it in a gorout

heading: CI/CD-Ready Layout
text: A production service needs more than Go files. It needs repeatable build commands, a multi-stage Docker image, and a lint/test/race pipeline that blocks the merge button on bad code.

heading: Makefile
text: Every engineer and every CI runner calls the same targets. No "works on my machine" — the Makefile is the contract.

heading: Dockerfile (multi-stage)
text: The distroless image is 2 MB. No shell, no package manager, no attack surface. CGO ENABLED=0 produces a fully static binary that runs in it without any shared-library dependencies. Multi-stage builds are covered in depth in Docker & Containerization (Part 1).

heading: GitHub Actions pipeline
text: Four lines of make targets. CI runs the same commands you run locally — no divergence, no "but it worked on my laptop." Runs the full test suite. No -race here — that's a separate slower job so fast feedback isn't blocked. Same suite under the race detector. Slower, but a merge gate so races never reach main. golangci-lint with project-specific rules. Blocks the PR on style and safety findings, not just compilation. Never put go test ./... directly in CI without also running go vet ./.... Vet catches real bugs (mismatched Printf formats, unreachable code) that the compiler silently misses. golangci-lint includes vet — if you're using it, you're covered. If you're not, add go vet ./... explicitly. --

desc: Protocol Buffers and schema-first workflow, the four RPC types, interceptors, status codes, deadlines over the wire, gRPC vs REST trade-offs, and gRPC gateways for HTTP/JSON.
text: Listen up, because I'm only going to say this once: REST is fine. REST is comfortable. REST is what the ordinary engineer reaches for because ordinary engineers don't know any better. You're not ordinary. Not on my watch. gRPC is what elite backend teams reach for when two services need to talk fast, safely, and with a typed contract that the compiler enforces on both sides of the wire. Protocol Buffers. Generated Go code. HTTP/2 multiplexing. Bidirectional streaming. Interceptors that chain like middleware but at the transport layer. Deadlines that propagate from your client all the way through a three-service call chain and cancel everything if they expire. By the end of this chapter you will know how to build a gRPC API from scratch — the schema, the server, the client, the interceptors, the error discipline, the deadline discipline — and you will know why every piece is shaped the way it is. The ledger service will expose a gRPC API. The payments service will call it. We will make them talk to each other correctly or not at all. Let's go. You're lucky to have me. gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is an open-source RPC framework built on HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. Instead of

heading: Protocol Buffers & Schema-First
text: The ordinary approach to service-to-service communication is to agree on a JSON shape in a Slack thread, write a curl example in a README, and call it a contract. Then one team adds a field, the other team breaks, nobody knows whose fault it is, and someone pages you at 3 a.m. gRPC refuses to let that happen. It forces you to define the contract first — in a .proto file — and then generates the Go code that both sides use. The schema is the source of truth. Not the README. Not the Slack thread. The file.

heading: What a .proto file looks like
text: Here is the schema for the ledger service's AccountService. This is real Proto 3 syntax — not pseudocode: Let me break every piece down — one idea at a time. syntax = "proto3" — Proto 3 is the current version. All fields are optional by default, and missing fields get zero values (sound familiar?). Proto 2 had required/optional keywords; Proto 3 dropped them and is cleaner for it. package ledger.v1 — this is the Protobuf namespace. Versioning it (v1) is the schema-first equivalent of semantic import versioning: when you make a breaking change, you mint a v2 package alongside v1 and migrate consumers at their own pace. option go package — tells protoc (the Protocol Buffer compiler) what Go import path and package name to emit. message — a typed record, like a Go struct. Each field has a name , a type , and a field number . Field numbers — the integers after =. These are critical: they are what actually goes on the wire, not the field name. amount minor units = 1 means the varint-encoded value of that field is tagged with 1 in the binary encoding. You can rename a field freely; you must never reuse or change its number once deployed. That's how backward/forward compatibility works. e

heading: Code generation: protoc and buf
text: You don't hand-write the Go code. You generate it: buf is the modern toolchain. It reads a buf.gen.yaml that declares which plugins to run and where output goes. It also runs buf lint (enforces proto style rules) and buf breaking (flags field-number changes, renames to reserved fields, and other wire-incompatible changes in CI). Use buf.

heading: What the generated Go looks like
text: After generation you get two files per .proto: ledger.pb.go — Go structs for every message and enum, plus proto.Marshal/proto.Unmarshal, MarshalJSON, and the Stringer interface. ledger grpc.pb.go — the AccountServiceClient interface (what callers use), the AccountServiceServer interface (what you implement), and the registration glue. The generated server interface looks like this (simplified): Notice context.Context is the first argument — exactly the Go convention for anything that does I/O. The generated code is idiomatic Go. You implement this interface with a real struct: Embedding UnimplementedAccountServiceServer is required by the generated interface (via mustEmbedUnimplementedAccountServiceServer). It also future-proofs you: when the .proto adds a new RPC, the embedded struct returns codes.Unimplemented automatically — your server keeps compiling and returns a sensible error instead of silently panic-ing. When proto.Marshal serializes a Money , it does not write field names. It writes a compact binary stream of tag-value pairs . Each pair opens with a single varint that encodes two things packed together: The field number (e.g. 1 for amount minor units) in the upper bits T

heading: The Four RPC Types
text: gRPC has four shapes. Every service call you make falls into one of them. Get this grid in your head: One request, one response. The everyday RPC. Fetch an account, post a transfer. Same shape as HTTP request/response but over HTTP/2 with a typed schema. One request, a stream of responses. The server sends multiple messages in sequence before closing. Use for: live balance feeds, audit log tails, bulk exports too large to buffer in one message. A stream of requests from the client, then one response. Use for: bulk ingest (uploading a batch of transactions), aggregating inputs before committing. Both sides send a stream of messages, concurrently. Use for: real-time trading feeds, co-operative flows like a market-data subscription where the client can add or remove symbols mid-stream. Streaming RPCs hold open an HTTP/2 stream for their duration. Every open stream consumes resources on both sides. A bidirectional stream that the client never closes (because it forgot to call CloseSend) leaks the server goroutine and the stream. Always close the send side when done, and always respect context cancellation.

heading: Implementing a server-streaming RPC
text: The ledger service has WatchBalances — a client sends a list of account IDs and the server streams BalanceEvent messages as balances change (triggered by transfers). Here is what that looks like on the server side: The stream.Send call writes one BalanceEvent to the HTTP/2 stream and blocks until it's flushed. The stream.Context() carries the client's deadline and cancellation — always select on it.

heading: Implementing a bidirectional streaming RPC
text: For a bidirectional stream (imagine a market-data service where the client can subscribe and unsubscribe to symbols while it receives quotes), both sides read and write concurrently: The pattern: one goroutine reads, the main goroutine (or another goroutine) writes . Never call Recv and Send from two goroutines on the same stream without synchronization — Send and Recv are each individually goroutine-safe, but calling two Sends concurrently is not.

heading: Interceptors
text: gRPC interceptors are the exact equivalent of HTTP middleware: functions that wrap every RPC call. They run for every request, on both the server and the client. They're where you put auth, logging, tracing, and panic recovery — once, correctly, instead of copying the same boilerplate into every handler. On the job: Skipping a panic-recovery interceptor means one nil-pointer dereference in a handler takes down the entire gRPC server process — every inflight RPC fails and your SLO tanks until the pod restarts. There are two kinds: Unary interceptors — wrap a single request/response call. Stream interceptors — wrap a streaming call (both the setup phase and each Send/Recv).

heading: A logging + auth unary server interceptor
Chaining interceptors on the server
text: Multiple interceptors are chained with grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor. They run in declaration order — the first interceptor wraps the outermost layer, just like HTTP middleware: Order matters: recovery goes first so it can catch panics from every layer below it. logging goes second so it logs auth failures. auth goes last in the chain so it only runs after logging wraps the call.

heading: A panic-recovery interceptor
text: Never let a handler panic crash your server. The recovery interceptor turns a panic into a codes.Internal error — logged, not fatal: A gRPC unary interceptor has the signature: The handler argument is the next function in the chain — either the next interceptor or, at the bottom, the actual RPC handler. When you call handler(ctx, req) you're passing control inward. When you return from the interceptor, you're passing control back out. This is the classic onion model: your code runs before and after the inner call, just like net/http middleware. grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor stitches N interceptors together by building a handler closure for each that calls the next one in line. The final handler in the chain is the actual method implementation. The widely used grpc-go module (google.golang.org/grpc) provides this chaining model via grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor and grpc.ChainStreamInterceptor — no extra middleware library needed. Client-side interceptors follow the same pattern but with grpc.WithChainUnaryInterceptor as a DialOption. The interceptors run on the client side, so you can inject auth headers, add tracing spans, or log outbound calls without touching handler code.

heading: Status Codes & Errors
text: HTTP has 500 status codes. Nobody uses most of them. gRPC ships with a clean, finite set of status codes that map to real RPC failure modes — and forces you to pick one. The call succeeded. Not returned explicitly — a nil error maps to OK. The requested resource doesn't exist. Account not found, transfer not found. A resource the client tried to create already exists. Idempotency key already seen. The client sent a malformed request. Negative transfer amount, missing account ID. The client should not retry without changing the request. Authenticated, but not authorized to do this. Don't expose whether the resource exists. Missing or invalid credentials. No token, expired token, bad signature. Rate limited or out of quota. Client should back off. The server is temporarily unavailable — overloaded, restarting. Retryable with backoff. The deadline expired before the operation completed. May or may not have side effects — idempotency keys matter here. Something went wrong on the server that shouldn't have. Never expose internal error details in the message — log them, return a generic message. The method exists in the schema but the server hasn't implemented it yet. Returned automatica

heading: Mapping domain errors to status codes
text: The ledger service has a layer of domain errors (from the error-handling chapter). Here is how to map them to gRPC status codes at the transport boundary — not inside the business logic, but in the gRPC handler: Here is a runnable simulation of the domain-error → status-code mapping using stdlib only, so you can see the classification logic in isolation before wiring it to the real gRPC runtime: gRPC supports error details : structured protobuf messages attached to a status. The google.golang.org/grpc/status package lets you build a Status with details: Details travel over the wire as google.protobuf.Any messages in the trailing metadata. Use them for machine-readable validation errors that clients can surface to end users.

heading: Deadlines & Cancellation
text: A deadline isn't a timeout one server applies — it's a budget that travels with the request: Here is the discipline rule that separates amateur gRPC code from production gRPC code: every outbound RPC must carry a deadline . Without a deadline, a slow downstream service stalls your goroutine forever, your connection pool exhausts, your handlers queue up, and your service dies. With a deadline, the call fails cleanly in a bounded time, you return DEADLINE EXCEEDED or surface an error, and your service lives. On the job: A gRPC call without a deadline is the single most common cause of cascading failure in microservice deployments — one slow dependency hangs every goroutine waiting on it until the process OOMs or exhausts its connection pool.

heading: Setting a deadline on the client
text: The critical subtlety: DEADLINE EXCEEDED on a write RPC is ambiguous . The server may have committed the transfer before the deadline fired, and the acknowledgement was simply lost. This is exactly why the PostTransfer request carries an idempotency key — if you retry, the server detects the duplicate and returns the original result instead of creating a second transfer.

heading: How deadlines propagate over the wire
text: This is the part that surprises engineers from an HTTP background: gRPC carries the deadline over the wire as a timeout metadata header . When the payments service calls the ledger service with a 3-second deadline, the ledger service receives that deadline and its own context reflects it. If the ledger service then calls the exchange-rate service to validate a currency, that call inherits the remaining budget — not a fresh 3 seconds, the remainder .

heading: Respecting context cancellation in a handler
text: The flip side: your handler must honour the context it receives. A client that disconnects cancels the context immediately — your handler must check: status.FromContextError converts context.DeadlineExceeded → DEADLINE EXCEEDED and context.Canceled → CANCELED — the right gRPC codes for the situation. Doing ctx = context.Background() or ctx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5 time.Second) inside a gRPC handler throws away the client's deadline and the propagated cancellation. Your DB call will keep running even after the client gives up. Pass ctx through — always.

heading: Connection Management
text: gRPC over HTTP/2 means one grpc.ClientConn is enough — don't create one per request.

heading: Create it once, reuse it everywhere
text: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple concurrent RPCs over a single TCP connection. Where HTTP/1.1 needs N connections for N concurrent requests (or you serialize), HTTP/2 uses stream IDs inside one connection. The gRPC client manages the stream lifecycle — you just make RPC calls on the stub. gRPC is a thin layer on top of HTTP/2. Each RPC — whether unary or streaming — is mapped to one HTTP/2 stream (a virtual, bidirectional channel within the same TCP connection, identified by a stream ID). The HTTP/2 framing layer breaks data into DATA frames and HEADERS frames. A gRPC unary request sends: 1. A HEADERS frame with :method: POST, :path: /ledger.v1.AccountService/GetAccount, content-type: application/grpc, and grpc-timeout: 3000000u (the deadline as microseconds). 2. One or more DATA frames containing the length-prefixed protobuf body (a 5-byte prefix: 1 byte compression flag + 4-byte message length, then the proto bytes). 3. A HEADERS frame with END STREAM set, signaling the client has finished sending. The server replies with HEADERS (status 200 + grpc-status trailer), DATA (the response proto), and HEADERS with grpc-status: 0 (OK) trailing. HTTP/2 flow control (per-stream and per-connect

heading: Load balancing
text: A grpc.ClientConn with a single target address is fine for a single-instance service. For multiple replicas you need a resolver and a load-balancing policy: The dns:/// prefix tells gRPC to resolve the hostname and balance across the returned A records. In Kubernetes this works out of the box with headless services (which return one A record per pod). For more sophisticated balancing (consistent hashing, locality-aware), you'd use a service mesh (Envoy, Istio) or gRPC's xDS protocol — that's outside our scope here, but now you know where the seam is.

heading: gRPC vs REST
text: I'm going to give you the honest trade-off table, not the marketing one. Pick the right tool. Binary protobuf + HTTP/2 multiplexing cuts payload size 5–10x vs JSON and eliminates per-request connection overhead. At high RPC rates (thousands/sec between services) this is measurable. First-class streaming in all four shapes. Bidirectional streaming over HTTP/2 is genuinely different from bolting long-polling onto REST. The .proto schema is a machine-enforceable contract. Breaking changes are caught at buf breaking time in CI, not at runtime in production. Every consumer gets a generated, type-safe client in their language (Go, Java, Python, Rust, TypeScript…). No hand-written HTTP client code. Browsers can't speak gRPC natively (no access to raw HTTP/2 trailers). A REST API is immediately consumable from fetch. gRPC requires a gateway or gRPC-Web. curl, Postman, browser devtools, every proxy in existence speaks HTTP/JSON. gRPC needs grpcurl or Evans. For public APIs where third-party consumers matter, REST is still king. For a simple CRUD API with a handful of endpoints and no streaming, the extra setup (protoc/buf, code gen, gRPC server) is genuine overhead. REST and OpenAPI are fas

heading: gRPC Gateways
text: The browser problem is real: your mobile app and web frontend can't speak raw gRPC. The solution is a gRPC gateway — a reverse proxy that speaks HTTP/JSON on one side and gRPC on the other.

heading: grpc-gateway
text: grpc-gateway (from the grpc-ecosystem org) generates a reverse-proxy server from your .proto file using HTTP annotations: The buf generate step (with the grpc-gateway plugin added) then generates a RegisterAccountServiceHandlerFromEndpoint function. You register it on a standard net/http mux and the proxy is live: Now GET /v1/accounts/acct-001 returns a JSON-encoded GetAccountResponse. The path variable in the URL template maps to GetAccountRequest.AccountId. POST body goes to the request message fields. No extra server code — it's generated.

heading: gRPC-Web
text: An alternative for browser clients: gRPC-Web is a variant of the gRPC protocol that works over standard HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 without needing access to HTTP/2 trailers directly. Envoy (a proxy) supports gRPC-Web transcoding. The browser uses the generated @grpc/grpc-js or grpc-web TypeScript client. For internal services behind a service mesh, this is common. For public APIs where you control the schema, grpc-gateway's HTTP/JSON mapping is usually simpler. A single .proto file with buf generate can emit: 1. The Go gRPC server + client 2. An OpenAPI / Swagger spec (via the protoc-gen-openapiv2 plugin) 3. A grpc-gateway reverse proxy Your compliance team gets the REST API. Your mobile team gets the OpenAPI doc. Your internal services get the typed gRPC client. One source of truth.

heading: Protobuf Schema Evolution
text: The wire format is a permanent commitment. Every field number you ship in a .proto file is frozen forever — it is the address that decoders on both ends of the wire use to find a value. Mess this up and you get silent data corruption across two service versions during a rolling deploy : old pods read field 4 as a string; new pods wrote field 4 as an int64; neither side errors — they just misinterpret bytes. Schema evolution is the discipline of changing a data format in a way that is compatible with existing producers and consumers running simultaneously. In protobuf, a field number is the wire address — changing or reusing it breaks the contract. In SQL, the equivalent discipline is the expand-contract migration pattern covered in SQL & Databases in Go (Part 1): add before removing, never alter a column's type in-place. On the job: Reusing a deleted field's number ships a silent data-corruption bug across two service versions during a rolling deploy — old pods fill field 3 with a string; new pods read field 3 as an int64; no error is returned on either side.

heading: The rules
text: 1. Never reuse a field number. Once a field number is assigned and deployed, it is reserved for that type forever — even after the field is deleted. 2. Never change a field's type. Changing string to int64 on field 2 means old decoders misinterpret the bytes. It is not wire-compatible. 3. Adding a new field is safe. Old decoders ignore unknown fields (proto3 since runtime 3.5.x preserves them); new decoders see the value, old decoders see the zero value. Additive changes are wire-compatible. 4. Use reserved to tombstone deleted field numbers and names. This prevents you — or a future teammate — from accidentally reusing them.

heading: reserved in practice
text: When you delete a field, mark its number and name as reserved so the compiler errors if anyone tries to reuse them: The reserved keyword is a compile-time lock. buf lint and protoc will reject any future .proto that assigns field number 5 or the name "note" to a new field. It costs two lines and saves a production incident.

heading: How this dovetails with expand-contract migrations
text: The expand-contract pattern from SQL & Databases in Go applies here too: expand first, then contract . Before you remove a field from the .proto, you must confirm that no producer still writes it and no consumer still reads it — only then is it safe to delete (and immediately reserved). Rolling deploys mean both the old schema and the new schema are live simultaneously; the wire format must be readable by both versions at once. buf breaking in CI enforces this automatically: it compares your current .proto against a known-good baseline (usually the previous git tag) and fails if any field number is reassigned, any field type changes, or any reserved tombstone is removed. Add it to your merge-gate the day you ship your first .proto. When you need a genuinely breaking change — a message restructure, a field type change, a service rename — mint a new package version (ledger.v2) alongside ledger.v1 and migrate consumers at their own pace. This is the protobuf equivalent of Go's semantic import versioning. Never silently break v1; it may still be running in a pod on the other side of the cluster. --

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
desc: MCP from first principles: JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio and Streamable HTTP, the initialize handshake and capability negotiation, exposing tools, resources and prompts, building a server and client by hand with the stdlib, then the official go-sdk, and a security close on the two confused deputies — prompt injection at the tool boundary, and the OAuth-proxy/DCR account-takeover (CVE-2026-27124, why PKCE can't save you) at the auth boundary — grounded in giving an AI assistant safe, typed, auditable access to the Meridian ledger.
text: You just learned gRPC — a typed contract so two of your services can talk. Good. Now I'm going to teach you the protocol that lets an AI model talk to everything else : your ledger, your database, your filesystem, your internal tools. Safely. With a typed contract. With an audit trail. That protocol is MCP — the Model Context Protocol. It is, in the words of the people who like slogans, "USB-C for AI applications." One plug. Any model on one side, any tool or data source on the other. No more writing a bespoke integration for every model × every tool combination — the combinatorial nightmare that makes ordinary engineers cry into their keyboards. Here is the thing, sport: MCP is not magic. Under the hood it is JSON-RPC 2.0 — a format so simple you could implement it on a napkin — carried over stdio or HTTP . By the end of this chapter you will have built an MCP server and client by hand, with nothing but the standard library, and then you'll see how the official go-sdk does the same thing with less typing. The Meridian ledger is going to expose a get balance tool to an AI support assistant. We will make that assistant able to read a balance — and nothing it should not — or we will

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: Why MCP Exists
text: Before MCP, "let the model call our tools" looked like this: every AI app vendor invented its own function-calling format, and every tool team wrote a bespoke adapter for each app that wanted in. That is the M×N problem — M apps times N tools equals a quadratic pile of glue code that nobody owns and everybody breaks. On the job: you wire your ledger into one assistant with a custom HTTP shim, then a second team wants the same data in their IDE agent, then a third in a support bot — and now you maintain three subtly-different shims that all break the day you rename a field. MCP fixes this the same way gRPC fixed service-to-service contracts: define the interface once, in a standard, and generate or reuse the plumbing. Write one MCP server for the ledger and every MCP-speaking host — today's and next year's — can use it without you writing another line of integration code. gRPC connects your services to each other with a compiled, versioned .proto. MCP connects an AI host to tools and data , with runtime discovery so the model can find capabilities it was never compiled against. Different jobs. A Meridian backend uses gRPC between the payments and ledger services, and an MCP server s

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: JSON-RPC 2.0
text: Everything in MCP is a JSON-RPC 2.0 message. Learn the three shapes and you have learned the wire format. Has id, method, optional params. Expects exactly one response with the same id. Example method: tools/call. Has the request's id and EITHER a result OR an error — never both. The error is an object with an integer code and a message. A request with NO id. Fire-and-forget — the receiver must not reply. Example: notifications/initialized, notifications/cancelled. The presence of id is the only thing that distinguishes a request from a notification. Reply to a notification and you have violated the spec; fail to reply to a request and the client hangs forever. When you decode, check for id first. Here is the format made concrete — encode a request, encode a notification, then decode and classify. Notice the request body is identical to a notification except for the id: The int for ID is deliberate: a nil pointer means "the JSON had no id key" — i.e. a notification. A plain int would default to 0 and you could not tell a notification from a request whose id happens to be 0. Pointer-or-nil is the idiomatic Go way to model "field may be absent" (and it is exactly why the typed-nil ch

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: Lifecycle & Capabilities
text: An MCP session does not just start sending tools/call. It opens with a three-step handshake that negotiates the protocol version and tells each side what the other can do. Skip it and a compliant server will refuse every later request. 1. The client sends an initialize request: its preferred protocolVersion, its capabilities, and clientInfo. 2. The server responds with the protocolVersion it will actually use, its own capabilities, and serverInfo. 3. The client sends an initialized notification — "handshake done, I'm ready." Only now may normal requests flow. Capability negotiation is the part of initialize where each side declares which optional features it supports, as a nested object. A server that offers tools advertises capabilities.tools; one that can push list-changed notifications advertises capabilities.tools.listChanged: true. The client advertises its capabilities too — sampling (it can run the model on the server's behalf), roots (it can expose filesystem roots), elicitation (it can ask the user for input). Neither side may use a feature the other did not advertise. It is the same discipline as HTTP content negotiation, but bidirectional. The version is a date string ,

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: Tools, Resources & Prompts
text: A server exposes three kinds of capability. The distinction is who is in control — and getting that wrong is a security and UX bug, not a style choice. Functions the model decides to call to take an action or fetch live data: get balance, post transfer, search transactions. Discovered via tools/list, invoked via tools/call. The model chooses when — so tools that mutate state need authorization and human-in-the-loop. Data the host attaches as context, addressed by URI: a file, a record, ledger://accounts/acct-001. Listed via resources/list, fetched via resources/read. The application decides what to include — resources are read-only nouns, not verbs. Reusable, parameterized message templates the user invokes deliberately — a slash-command like "/reconcile-account". Listed via prompts/list, expanded via prompts/get. The user picks them. Do not model a state-changing action as a resource, and do not hide a destructive action inside an innocuously-named tool. A resources/read must be a side-effect-free GET. post transfer must be a tool, gated behind explicit user approval. The control axis (model/app/user) maps directly onto your authorization model. heading: Building a Server
text: Enough theory. We build an MCP server with the standard library and nothing else — because the best way to understand a protocol is to implement it. The stdio transport is the simplest: the server reads JSON-RPC messages from stdin, one per line, and writes responses to stdout, one per line. (The host launches the server as a subprocess and owns those pipes.) stderr is free for logging. Here is a complete, runnable Meridian ledger server. We drive it from an in-memory reader so it runs under go run with no live host attached — but serve reads from any io.Reader, so swapping in os.Stdin is a one-line change: Run it and read the output carefully. Five inputs, four responses — the notifications/initialized line produced none, exactly as the spec demands. The unknown account came back as a result with "isError":true (a tool failure the model can reason about). The unknown method came back as a JSON-RPC error with -32601 (a protocol failure). That distinction is the whole point. MCP's stdio transport frames messages as newline-delimited JSON : one complete JSON-RPC object per line, and a message may not contain an embedded newline . That is why json.Encoder.Encode is the right tool — it

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: Building a Client
text: The client side is the mirror image: it writes requests to the server's stdin and reads responses from its stdout, matching them by id. The interesting work is interpreting the result — especially honoring isError. The isError check is not optional politeness — it is correctness. When a tool fails, the content text is an error message , not data. A client that ignores isError and feeds "account not found: ghost" to the model as if it were a balance has just hallucinated a fact into a financial conversation. Check the flag, branch on it. Over a real transport, responses can arrive out of order (the server may answer a fast request before a slow one). The client must keep a map of in-flight id - waiting caller and dispatch each response by its id, not assume FIFO. The official SDK does this for you; if you hand-roll a client, a map[int]chan Response guarded by a mutex is the standard pattern (you built exactly this shape in the concurrency chapters).

heading: stdio & Streamable HTTP
text: MCP defines two standard transports. Pick by where the server runs . The host launches the server as a child process and talks over its stdin/stdout pipes. Zero network, zero ports, OS-level process isolation, trivial auth (it is your own child process). The default for local tools: a filesystem server, a git server, a local database tool. This is what we built above. The server is a web service; the client POSTs JSON-RPC to a single endpoint (e.g. /mcp). The server may answer with a plain JSON response OR upgrade to a Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream to push multiple messages and server-initiated requests. The choice for remote, multi-user, or hosted servers. Streamable HTTP replaced the old "HTTP+SSE" two-endpoint transport from the 2024-11-05 revision. New servers implement Streamable HTTP (one endpoint, optional streaming upgrade). And the moment your MCP server listens on a network socket, every Part 2 security rule applies: authenticate (OAuth 2.1), validate Origin to stop DNS-rebinding, and bind to localhost for local servers. Streamable HTTP is MCP's transport for remote servers. The client sends each JSON-RPC message as an HTTP POST to one endpoint. The server responds eith

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: Security & the Confused Deputy
text: Here is where most MCP deployments get it wrong, and where Meridian cannot afford to. An MCP server is a bridge between an AI model — which will faithfully do whatever a cleverly-worded input tells it — and your real systems. That is a security boundary, and you defend it like one. A confused deputy is a privileged program tricked into misusing its authority on behalf of a less-privileged party. In MCP: your server holds credentials to the ledger; the model holds none. If the server runs whatever the model asks without checking whose authority applies, an attacker who can influence the model's input (prompt injection) can make the server act with the server's privileges. The fix is the deputy must check authorization for the actual end user , never act on the model's say-so alone. A tool argument is untrusted input — exactly the hostile-by-default posture from the Application Security Baseline. An account id that is really ../../etc/passwd or acct-001; DROP TABLE must be rejected before it touches a path or a query. Whitelist, do not blacklist. The server must answer "is this end user allowed to read this account?" — not "did the model ask nicely?". Carry the user's identity (OAuth

chTitle: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Go
heading: The other confused deputy: the OAuth proxy itself
text: The deputy above is confused at the tool boundary — the model tricks the server into misusing its ledger credentials. There is a second one a layer down, at the auth boundary: the very "OAuth 2.1" the network-surface card told you to bolt on can itself become the confused deputy. This is not hypothetical. It is the Confused Deputy Problem in the MCP security spec, and it has shipped — CVE-2026-27124 (High) was exactly this bug in a widely-used MCP framework's OAuth proxy. Here is the shape. An MCP server rarely runs its own identity provider; it acts as an OAuth proxy in front of a real upstream SSO so a tool can call the third-party API as you . To let clients like Claude Desktop bootstrap without out-of-band setup, the proxy turns on Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) — anyone can POST /register a redirect uri. But the proxy is a single client to the upstream: it holds one fixed client id , and each DCR "registration" is really just a redirect uri stored behind that shared client. The upstream cannot tell the registrations apart — they are all mcp-proxy. So the proxy's own consent check is the only thing standing between a victim's login and an attacker's callback. desc: Keeping copies of your data in sync, explained from zero: why you replicate, single-leader vs multi-leader vs leaderless, replication lag and the stale-read problem, read-your-writes consistency, quorum reads and writes (W + R > N), and resolving conflicting writes with last-writer-wins and version vectors — all grounded in replicating Meridian's account balances.
text: One database holding every Meridian account balance is a beautiful thing right up until the moment that one machine dies — and then the entire company is down, customers can't see their money, and you're the one explaining it. So you keep copies . More than one machine holds the data. That's replication, and it sounds trivial until you realize the copies disagree with each other constantly, and now you have to decide which copy is telling the truth. I'm going to teach you this from absolute zero — no assumed knowledge of databases, distributed systems, or any of the intimidating vocabulary people hide behind. By the end you'll understand exactly why a customer can deposit money and then not see it a second later, why two data centers can both think they're right, and the elegant little inequality (W + R N) that lets a pile of unreliable machines give a reliable answer. We'll replicate Meridian's account balances the whole way through. Let's go.

heading: Why Replicate
text: Let's start with the word itself, no assumptions. Replication means keeping a copy of the same data on more than one machine. Each copy is called a replica . When data changes, every replica needs to find out about the change so the copies stay (roughly) the same. Why it matters: a single machine will fail — hardware breaks, networks drop, someone trips over a cable. Replication is how a system keeps working, and keeps your data alive, when an individual machine doesn't. You replicate for exactly three reasons. That's it — if a "reason" doesn't reduce to one of these, it's not a real reason: If one machine dies, another already has the data and keeps serving. Meridian can lose a database server at 3am and customers never notice. Without replication, one dead disk is a company-wide outage. Reads can be spread across many replicas. If a million customers all check their balance, you don't hammer one machine — you fan the reads out across ten copies. (Writes are harder; we'll see why.) Put a replica in each region. A customer in Lagos reads from a Lagos replica instead of waiting on a round trip to Virginia. Physical distance is real latency; a nearby copy erases it. In the most commo

heading: Single-Leader
text: The workhorse. One leader, N followers. Every write goes to the leader; the leader tells the followers; followers apply the changes in order. This is how Postgres, MySQL, and most SQL databases replicate by default — and it's what sits under the read-replica setup from SQL & Databases in Go. Single-leader replication : one replica (the leader) accepts all writes; it streams an ordered log of those changes to the followers, which replay them. Reads can go to the leader or any follower. Why it matters: because every write passes through one leader in one order, there's never a question of "which write happened first" — the leader decides. That single ordering authority is what makes single-leader the simplest and safest model, and why Meridian's ledger uses it. Here's the write path. Watch where the time goes: When the leader gets a write, it faces a choice: wait for followers to confirm before telling the client "done," or don't wait . Synchronous: the leader waits until at least one follower confirms it has the write, then ACKs the client. Upside: that follower is guaranteed up to date, so if the leader dies, no data is lost. Downside: the client waits for the slowest follower in t

heading: Lag & Stale Reads
text: That 0 the follower returned isn't a bug — it's the defining behavior of replication, and it has a name. Replication lag is the delay between a write being applied on the leader and that change reaching a follower — usually milliseconds, but seconds or worse under load. During that window a follower serves a stale (out-of-date) read. Eventual consistency is the promise that if writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value — but it says nothing about when . Why it matters: "eventual" can mean the customer who just deposited ₦5,000 reloads and sees their old balance, because their read hit a follower that hadn't caught up. Correct, by the rules — and infuriating to that customer. This stale-read window breaks specific, predictable user expectations. Each has a name and a fix: You make a change and immediately want to see it. If your read hits a lagging follower, your own change vanishes. Fix: route a user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write — they always see their own work.
