heading: ACID & Isolation Levels
text: Before a single dollar moves, you need to understand the contract your database is making with you. That contract has four clauses. Every professional knows them cold. ACID is the set of four guarantees a database transaction makes: A tomicity (all operations in the transaction succeed together or none are visible), C onsistency (every transaction takes the database from one valid state to another — your invariants hold before and after every commit), I solation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's in-progress work), and D urability (once a transaction commits, it survives crashes). You care about ACID because without it, concurrent money movement corrupts balances silently — no exception thrown, no error logged.

heading: The four properties
text: A transaction is a group of operations that the database treats as a single unit. You've used them: BEGIN → do work → COMMIT (or ROLLBACK). The database promises four things about that unit: All operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are visible. A transfer that posts a debit and a credit either completes both or neither. No half-posted transfers. Ever. Every transaction must take the database from one valid state to another. Your invariants — like "debits must equal credits" — hold before and after every commit. The DB enforces constraints; you enforce your domain rules in the transaction. Concurrent transactions must not see each other's in-progress work. The degree to which they're shielded is the isolation level. This is the one that bites people in fintech. Once a transaction commits, it's permanent. A crash, a power cut, a cosmic ray — the committed data survives. The write-ahead log (WAL) is how Postgres makes this true. Atomicity and durability are either on or off — you don't configure them. Isolation is a dial.

heading: Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent
text: An isolation level controls how much a transaction can see of concurrent in-progress work from other transactions. The SQL standard defines four levels — Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable — each buying protection against a specific class of anomaly. Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more contention; lower isolation means more concurrency but more subtle bugs. Postgres defaults to Read Committed , which is safe for many workloads but not for concurrent balance updates. The SQL standard defines four isolation levels. Each one buys protection against specific anomalies. Here they are, strongest to weakest: You read a row that a concurrent transaction has modified but not yet committed. If that transaction rolls back, you saw data that never existed. Postgres doesn't allow this at any isolation level. You read a row, a concurrent transaction commits a change to it, you read it again and get a different value. Two reads of the same row in one transaction return different data. You run a query with a WHERE clause, another transaction inserts rows that would match, you run the same query and get more rows. The "phantom" rows appeared between your

heading: The Lost-Update Problem
text: Enough theory. Let's watch the disaster happen in real time. The lost-update problem occurs when two transactions both read the same value, each independently computes a new value based on that read, and both write back — so the second write silently overwrites the first. No error is raised. No constraint is violated. The database happily commits both transactions. In a balance update, this means real money either disappears or gets created from nothing. On the job: At Meridian, POST /transfers is hit by payment processors, mobile clients, and batch jobs simultaneously. Any read-compute-write pattern on accounts.balance cents without a lock is a lost-update waiting to happen — and it only manifests under load, not in unit tests. Two customers are pulling money from the same account simultaneously. Gwendolyn wants to send $30. Marcus wants to send $40. The account has $100. After both transfers succeed, the balance should be $30. Watch what happens without any locking: That's the lost-update problem. In a real system it means real money either disappears or gets created from nothing. No exception is thrown. No error is logged. The database happily committed both transactions. It was

heading: Pessimistic Locking
text: The fix for the lost-update problem at the database level is pessimistic locking: acquire a lock on the row before you read it, hold that lock until you commit. No other transaction can read or write that row while you hold the lock. You're pessimistic — you assume someone will race you, so you prevent it up front. Pessimistic locking means acquiring an exclusive lock on a resource before reading it, holding that lock for the duration of the transaction. In Postgres, the SQL clause is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. It says: "read this row AND lock it — no other transaction may lock or write it until I commit or roll back." You're paying the overhead of lock management on every read, whether or not there's a race. The payoff: zero possibility of a lost update on that row. On the job: Use pessimistic locking on Meridian's account rows any time you do a read-compute-write on balance cents. High-volume accounts (a prize pool, a merchant settlement account) can see hundreds of concurrent transfers — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is the only correct tool there. In Postgres (and most SQL databases), the spell is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. The FOR UPDATE clause does two things: 1. It reads the row and acquire

heading: Optimistic Locking
text: Pessimistic locking is correct, but it serializes all writes to a row. If contention is low — most of the time nobody races you — you're paying the overhead of lock management and blocking for a scenario that rarely happens. Optimistic locking assumes you won't be raced, and detects the collision after the fact instead of preventing it up front. Optimistic locking lets a transaction proceed without acquiring any lock, then checks at commit time whether the data changed under it. The standard implementation adds a version column — an integer that increments on every update. At write time, the UPDATE includes WHERE version = $old version: if zero rows are affected, another transaction won the race and changed the version first. The current transaction retries from scratch. Optimistic locking wins when contention is low (most writes don't race); it degrades into a thundering-herd problem when contention is high. On the job: Optimistic locking is the right choice for Meridian's user profile updates or currency preferences — fields that are rarely written concurrently. It's the wrong choice for balance cents on a high-volume account. The pattern uses a version column : an integer that i

heading: When to choose optimistic vs. pessimistic
text: Contention is high — the same account is hit by many concurrent transfers. A payment processing queue where many workers drain one account. You cannot afford retries (strict latency SLAs). The operation has expensive side effects you don't want to repeat. Contention is low — most transfers hit different accounts. You're writing a distributed system where lock-holding across network calls would be disastrous. Retries are cheap and safe. The happy path (no conflict) must be as fast as possible. Never use optimistic locking for the account balance if your service handles burst traffic on popular accounts (e.g., a prize account hit by 10,000 concurrent claimants). At high contention, every transaction retries repeatedly, and you've turned a locking problem into a thundering-herd problem. Use FOR UPDATE there.

heading: Safe Concurrent Transfers
text: Now we put it all together. A production transfer between two accounts — with both sides locked, a funds check, and the double-entry ledger posted inside the same transaction. But first: deadlocks . A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are each waiting for a lock held by the other, forming a cycle in the wait-for graph. Neither can proceed. Example: TX 1 locks account A then waits for account B; TX 2 has locked account B and is waiting for account A. Postgres detects this within deadlock timeout (default 1 second) and aborts one transaction with ERROR: deadlock detected. The aborted transaction must be retried from scratch. Prevention is better than detection — lock multiple rows in a deterministic order. On the job: Deadlocks between transfers are the most common liveness bug in fintech database code. They're invisible in single-threaded tests and emerge under concurrent load. The fix costs one comparison. If TX 1 locks account A then tries to lock account B, while TX 2 locks account B then tries to lock account A — they deadlock. The fix is a deterministic lock order: always lock accounts in ascending order of their ID, regardless of which is the sender and which is th

heading: Sagas & Compensating Actions
text: ACID transactions are powerful, but they have a hard limit: they work when all the operations you need to make atomically live inside one database . Reality is messier. Consider this Meridian transfer: debit the user's wallet in the ledger service, then credit their external bank account via the ACH network. These are two different systems. You cannot put them in one BEGIN/COMMIT block. If the ACH call succeeds but the ledger service crashes before recording it, or vice versa — you have a split-brain transfer. This is the problem sagas solve. Forward until something breaks, then compensate BACKWARD — the whole shape of a saga in one run: A saga is a sequence of local ACID transactions, one per service or system, each of which commits independently. Instead of one global atomic commit across multiple systems (which is impossible without a distributed coordinator), a saga achieves eventual consistency — with the guarantee that if any step fails, every preceding step is reversed by a compensating action . A saga is not a hack; it's the correct model for multi-system money movement, used in production at every major payments company. On the job: Meridian's cross-bank transfer is a saga

heading: What a saga is
text: A saga is a sequence of local transactions , where each step commits to its own database. Instead of a global atomic commit, you get eventual consistency — with the guarantee that if any step fails, every preceding step is undone by a compensating action . A compensating action (also called a compensating transaction) is a new, committed database transaction that reverses the business effect of a previously committed step. It is NOT a ROLLBACK — that would make the change invisible. A compensation is a new ledger entry that is permanently visible in the audit log. Example: a debit of $200 is compensated by a credit of $200 — both appear in the ledger, and together they net to zero. This is mandatory for regulated financial systems: auditors need to see what happened and that it was corrected, not a sanitized view where the failure never occurred. heading: Orchestration vs. choreography
text: Orchestration uses a central saga orchestrator — a dedicated service or state machine — that knows the full step sequence, calls each step, and triggers compensating actions on failure. The orchestrator is the single source of truth for saga state. Choreography uses no central coordinator: each service publishes events ("DebitSucceeded") and subscribes to events from others ("ACHFailed"), and the saga emerges from the event flow. Orchestration is easier to reason about and observe; choreography is more decoupled but harder to trace. For money movement at Meridian, prefer orchestration — a money transfer needs a clear, auditable state machine. On the job: Choreography sounds elegant until you have to debug a half-executed saga in production at 2am. An orchestrated saga has a saga state table — you can query it. A choreographed saga's state is implicit in a dozen event handlers across five services. A central saga orchestrator (a dedicated service or state machine) knows the full sequence. It calls step 1, waits for success, calls step 2, and so on. If any step fails, it calls the compensating actions in reverse order. The orchestrator is the single source of truth for saga state. Ea

heading: Combining the saga with the transactional outbox
text: There's a subtle bug lurking in a naive saga implementation: what if the orchestrator successfully calls DebitSender but crashes before it can record that step 1 succeeded and trigger step 2? On restart, does it retry step 1 (double-debit!) or skip it (inconsistent)? The answer is the transactional outbox — covered in depth in the Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics chapter. The short version: every state transition in the saga is written to an outbox table inside the same local ACID transaction as the saga state update. A separate outbox relay process reads unprocessed outbox records and fires the next saga step (or the compensating action) reliably — with at-least-once delivery and idempotent handlers. If the orchestrator crashes, the relay picks up where it left off, using the outbox as a durable work queue. A database ROLLBACK is invisible: it undoes changes as if they never happened, and nothing appears in the audit log. A saga compensation is the opposite: it is a committed transaction that explicitly reverses a business effect, and both the original action and the compensation are permanently visible in your ledger. desc: Idempotency keys, deduplication, at-least-once vs exactly-once, safe payment retries, and the transactional outbox pattern.
text: Listen up, sport — because what I'm about to teach you is the difference between a payment system that works and one that silently double-charges customers at 3am while your on-call engineer stares at a dashboard in horror. Here's the thing: networks lie. Clients retry. Servers crash mid-write and come back up not knowing if they succeeded. In this environment, "just don't send the request twice" is not a strategy — it's a wish. What you need is a system that can receive the same request a hundred times and produce exactly the outcome it would have produced once. That property has a name: idempotency . And it's not optional in fintech. It's the floor. By the end of this chapter you will understand idempotency keys, deduplication, the honest truth about exactly-once semantics, safe retry patterns, and the transactional outbox — the pattern that keeps your database and your message broker from ever disagreeing about what happened. I built systems like this. You're about to learn how. Pay attention.

heading: Why idempotency matters
text: The scene that motivates this whole chapter — one webhook, delivered three times: An operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times produces the same result as applying it once. A payment "charge $149.99 for order 4201" must be idempotent: if the client retries after a timeout, Meridian charges once , not twice. We need idempotency because networks retry, and a retried charge that is not idempotent creates money out of nothing — it is a bug that shows up in production under load, not in unit tests. On the job: you hit idempotency the moment any client can retry a mutating call — mobile apps, service-to-service RPCs, background workers, webhook processors. Every POST /v1/charges at Meridian must be idempotent. Every event consumer must be idempotent. Getting it wrong means duplicate charges, double-booked transfers, and a support queue that grows faster than your team. Let me set the scene with the exact scenario that wakes fintech engineers up at night. A customer clicks "Pay Now" for a $149.99 subscription. Meridian's mobile client sends a POST /v1/charges to the payment API. The request crosses the Atlantic, the server processes the charge, deducts the balance, writes the

heading: Idempotency keys
text: An idempotency key is a unique token that the client generates once per logical operation — not per HTTP request. The client sends it with every attempt, including retries. The server stores the mapping from key → result. On a repeated key, the server returns the stored result without re-executing the operation. The key is usually a UUID v4 or ULID. It must be unique per logical operation — not per session and not per user. On the job: Stripe, Adyen, and every mature payments API require an Idempotency-Key header on all mutating calls. If you forget to send one, retries become double charges. If you regenerate the key on retry (a common bug), idempotency is silently defeated. An idempotency key is a unique token the client generates for each logical operation — not each HTTP request. The client sends the key with every request, including retries. The server stores the mapping from key to result. On a repeated key, the server returns the stored result without re-executing the operation. The lifecycle of an idempotency key has three states: 1. In-flight — the key has been seen but the operation has not finished yet. 2. Completed — the operation finished; the result is stored and will

heading: Claiming a key atomically — the race condition
text: Here is where amateurs get it wrong. What happens when two copies of the same retry arrive simultaneously — say, a client is using HTTP/2 and fires two parallel attempts? You cannot let both of them race to process the charge. The solution is a unique constraint on the idempotency key column and an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT clause. This is the database's atomic test-and-set. Only one insert wins; the loser finds the row already exists and knows it must wait for the winner to finish, then return the stored result. ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING is atomic at the database level — it cannot race with another identical insert. The unique index on key guarantees only one insert succeeds. This is not application-level locking; it is a hard database guarantee. If the process crashes between Claim and Complete, the key is stuck as an empty placeholder. On restart, the key entry is gone and a new request could re-execute the charge. The database-backed version is durable and atomic in a deeper

heading: The concurrent race test — a mandatory Meridian verification
text: The most important test for an idempotency system is not a sequential one. It is a concurrent one: fire N identical requests simultaneously and verify that exactly one charge occurs. Run this with -race always. If there is a data race in your idempotency logic, the race detector will find it. This test must be green before any payment handler ships.

heading: Deduplication
text: Deduplication is the practice of detecting and discarding duplicate messages or events before they can be processed twice. Where an idempotency key is client-supplied (your own mobile app, your own service), a natural dedup key comes from the event payload itself — the card network's authorization ID, a bank's ACH trace number, a webhook's event id. Both strategies use the same underlying primitive: an atomic insert into a table with a unique constraint. On the job: dedup keys matter most at event consumer boundaries. A payment processor (Stripe, Adyen) delivers webhooks at-least-once — your consumer will receive the same payment intent.succeeded event more than once during network blips and retries. Without deduplication, you credit the customer twice. Idempotency keys work when clients cooperate — they generate and send the key. But what about deduplication at the message or event level, where the producer may be a third-party system or a broker delivering events at-least-once? Message-level deduplication uses a different strategy: you build a dedup table that records which messages you have already processed, keyed by a natural key — an identifier that comes from the event paylo

heading: At-least-once vs exactly-once
text: These are the three delivery guarantees a messaging system can offer: At-most-once : fire and forget — the message may never arrive. No retries. Used where loss is acceptable (telemetry, UDP). At-least-once : the message will arrive, but may arrive more than once . The sender retries until it gets an acknowledgement. This is the standard for reliable systems — Kafka, SQS, most webhook implementations. Exactly-once delivery : the message arrives exactly once, never duplicated, never lost. Theoretically impossible in an asynchronous distributed system (see the Two Generals Problem and FLP impossibility). What brokers call "exactly-once" is always at-least-once + a dedup layer. Exactly-once processing — also called effectively-once — is the achievable goal: at-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent handler. The broker may deliver the message twice; the handler detects the duplicate (via a dedup table or idempotency key) and makes the second delivery a no-op. The effect on your system is as if the message was processed exactly once. On the job: "we need exactly-once delivery" is a common requirement in payments. The correct response is: "we implement at-least-once delivery wit

heading: Safe payment retries
text: Retries without idempotency are dangerous. Retries with idempotency plus proper backoff are the standard for resilient payment systems. The retry strategy for payment API calls combines three things: 1. Idempotency key — same key on every retry, so the server can absorb duplicates. 2. Exponential backoff — wait longer after each failure to avoid hammering a struggling upstream. 3. Jitter — randomize the backoff slightly so a fleet of clients does not retry in lockstep (the "thundering herd"). The canonical backoff formula: sleep = base 2^attempt + random jitter. Not every error is retryable. A 400 Bad Request (invalid card number) is permanent — retrying it will not fix it. A 500 Internal Server Error or a network timeout is transient — worth retrying. Your retry logic should inspect the error type and only back off on transient failures. Retrying a permanent error wastes time and burns your idempotency key's retry window. As of Go 1.26, errors.AsType[T] provides a generic helper for unwrapping typed errors — useful when your payment processor client returns a typed APIError carrying a status code, letting you branch on transient vs permanent without a manual type assertion. heading: The transactional outbox
text: The dual-write problem occurs when you need to update two separate systems atomically — typically a database and a message broker — but have no distributed transaction spanning both. If the process crashes between the two writes, one system is updated and the other is not: either the event is lost (DB committed, broker publish never happened) or a phantom event exists (broker published, DB rolled back). There is no network call that can make two independent systems commit together without a coordinator. The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem without a distributed transaction. Instead of writing directly to the message broker, you write the event to an outbox table inside the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay process reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, then marks them sent. The DB transaction guarantees atomicity between the business write and the outbox write. The relay delivers at-least-once (it may publish twice if it crashes between publish and mark-sent), but your consumers are idempotent — so that is fine. On the job: every Meridian transfer that must notify a downstream service (fraud check, notif

heading: The dual-write problem in detail
text: The problem: you are processing a payment transfer at Meridian. You need to: 1. Write the transfer record and update balances in PostgreSQL. 2. Publish a TransferCompleted event to Kafka so downstream services (notifications, analytics, fraud-check) can react. The naive approach: write to Postgres, then publish to Kafka. What could go wrong? What if you reverse the order — publish to Kafka first, then write to Postgres? If Kafka succeeds, but the PostgreSQL write fails (e.g. a unique constraint violation on account limits or database connection pool exhaustion), downstream services receive an event for a transfer that never actually happened in the database . That is a phantom event , and downstream microservices may ship goods or credit rewards for money that was never moved. Why not use a distributed transaction (Two-Phase Commit / XA)? 2PC requires a central transaction coordinator that holds locks across network boundaries across all participants. Modern message brokers like Apache Kafka and AWS SQS do not support XA protocols with relational databases. Furthermore, 2PC is notoriously slow, brittle, and introduces a single point of failure that stalls if any node becomes unreac

heading: Writing domain state + outbox event in a single ACID transaction
text: The solution: write the domain state mutation AND the event into an outbox events table within the exact same database transaction . Either both commit together, or both roll back together. heading: Relaying outbox events: polling vs Change Data Capture (CDC)
text: Once the event row is durably stored in PostgreSQL, how does it get published to Kafka? There are two primary relay architectures: 1. The Polling Relay with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED A background Go worker periodically queries the outbox table for unsent rows, publishes them to Kafka, and updates sent = TRUE. To support multiple relay workers running in parallel without stepping on each other, PostgreSQL provides FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Each worker locks a batch of rows; any other worker running concurrently skips those locked rows and immediately grabs the next available batch without waiting or deadlocking. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is a PostgreSQL locking hint that makes running multiple relay workers safe and horizontally scalable. When relay worker A locks a batch of outbox rows with FOR UPDATE, any concurrent worker B that queries the same rows will SKIP them (not block) and process a different batch. Without SKIP LOCKED, multiple relay workers would serialize on the same rows, negating the benefit of horizontal scaling. With it, each worker grabs a non-overlapping slice of unsent rows and works in parallel. The rows are never processed twice by two different relay workers i

heading: Guaranteed at-least-once publishing to Kafka
text: The Transactional Outbox guarantees at-least-once delivery from your database to Kafka: 1. The domain mutation and outbox row are committed atomically. 2. The relay worker (or CDC engine) reads the row and publishes it to Kafka with acks=all (ensuring Kafka replicates the message across in-sync replicas before returning success). 3. The relay marks sent = TRUE in the database. If the relay worker crashes after step 2 (Kafka received the event) but before step 3 (database marked as sent), the relay restarts, re-reads the un-marked row, and publishes the event to Kafka a second time. Because network retries and relay restarts can produce duplicate events on Kafka topics, the producer side is complete only when paired with idempotent consumers on the receiving side. event never published. err = kafka.Publish(ctx, event) if err != nil } good= /

heading: Idempotent consumer & inbox pattern
text: The transactional inbox pattern is the consumer-side counterpart to the transactional outbox. When consuming messages from an at-least-once message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS), the consumer records incoming event IDs in an inbox events table inside the same database transaction that applies the business logic. If a redelivered message arrives, the unique constraint on the event ID detects the duplicate and causes the handler to skip business logic execution while safely acknowledging the message to the broker. An idempotent consumer is a message consumer designed such that receiving the same message multiple times produces the exact same outcome as receiving it once, without duplicate side-effects. This is achieved through natural deduplication keys, unique constraints, or the transactional inbox pattern. On the job: message brokers only guarantee at-least-once delivery. If your consumer crashes after executing a database write but before committing its Kafka offset, Kafka redelivers the message on restart. Without an inbox pattern, your consumer executes the transfer a second time.

heading: The consumer-side dual-write dilemma
text: Just as producers face a dual-write problem when writing to PostgreSQL and publishing to Kafka, consumers face a dual-write dilemma when processing an event: 1. Apply the state change to the consumer database (e.g. credit account balance, send notification). 2. Commit the message offset to Kafka (CommitOffsets or session.MarkMessage). Consider the failure modes: Commit offset AFTER database write: The consumer processes the message, updates the database, and is about to commit the offset to Kafka. Suddenly, the container is killed (pod restart, OOM, deployment). The offset was never committed. When the consumer comes back up, Kafka redelivers the message. The consumer executes the database write again . Result: duplicate payment credit. Commit offset BEFORE database write: The consumer commits the offset to Kafka first, then attempts to update the database. If the database write fails or the process crashes mid-write, the message is permanently marked as processed in Kafka, but the database change was never applied. Result: message loss (at-most-once disaster).

heading: Dead Letter Queues (DLQs) for poison pills
text: What happens when an event has malformed JSON or triggers an unrecoverable business error (e.g. references an account ID that was permanently deleted)? If the consumer simply errors and rolls back, Kafka will redeliver the message repeatedly, causing an infinite retry loop that blocks the entire partition. This is a poison pill . The solution is a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) strategy: 1. Catch unrecoverable errors (e.g. deserialization errors or permanent invariant failures). 2. Write the failing event and error reason into an inbox dead letters table or publish to a transfers.dlq Kafka topic. 3. Mark the inbox status as 'failed'. 4. Commit the Kafka offset so consumer progress resumes on subsequent healthy messages. 5. Fire an alert for on-call engineers to inspect and replay the DLQ message once investigated. desc: The broker-agnostic mental model: queues vs topics, producers/consumers, push vs pull, delivery guarantees, ordering, acks and dead-letter queues.
text: Listen up, sport. You've got a payment service that fires off a payment.completed event — and your ledger service, your notifications service, and your analytics pipeline all need to hear about it right now . The naive move? Call all three directly, in sequence, from inside the payment handler. Then one of them is slow. Or down. Suddenly a perfectly good payment is timing out, or worse, half your side effects ran and half didn't. That's not a system. That's a house of cards in a hurricane. A message broker exists specifically to save you from that fate. By the end of this chapter you'll understand exactly how it does that — queues, topics, delivery guarantees, acknowledgements, dead-letter queues, and back-pressure — without needing to name a single vendor. These are the concepts Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, and every other broker are built on. Learn the foundation here, and those tools become obvious. You're exceptionally lucky I'm the one teaching you this.

heading: What a Broker Is
text: Let's nail the problem before we build the solution. Here's the scene: Your payments service just settled a payment.completed event for order ORD-7823. Three things need to happen: 1. The ledger service posts the double-entry accounting lines. 2. The notification service emails the customer. 3. The analytics pipeline records the conversion. The synchronous version — calling each service directly from the payment handler — looks like this: That err chain is a lie dressed as safety. If notifier.Send is down for a rolling deploy, you've got ledger entries with no notifications. If analytics.Record times out at 2 a.m., you've got a partially applied side-effect set with no idempotency key to replay safely. You've tightly coupled three independent services behind a single synchronous call chain. On the job: You hit this pattern the moment your payment handler has more than one downstream side effect. The failure mode — partial execution with no clean retry path — is one of the most expensive bugs to debug in production, because the ledger and the notification system are now out of sync with no record of why. A message broker is an intermediary that accepts messages from producers and de

heading: Queues vs Topics
text: Here's where most developers get confused. A broker can operate in two fundamentally different modes, and knowing which one you want is the difference between a system that works and one that loses data silently. A queue is a point-to-point channel where each message is delivered to exactly one consumer from a competing pool. Multiple workers read from the same queue; each message goes to whichever worker has capacity. Use a queue when you want to distribute work across a pool — receipt emails, report generation, image resizing — and each job should be done once, not N times. A topic is a publish/subscribe channel where each message is delivered to every subscriber independently . Each subscriber gets its own copy; the broker tracks each subscriber's progress separately. Use a topic when multiple independent downstream services all need the same event — a payment.completed event that ledger, notifications, and analytics all need to handle. Fan-out is what a topic does: one published message is copied and delivered to every subscriber. It's the messaging equivalent of broadcasting — the producer sends once, N consumers each receive once. Contrast with a queue, where one message goes

heading: The Work Queue: one message, one worker
text: In a work queue (also called a point-to-point queue), a message is consumed by exactly one worker . You have multiple workers competing for messages; each message goes to one of them. This is load distribution. Picture Meridian's receipt-email job queue. You enqueue one job per completed payment. You run three worker pods. Each job gets picked up by whichever pod has capacity — you don't want all three workers processing the same email.

heading: The Topic: one message, every subscriber
text: In a topic (publish/subscribe), a message is delivered to every subscriber independently . This is fan-out. Back to Meridian's payment.completed event: ledger, notifications, and analytics all need it. They're independent subscribers on the same topic. Each gets their own copy of the message.

heading: Queue vs Topic side by side
text: One message → one consumer. Used when you want to distribute work across a pool (receipt emails, image resizing, report generation). Adding workers scales throughput. One message → all subscribers. Used when multiple independent systems need the same event (payment events going to ledger + notifier + analytics). You care about one worker owning each delivery attempt. Pair it with acking, retries, and idempotency when the job must survive crashes. Multiple independent downstream services need the same information. The producer shouldn't know or care who they are. Some brokers blur the line — Kafka topics with consumer groups give you queue semantics within a group and fan-out across groups. The mental model still holds: within a group it's work-queue distribution; across groups it's fan-out. Get this chapter's model right and Kafka makes immediate sense.

heading: Producers, Consumers & Delivery
text: Now let's name the actors cleanly. A producer is any service or process that sends messages to the broker. A consumer (or subscriber) is any service or process that reads messages from the broker. These roles are asymmetric by design — the producer needs to know the destination (topic name or queue name); the consumer only needs to know what it wants to read. The payment service is a producer; the ledger service, the notification service, and the analytics pipeline are each consumers. A producer is anything that sends messages to the broker. A consumer (or subscriber) is anything that reads them. These roles are asymmetric by design — the producer needs to know the destination (topic name or queue name); the consumer only needs to know what it wants to read.

heading: Push vs. Pull
text: Push delivery : the broker sends messages to consumers as soon as they arrive — the broker initiates. Low latency, but the broker needs to track consumer state and risks overwhelming a slow consumer with more messages than it can handle. Pull delivery : the consumer polls the broker when it is ready for more messages — the consumer initiates. The consumer controls its own ingestion rate, which naturally provides back-pressure. Kafka, SQS, and most high-throughput production systems use pull. On the job: Push vs pull is not just a configuration choice — it determines who owns the flow-control signal. In a push system, a slow consumer that can't keep up either drops messages or crashes under load. In a pull system, the slow consumer simply stops pulling; the broker buffers and the system degrades gracefully. For Meridian's ledger consumer — which involves a DB write on every event — pull is the right default. There are two ways a message gets from broker to consumer: Push : the broker sends messages to consumers as soon as they arrive. Low latency, but the broker needs to track consumer state and risks overwhelming a slow consumer. Pull : the consumer polls the broker when it's ready

heading: Delivery Guarantees
text: Now for the part that bites every system at scale. When you publish a message, what promise does the broker make about whether (and how many times) a consumer processes it? On the job: Delivery guarantee mismatches are silent killers. A team that thinks they're running at-least-once but accidentally configured at-most-once will lose financial events with no error, no alert, and no stack trace. Define the guarantee explicitly in your service contracts. There are three tiers: The producer sends the message and moves on. No retry. If the network drops, if the broker crashes, if the consumer dies mid-processing — the message is gone . No duplicate risk, but possibly no delivery either. Appropriate for metrics, telemetry, and health pings where a missed sample is acceptable. Never appropriate for financial events. The broker retains the message until the consumer acknowledges it. If the consumer crashes before acknowledging, the broker redelivers. The consumer may process the same message more than once. This is the correct default for financial events — paired with idempotent consumers (see Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics), it becomes safe. The cost of redelivery is paid; the cost

heading: At-most-once (fire and forget)
text: The producer sends the message and moves on. No retry. If the network blips, if the broker crashes, if the consumer dies before processing — the message is gone . No duplicate. But possibly no delivery either. Use case: metrics, telemetry, system-health pings where a missed sample is fine. Never use this for financial events.

heading: At-least-once (the workhorse)
text: The broker retains the message until the consumer acknowledges it. If the consumer crashes before acking, the broker redelivers. The consumer may process the same message more than once. This is the default for most production systems. The trade-off: you must make your consumers idempotent — processing the same message twice must produce the same result as processing it once. We covered exactly how to do this with idempotency keys in Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics. The two chapters are designed to work together.

heading: Exactly-once (expensive and conditional)
text: The effect happens exactly once, with duplicates suppressed and losses avoided. In theory. In practice, true end-to-end exactly-once effects require coordination between the broker, the consumer, and its downstream store — it's expensive, limits throughput, and often depends on broker-specific features (Kafka's idempotent producer + transactional API, for example). In fintech, the pragmatic answer is " effectively exactly-once ": use at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers. You may receive a message twice; you handle it as if it arrived once. This is the pattern the industry uses — the outbox pattern from the previous chapter is exactly this. Send and forget. May lose messages. Zero duplicate risk. Fine for metrics; catastrophic for payments. Broker retains until acked. May redeliver. Consumers MUST be idempotent. The correct default for financial events. No loss, no duplicates. Expensive and broker-specific. In practice, implemented as at-least-once + idempotent consumers ("effectively once"). Never use at-most-once for any financial event. A missing payment.completed means the ledger never posts. "It probably got there" is not an auditing strategy.

heading: Ordering & Acknowledgements
text: Two more pieces of the mental model that trip up engineers in production. An acknowledgement (ack) is the signal a consumer sends to the broker to say "I have finished processing this message and the result is durable." Only after receiving an ack does the broker discard the message. A negative acknowledgement (nack) tells the broker "I failed to process this — redeliver it." The timing of the ack is critical: ack on receipt (before processing) means a crash during processing silently loses the work. Ack after the commit to durable storage is the correct pattern. On the job: The single most common ack bug is acking on receipt — the moment the message arrives in your process, before you've done anything with it. It looks harmless; it's catastrophic under failure. Add a code review checklist item: "Where does this consumer ack? Is it after the DB commit?"

heading: What an ack really means
text: The naive implementation acks a message when it's received — the moment it lands in the consumer's process. That's wrong. An ack must mean " I have finished processing this message and the result is durable. " If you ack on receipt and then crash while writing to the database, the broker thinks you're done. It discards the message. The work was never done. You've silently lost a financial event. Ack after processing. Ack after the commit. Not before.

heading: Ordering guarantees
text: Global ordering across all producers and all consumers is extraordinarily expensive — it requires a single sequential bottleneck. Most brokers don't provide it. What they do provide is per-partition or per-queue ordering. Within one partition, messages from one producer arrive at consumers in the order they were sent. Across partitions, all bets are off. For fintech, this usually means: use a partition key tied to the entity being modified (e.g., account ID). All events for account ACC-42 go to the same partition, so they're processed in order. Events for different accounts can be processed in parallel across partitions. Here's the precise mechanism. When a broker delivers a message, it starts an ack timer (the visibility timeout in SQS, the ack deadline in Pub/Sub, the session timeout in Kafka). During this window the message is invisible to other consumers — it's been handed off to one. If the consumer acks within the window: the broker discards the message. Done. If the consumer does NOT ack within the window (crash, timeout, slow processing): the broker's timer fires. The message becomes visible again and is redelivered to another consumer (or the same one, recovered). This is

heading: Dead-Letter Queues & Back-pressure
text: Two more production essentials that every system eventually needs. A dead-letter queue is a separate queue where messages are routed after they have exceeded their maximum retry count. Instead of retrying a failing message forever (blocking everything behind it) or silently discarding it, the broker moves it to the DLQ. Operations teams can then inspect it, diagnose the root cause, fix the underlying issue, and replay the message — or discard it with an audit trail. Without a DLQ, one malformed message (a poison message) can halt an entire consumer indefinitely. Backpressure is the mechanism by which a consumer signals upstream producers to slow down when it cannot keep up. Without backpressure, producers publish faster than consumers can process, messages pile up, and the broker's buffer — memory or disk — fills until something crashes. In Go, a buffered channel is a built-in backpressure mechanism: once full, sends block and the producer stalls naturally. Real brokers implement backpressure through fetch-size limits, consumer-lag monitoring, and flow-control protocols. On the job: DLQs and backpressure are the two features teams skip when they're moving fast — and the two they be

heading: Dead-letter queues (DLQs)
text: What happens when a message fails processing not because of a transient glitch, but because it's genuinely bad — a malformed payload, a missing field, a downstream service that rejects it every single time? Without a DLQ, that message retries forever, clogging the queue for every other message behind it. That's called a poison message , and it will bring your consumer to its knees. A dead-letter queue is where messages go after they've exceeded their retry limit (max delivery attempts). Instead of retrying forever or discarding, the broker routes the message to a separate DLQ. There, ops teams can inspect it, fix the underlying issue, and replay it — or discard it with an audit trail.

heading: Back-pressure
text: What happens when producers are publishing faster than consumers can process? Messages pile up. Memory fills. The broker's disk fills. Consumers start lagging further and further behind. Backpressure is the mechanism that signals upstream — "slow down, I'm full." Without it, the buffer grows unbounded until something crashes. In Go, a buffered channel is a built-in backpressure mechanism. Once it's full, the send blocks. The producer stalls. That's backpressure — the consumer's capacity limits the producer. Real brokers implement back-pressure through fetch size limits (consumers request N messages at a time), consumer lag monitoring, and flow control protocols. The mental model — "consumer capacity limits producer rate" — is the same whether the backpressure signal travels through a buffered channel or a Kafka consumer-group lag metric. Messages that fail processing after max retries are routed here instead of retrying forever. Enables inspection, debugging, and replay without blocking the main queue. chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
desc: Before you reach for a broker: an in-process, type-safe pub/sub event bus built from channels, generics and reflection — the actor model, total event ordering, and backpressure — grounded in decoupling Meridian's modules and read against Tailscale's production util/eventbus.
text: Listen up, sport. Last chapter I handed you the whole broker-agnostic mental model — topics, fan-out, acks, backpressure — and you earned it. But here's the thing nobody tells you before they sell you a Kafka cluster: you might not need a network at all. Meridian isn't six services yet. Right now it's one binary : the transfers module, the ledger module, the notifications module, the fraud module — all running in the same process, sharing the same memory. And they're calling each other directly, which means they're welded together. Change one, recompile all. One slow module stalls the request. That's not architecture, that's a single point of seizure. An in-process event bus breaks that weld without a broker, without a network hop, without serialization. Same publish/subscribe model you just learned — but the "wire" is a Go channel and the "message" is a struct that never leaves the heap. Tailscale runs exactly this pattern in production to keep their daemon's subsystems from strangling each other, and by the end of this chapter you'll have built it yourself, from channels up through generics and reflection, and then read theirs and understood every line. I've decoupled bigger syst

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: The Coupling Problem
text: Let's see the weld before we cut it. Meridian's monolith settles a transfer. The instant POST /transfers commits, four things must happen: the ledger posts the double-entry lines, the notifier emails a receipt, the fraud module updates its rolling risk score, and the analytics module records the conversion. Today the transfers handler just... calls all four. Look at what this Handler now knows . It imports ledger, notifier, fraud, and analytics. It knows the order they run in. It knows their method names. Add a fifth consumer — a webhook dispatcher — and you edit this function and recompile the transfers module to teach it about a module it has no business knowing. That is the definition of tight coupling : a change there forces a change here . On the job: you hit this the moment a second module cares about something the first module did. The transfers handler should know how to move money. The instant it also has to know who's watching it move money, every new feature becomes a surgery on the hottest code path you own — and a slow notifier turns a successful transfer into a timed-out request. An event bus is an in-process publish/subscribe mediator. A component publishes a typed e

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: A Naive Channel Bus
text: Let's build the simplest thing that works, then watch it fail in an instructive way. You already know channels are Go's in-process pipe. So the crudest possible bus is: keep a slice of subscriber channels; to publish, send the value to each one. Here it is, carrying Meridian's TransferCompleted event to a ledger listener and a notifier listener. That works. It decouples transfers from ledger and notifier — exactly what we wanted. So what's wrong with it? It carries one type. The day the fraud module wants to hear about AccountFrozen, and the analytics module wants LimitRaised, you are writing AccountFrozenBus and LimitRaisedBus, each an identical copy-paste with the type swapped. A bus per event type is not a bus — it's a parking lot full of one-seat cars. We want one bus that any module can publish any event type onto, and subscribers pick out only the types they asked for. Two instincts are both half-right, and seeing why each fails is the whole lesson: One bus, one chan any, send anything. But now every subscriber receives every event and must type-assert each one in a giant switch — and the bus has thrown away which channel wants which type. We lost routing. Bus[T] is type-safe

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Typed Edges with Generics
text: Here's the design in one sentence: the caller only ever touches Publisher[T] and Subscriber[T]; inside, everything is boxed to any and routed by reflect.Type. Start with the typed facades. A Publisher[T] is a thin wrapper that knows its event type T and forwards values into the untyped bus. A Subscriber[T] is a thin wrapper that pulls untyped values out and asserts them back to T before the caller sees them. The type safety lives entirely at these two edges. Notice what the caller sees: p.Emit(TransferCompleted ) won't compile if you hand it an AccountFrozen. for ev := range sub.Events() gives you a TransferCompleted, statically — no assertion, no , ok, no switch. The generics buy compile-time safety at the call site . The reflection we're about to add buys runtime routing in the core . Neither could do the other's job.

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Routing by Type
text: Now the core. The bus keeps a map from event type to the list of subscriber channels that want that type. The key is a reflect.Type — Go's runtime handle for "the type TransferCompleted," usable as a comparable map key. One bus. Two event types. Each event reaches only its type's subscriber, with full static typing at both ends. That's the whole trick — and it's the architecture Tailscale ships. Three mechanics make this work, and each has a price worth knowing. 1. Boxing into any. When Emit passes v T to publish(v any), Go puts v into an interface value: a two-word pair (type-pointer, data-pointer). The type-pointer references the runtime. type for TransferCompleted; the data-pointer references the value (heap-allocated if it escapes, which here it does because it flows through a channel into another goroutine). So each published event is one small interface header plus, usually, one heap allocation for the value. That's the cost of erasing the static type — and it's why a hot path that fires millions of events still measures this. 2. reflect.Type as a map key. reflect.TypeOf(v) reads the type-pointer straight out of that interface header — it's nearly free, just a field read. The

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Backpressure & the Pump
text: Our teaching bus has a hidden flaw, and it's the same one every real bus must answer: what happens when a subscriber is slow? In our publish, the fan-out loop does ch Backpressure is the resistance a slow consumer exerts back on its producer. When a subscriber can't keep up, its buffer fills; once full, the producer must either block (wait — preserving every event, at the cost of slowing the producer), drop (discard events — protecting the producer's speed, at the cost of losing data), or grow an unbounded buffer (preserve everything and stay fast — at the cost of unbounded memory, i.e. an eventual OOM). There is no fourth option; every event bus picks among these three, and the choice is the design. The naive answer — make every channel buffer enormous, or unbounded — just trades a stall for an out-of-memory crash under sustained load. The production answer is a single dispatch goroutine (call it the pump ) with a bounded internal queue, that imposes a clear ordering and a predictable backpressure point. One goroutine owns the timeline: it reads published events one at a time and hands each to the right subscribers. Because one goroutine sequences everything, you get a property th

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: The Actor Model
text: Step back from channels for a second, because the bus is really a vehicle for a design discipline , and that discipline has a name. The actor model structures a program as independent actors , each owning its own private state, that never touch each other's memory. An actor changes the world in exactly two ways: it emits messages, and it reacts to messages it receives. There is no shared mutable state to lock, because there is no sharing — coordination happens entirely through message passing. An event bus is the message-passing substrate; each subscribing module is an actor. Tailscale's bus documentation says it plainly: structure each component to hold authority over its own state and interact with everything else only by emitting and receiving events. The ledger module owns the ledger. Nobody reaches into it; they publish facts, and it decides what to do. The fraud module owns its risk scores. Nobody mutates them; they publish TransferCompleted and fraud updates itself . This is why the bus guarantees a total order ("one true timeline," in their docs): if every actor only reacts to a single, agreed sequence of events, then every actor sees the same history, and the system as a w

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Why So Many Parts
text: Here's the honest thing about reading util/eventbus cold: it looks like overkill . There's a Bus, a Client, a subscribeState, a subscriber interface, a Subscriber[T], a subscriberCore, a SubscriberFunc[T], a PublishedEvent, a DeliveredEvent, and a tangle of methods named dispatch, dispatchFunc, and dispatchTyped that call each other . The natural reaction is "why on earth does an event bus need ten types?" The answer is the best kind of lesson Go has to offer: every one of those parts exists to fix a specific problem the previous version created. Nobody designed this all at once. It grew, one forced move at a time. So let's grow it the same way — start from the naive bus you already built, and at each step, break it, see exactly why it breaks, and add the one part that fixes it. By the end, all ten types will feel not just sensible but inevitable . We'll keep using Meridian's two event types — TransferCompleted and AccountFrozen — as our stand-ins for any two unrelated events on one bus.

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 1 → the pump: ordering across publishers
text: You already met this in "Backpressure & the Pump," but now it's the first domino , so look again. In the naive bus, publish itself walks the subscriber slice and sends. So if the transfers goroutine and the fraud goroutine both publish at the same instant, each is running publish independently, sending to subscribers at its own pace. A subscriber listening to both types can see them interleaved in any order — and worse, two different subscribers can disagree on the order. For a stream of money events, "no agreed order" is a non-starter. The fix is the single pump goroutine: publishers stop sending directly and instead drop their event into one channel; one goroutine drains that channel and does all the delivery. Because one goroutine decides "next," there is now exactly one order — the "one true timeline."

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 2 → non-generic wrappers: the pump can't type-assert
text: Now the move that shapes everything else , and the single most important idea in this whole codebase. Watch what happens when we try to write the delivery step inside pump. To deliver, the pump must take the boxed any event and send it on a subscriber's typed channel — which means it must do the assertion evt.(TransferCompleted). But to write evt.(T), the code needs T in scope. And here's the wall: A type parameter like the T in func SubscribeT any exists only inside that generic function or method . A plain, non-generic function has no T — there is no type variable for it to name. So you can box a value into any anywhere, but you can only un box it with v.(T) somewhere that T is a visible type parameter. This is the constraint the entire bus is built around. The pump is a method on Bus. Bus is not generic — it has to hold subscribers of many event types at once, so it can't carry a single T. Therefore the pump has no T, therefore it cannot write evt.(T). The code simply won't compile. So the type assertion cannot happen in the bus . It can only happen back out at the edges, inside a generic function where T is in scope. Every awkward-looking part that follows is a consequence of s

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 3 → the Client: ordering across subscriptions
text: We fixed ordering across publishers with one pump. But if every call to Subscribe spins up its own subscribeState with its own goroutine, then a component that subscribes to both TransferCompleted and AccountFrozen has two independent goroutines pulling events — and they can fall out of order relative to each other again. The "one true timeline" leaks at the subscription boundary. The fix is the Client: a named handle that owns one subscribeState and therefore one dispatch goroutine, no matter how many event types it subscribes to. All of that client's subscriptions are served by that single goroutine, so they're delivered in the one true order. This is also why Bus.Client(name) wants a human name: it's the unit of "an actor," and the name shows up in the debugger so you can see which subsystem is behind a slow subscriber. To make the non-generic subscribeState able to call the generic Subscriber[T] it routes to, we need a contract between them that doesn't mention T. That's the subscriber interface : An interface is a set of method signatures; any type implementing those methods satisfies it, and you can hold it in a variable whose static type is the interface — without knowing th

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 4 → the queue + multi-way select: a slow subscriber can't stall the pump
text: The subscribeState delivers to a Subscriber[T] over a single channel. If that subscriber is slow and its channel fills, the send blocks — which blocks the subscribeState's goroutine, which blocks the bus pump feeding it, which blocks every publisher. One sluggish handler freezes the whole bus. The fix is to never let the delivering loop get stuck. The dispatch loop runs a multi-way select : one case tries to send the current event to the subscriber; another case, in the same select, keeps accepting newly-arriving events into an internal queue so the upstream pump is never blocked just because this one subscriber is slow; a third case handles shutdown. acceptCh() is a small function that returns the inbound channel — or nil when the queue is full, which (since a receive on a nil channel blocks forever) is exactly how you re-enable backpressure once the buffer is genuinely exhausted. (In our teaching bus we used a buffered channel for the same effect; this is the grown-up version with an explicit queue and an explicit "still accepting" case.)

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 5 → the subscriberCore: one itab instead of one per event type
text: Now a pure-Go cost problem, and the reason there's a subscriberCore at all. Subscriber[T] implements the subscriber interface. But Subscriber[TransferCompleted] and Subscriber[AccountFrozen] are different concrete types , so Go generates separate interface plumbing for each. When a concrete type is stored in an interface, Go builds an itab — an interface method table mapping the interface's methods to that concrete type's implementations, so a call like sub.dispatch(...) can find the right code at runtime. There's one itab per (interface, concrete type) pair. If Subscriber[T] implements subscriber, you get a fresh itab for every event type T ever used — plus a generic method body (a "stencil") per type shape. Each is only tens of bytes, but Tailscale's node software ships on every device and defines many event types, so "per-type" overhead in the binary is real and worth removing. The fix is to make a single, non-generic type implement the interface, so there's exactly one itab regardless of how many event types exist. That type is subscriberCore: But subscriberCore is non-generic — it still can't do the assertion itself. So how does its dispatch reach the one place that can , the

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 6 → SubscriberFunc: a friendlier API
text: Last part, and this one's a convenience, not a correctness fix. With Subscribe[T], the caller gets back a Concurrent publishers → no agreed order. One goroutine draining one channel imposes the single "true timeline." The non-generic pump can't do evt.(T). Carry events in PublishedEvent/DeliveredEvent and route to a non-generic subscribeState; defer every assertion to a generic edge. Per-subscription goroutines reorder across subscriptions. One Client = one subscribeState = one goroutine = ordered across all its subscriptions. A non-generic subscribeState must call a generic subscriber. The subscriber interface is the bridge that names no T. A slow subscriber stalls the whole pump. A multi-way select keeps accepting into a queue so upstream never blocks on one laggard. One itab per Subscriber[T] bloats the binary. A single non-generic subscriberCore implements the interface once; a closure captured where T lives reaches dispatchTyped for the assertion. Now re-read the file listing from the top of this section. Bus, Client, subscribeState, subscriber, Subscriber[T], subscriberCore, SubscriberFunc[T], PublishedEvent, DeliveredEvent, dispatch/dispatchFunc/dispatchTyped — not overkill.

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: The Saga Pattern
text: A saga is a design pattern for managing distributed transactions across decoupled services or modules without using two-phase commit (2PC). A saga breaks a distributed operation into a sequence of local transactions T1, T2, ..., Tn. Each local transaction updates an internal database and emits an event or command. If a step fails, the saga executes a series of compensating transactions Cn-1, ..., C1 in reverse order to semantically undo the committed changes. A compensating transaction is a forward-reversing operation that semantically undoes the effect of a previously committed local transaction. Unlike a database ROLLBACK (which physically discards uncommitted data), a compensating transaction runs after a local transaction has already committed and become visible to the world. It records a corrective entry (such as releasing a balance hold or refunding a charge) rather than erasing historical data. On the job: once you decouple Meridian's monolith into separate modules (Transfers, Accounts, Fraud, External Payouts, Notifications), you lose single-database ACID transactions. An operation like POST /transfers/cross-border touches three independent systems and an external clearing

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Why distributed transactions (2PC) fail at scale
text: When modules or microservices own their own databases, traditional ACID transactions across multiple databases require Two-Phase Commit (2PC) with an XA coordinator. In 2PC: 1. The coordinator asks all databases to prepare (locking rows across the network). 2. If all vote yes, the coordinator sends commit ; if any votes no, it sends abort . Why 2PC is avoided in modern financial systems: Lock amplification & blocking: Rows remain locked across all services throughout network round-trips. If the coordinator or any network link stalls, all locked rows remain unavailable, starving other transactions. Incompatible with external systems: External payment APIs (Stripe, Adyen, FedNow, SWIFT) do not participate in database 2PC protocols. You cannot ask a card network to "prepare" a charge and hold a lock for 5 seconds. Availability bottleneck: By the CAP theorem, 2PC sacrifices availability for strict consistency. A single partition brings the entire workflow to a dead stop. The Saga pattern (first formulated by Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem in 1987) replaces cross-service locking with eventual consistency and compensating actions .

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Compensating transactions: semantic rollbacks
text: In a Saga, every step $T i$ commits immediately to its own local datastore. Its changes become visible to the rest of the system. If step $T 3$ (e.g. External Bank Payout) fails, step $T 1$ (Reserve Sender Funds) and step $T 2$ (Log Compliance Entry) have already committed. We cannot run ROLLBACK. Instead, the Saga executes compensating transactions $C 2$ and $C 1$ in reverse order: Forward Action $T 1$: Hold $500 from sender account $\to$ Compensating Action $C 1$: Release $500 hold back to sender account. Forward Action $T 2$: Record compliance screening $\to$ Compensating Action $C 2$: Mark compliance record as voided/cancelled. chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Choreography vs Orchestration
text: There are two primary ways to coordinate a Saga: No central coordinator. Each service listens to events published on the bus, performs its local transaction, and publishes the next event. If a step fails, it publishes a failure event, and participating services listen and run their own compensations. Best for: Simple 2-3 step workflows where adding a coordinator is unnecessary overhead. Central coordinator. A dedicated Saga Orchestrator executes a state machine. It calls services directly (via RPC or command messages), waits for responses, records progress in a durable store, and explicitly triggers compensating actions if a step fails. Best for: Complex, multi-step financial flows (transfers, disbursements, KYC verification) requiring clear auditing and monitoring. Why high-stakes fintech uses Orchestration In Choreography, the workflow logic is scattered across multiple services. When a cross-border transfer stalls, answering "what step is this transfer currently waiting on?" requires querying distributed logs across five different services. This is commonly referred to as distributed spaghetti . With an Orchestrated Saga : The state machine is explicit and lives in one place. In
