chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: Prefix Sums
text: Two pointers and sliding window both do O(n) work to answer one query. Prefix sums do O(n) upfront work so that every subsequent range-sum query costs O(1). If you need to answer many queries on the same array, that trade is a steal. A prefix sum array pre where pre[i] holds the sum of all elements from index 0 through i-1. Build it once in O(n): pre[i+1] = pre[i] + nums[i]. Then any range sum nums[l..r] becomes a single subtraction: pre[r+1] - pre[l], costing O(1). Why it matters: a naive range-sum query re-traverses the subarray each time — O(n) per query. With a prefix sum table, you pay the O(n) build cost once and answer every subsequent query in O(1), so m queries costs O(n + m) instead of O(n·m). The same idea extends to 2D grids, XOR, and — combined with a hash map — powers the O(n) "subarray sum equals k" complement trick. The scenario: a bank's audit system needs to answer thousands of queries of the form "what is the total transaction value between index l and index r inclusive?" If you sum the subarray each time, that's O(n) per query. Build the prefix sum once, answer in O(1) forever.

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: Building and Querying
text: A prefix sum array pre has pre[i] = sum of all elements from index 0 through index i-1. With one-based indexing of pre, the range sum from l to r (both 0-indexed, inclusive) is pre[r+1] - pre[l].

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: Subarray Sum Equals K
text: Prefix sums power one of the trickiest medium problems: count subarrays that sum to exactly k. Without prefix sums, O(n²). With them, you use the complement trick: a subarray [l..r] sums to k if and only if pre[r+1] - pre[l] == k, i.e., pre[r+1] - k == pre[l]. So as you build the prefix sum, look up how many times you've seen that complement in a hash map. Pattern variations: 2D prefix sums: build a 2D table to answer rectangle-sum queries in O(1); used in image processing and matrix problems. Prefix XOR: replace addition with XOR to answer range-XOR queries. Difference arrays: the "inverse" of prefix sums — O(1) range updates, O(n) to reconstruct. Useful for range-increment problems. --

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: In-Place Tricks
text: Interviewers love in-place operations because they test whether you understand how memory works, not just the algorithm. The constraint: O(1) extra space. The tools: swapping, partitioning, and the classic "use the array as its own auxiliary structure."

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: The Swap Without Extra Space
text: You already saw swapping in the reverse. In Go, multi-assignment makes it zero-ceremony: Go's spec guarantees the right-hand side is fully evaluated before any assignment happens, so this is always safe — even when a and b are elements of the same slice.

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: Rotate Array
text: To rotate a slice right by k positions: reverse the whole slice, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the rest. Three reverses, O(n) time, O(1) space.

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: Dutch National Flag Partition
text: Three-way partitioning: given an array of values 0, 1, and 2, sort it in-place in one pass with three pointers — lo, mid, hi. This is Dijkstra's Dutch National Flag algorithm, and it generalizes to any three-bucket partition. Pattern variations: QuickSort partition: the Dutch Flag partition is the three-way partition step in three-way quicksort — faster on inputs with many repeated elements. Move zeros to end: a two-pointer fast/slow variant — slow marks the next write position for non-zeros; fast scans forward. Segregate even/odd (or negative/positive): same two-pointer partition logic with a different predicate. --

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: []byte vs string vs []rune
text: This section is not optional. Every year, people fail interviews because they write a string solution that silently corrupts multi-byte characters, or they convert strings to runes when they don't need to and get a memory hit they can't explain. Let me fix you before an interviewer has to. Three distinct types for "text" in Go, each with a different cost model. string — an immutable two-word header (ptr, len) over bytes, commonly UTF-8 but not required to be valid UTF-8. s[i] gives a raw byte, len(s) counts bytes. Zero-allocation slicing in current implementations. []byte — a mutable three-word slice (ptr, len, cap). Converting from a string ([]byte(s)) allocates and copies all bytes; converting back (string(b)) allocates again. Use when you must mutate content in-place — e.g., in-place reverse, cipher, URL encode. []rune — a mutable slice of 32-bit Unicode code points. []rune(s) decodes the string as UTF-8 into one int32 per decoded rune; len(runes) is then the rune count and runes[i] is the i-th rune. Costs 4× the memory of the byte slice. Use when you need correct rune-level indexing on non-ASCII input. The rule: keep string unless you need mutation ([]byte) or Unicode-correct i

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: The Mental Model
text: In Go, a string is an immutable, read-only byte sequence . It is a two-word header: a pointer and a length in bytes. That's it. Text is usually UTF-8, but the type itself permits arbitrary bytes. len(s) counts bytes , not characters. s[i] gives you a byte (uint8), not a character. Indexing a string to get a character is a bug for any non-ASCII input.

chTitle: Arrays & Strings: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
heading: When to Use Each
text: Use for passing text around, map keys, comparisons, and any place you don't need to mutate. Zero-copy slicing: s[l:r] creates a new header pointing into the same bytes — no allocation. Use when you need to mutate the content (e.g., in-place reverse, cipher, URL encoding). Convert with []byte(s) — this allocates and copies the bytes. Convert back with string(b) — another copy. Avoid round-trips in hot paths. Use when you need correct character indexing or length for Unicode text. []rune(s) decodes the entire string into a slice of 32-bit code points — one rune per character. Then len(runes) is the character count and runes[i] is truly the i-th character. Costs 4× the memory of the byte slice. Never index a string with s[i] when you mean "the i-th character." For ASCII-only data (English letters, digits, common symbols) it's safe. For any data that may contain accented characters, CJK, emoji, or any non-ASCII codepoint, s[i] gives you a byte, not a character. Bugs from this are silent and only surface on non-English inputs — exactly the kind of input that finds production bugs.

That's why string slicing is O(1) and zero-allocation — s[l:r] just creates a new header with an adjusted pointer and a smaller length, sharing the same underlying bytes. []byte is a three-word struct — (ptr byte, len int, cap int). When you write []byte(s), Go allocates a fresh backing array and copies the bytes into it. That's a real allocation and a real copy. When you write string(b), it allocates again and copies back. The compiler is allowed (but not required) to optimize away the copy in some specific, limited cases — when the []byte is used immediately in a comparison or as a map key inside a single expression. desc: Frequency maps, dedup, grouping, and set operations with map[T]struct{}.
text: Listen up, because this is where average engineers stay average and the ones I actually respect start to diverge. Hash maps. The single most decisive data structure in an algorithms interview — and 90% of candidates misuse them, under-use them, or stand there staring at an O(n²) solution when the answer is staring them in the face from the other side of a lookup table. You're prepping for interviews. This chapter is interview prep — not production engineering, not fintech. We're here to recognize patterns, name them, implement them flawlessly in idiomatic Go, and walk out of that room looking like the only person in the building who actually knows what they're doing. Which, after this chapter, you will be. Lucky you.

heading: Classic problem: anagram check
text: Two strings are anagrams if one is a rearrangement of the other. The frequency-map proof: build a freq map for one string, decrement for the other, then verify every count lands at zero. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space (the alphabet is fixed at 26 or 128 chars — bounded).

heading: Classic problem: first unique character
text: Scan twice. First pass builds the frequency map. Second pass finds the first index where the count is exactly 1. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space (bounded alphabet).

heading: Classic problem: top-K frequent elements
text: Here's where it gets interesting. Count frequencies in one pass, then pull out the top K. The trick: after counting, you need a min-heap of size K — push each element in, and if the heap exceeds K, pop the smallest. That keeps the K largest without sorting everything. Go's container/heap is clunky (it requires implementing an interface), but it's the tool the job calls for. Complexity: O(n log k) time, O(n + k) space.

heading: Classic problem: majority element
text: The element that appears more than n/2 times. You can do this in O(n) time and O(1) space with Boyer-Moore voting, but the frequency-map approach is clean and worth knowing — it's the pattern, not the trick.

heading: Dedup & Sets
text: Your user-facing API returns a list of recommended product IDs. It calls three upstream services, stitches the results together, and — because two services can recommend the same product — produces duplicates. You need to deduplicate in one pass without sorting. The pattern: map[T]struct as a set. The zero-size struct value costs zero bytes — you're using the map purely for its key-lookup. Insert a key to "add" it to the set; the comma-ok lookup to "test" membership. Go has no built-in set type. The idiom is map[T]struct : use the map's keys to represent set members, and struct (the zero-size type, 0 bytes) as the value — because you only care whether a key exists, not what it maps to. Adding an element: s[k] = struct . Membership test: , ok := s[k]. Why not map[T]bool? bool wastes 1 byte per entry; at a million entries that's 1 MB of useless data. More importantly, map[T]bool lets you accidentally write m[k] = false, which looks like "not a member" but the key is present — the comma-ok form is the only safe membership test either way.

heading: Contains duplicate
text: Return true if any value appears more than once. Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

heading: Intersection of two slices
text: Return the elements that appear in both a and b. Build a set from the first slice, then scan the second, collecting elements that land in the set. Complexity: O(n + m) time, O(min(n, m)) space.

heading: Grouping
text: An analytics service processes transaction records from five regional data centers. Before running aggregations, it needs to bucket transactions by region, by day, and by merchant category. Three different groupings, all with the same pattern. The pattern: map[K][]V — a key that categorizes, and a slice of everything that falls into that category. Build it in one pass; query any bucket in O(1). A grouping map associates each category key with a slice of all values in that category. The Go idiom groups[k] = append(groups[k], item) works even when k is new: append on a nil slice allocates a fresh slice, so you never need to pre-initialize the bucket. One pass builds every bucket simultaneously — O(n) time, O(n) space. On the job: bucketing transactions by region or merchant, grouping log lines by severity, partitioning tasks by worker — any "sort into buckets" problem without needing to sort. That generic version is Go 1.18+ and works for any key/value combination. The append to a nil slice works fine — append(nil, v) creates a new slice, so you need no initialization ceremony.

heading: Classic problem: group anagrams
text: Given a slice of strings, group them so anagrams end up together. The key insight: anagrams have the same sorted characters, so sort(word) is a canonical key. Complexity: O(n · k log k) where k is max word length. For fixed alphabets, a character-count signature (an array of 26 ints) turns this into O(n · k). Variation — character-count key: Sort-based keys are O(k log k) per word. You can squeeze this to O(k) by encoding a fixed-size character-count array as the key. In Go you can use [26]int directly as a map key (arrays are comparable). In Go, arrays (fixed-size, like [26]int) are comparable and can be used as map keys directly. Slices cannot — they are reference types with no defined equality. This is why the character-count signature uses [26]int instead of []int. Know this cold; it comes up repeatedly in hash-map problems.

heading: Two-Sum Family
text: Here is the canonical "trade space for time" trick — the move that separates people who think algorithmically from people who just write code. The scenario: a payment reconciliation job needs to find every pair of transaction amounts that sum to a target. The naive approach is O(n²): for every transaction, scan every other transaction. With a million rows that's a trillion comparisons. We have a Monday morning deadline. The insight: for every element x, its complement is target - x. If we've already seen target - x, we have our pair. A hash map lets us check "have I seen this value before?" in O(1). One pass: O(n) time, O(n) space — we trade memory for time. For each element x you scan, compute complement = target - x. If complement is already in the map, you found your pair — return both indices immediately. If not, store seen[x] = currentIndex and move on. The map remembers everything seen so far, so the complement check is O(1) instead of a second linear scan. This single-pass pattern — build the answer as you scan, check the map at each step — generalises to subarray sums (prefix maps), four-sum (split into two passes), and any "find two things that relate" problem. Equivalently: at index j, if we've already seen the prefix sum prefix[j] - k, there's a valid subarray ending here. Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

The control bytes store occupancy state and hash bits, letting Go reject non-matching entries without touching the actual key memory. Lookup in O(1) average. desc: Slices as stacks, ring/container/list queues, hand-rolled singly/doubly linked lists, and monotonic stacks.
text: Let me be direct with you, sport. Linear data structures are the interview's opening move — the thing they throw at you to calibrate whether you actually know Go or just think you do. A stack is three lines of code. A queue is where amateurs start bleeding. A linked list is where they invent pointer bugs they didn't know were possible. This is the chapter where I personally ensure you stop bleeding and start winning . Interview prep flag: this is Appendix Track material — DS&A interview prep, not production backend engineering. You're here to recognize patterns, write clean Go under time pressure, and name the complexity without stuttering. Let's go.

heading: Stacks
text: Here's the thing about stacks: Go gives you one for free, and it's sitting in plain sight. A slice is a stack. You don't need a library, you don't need a struct — you need append and a re-slice. A stack is a Last In, First Out (LIFO) collection: the most recently pushed item is always the first one popped. In Go, a plain []T slice is the idiomatic backing store — append to push, re-slice to pop. No wrapper struct needed for the basic case. You reach for a stack when you need to remember the current context and return to it : bracket matching (return to the outer bracket after the inner one closes), expression evaluation, DFS traversal (implicit call-stack or explicit stack), and the monotonic-stack problems later in this chapter.

heading: The Pattern
text: A stack is LIFO — Last In, First Out. Think of a browser's back history: the last page you visited is the first one you pop when you hit back. In Go, the canonical idiom is: Clean, idiomatic, no wrapper type needed for the basics. When you need a reusable generic stack, Go 1.18+ generics make that a five-liner.

heading: Classic: Valid Parentheses
text: Your interviewer's favorite warmup. Given a string of brackets — "()[] " — return true if every opener is closed in the right order. The pattern: push every opener; on every closer, check the stack top. If the top doesn't match, it's invalid. If the stack is empty at the end, it's valid. Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space (stack can hold up to n/2 openers).

heading: Classic: Evaluate RPN
text: Reverse Polish Notation — "2 3 + 4 " means (2+3) 4 = 20. Operands push onto the stack; operators pop two operands, compute, and push the result back. Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

text: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin — all O(1). The trick: carry a second "min-stack" in parallel that tracks the running minimum at each level. Complexity: O(1) all ops, O(n) space (two parallel slices). A Go slice is a three-word header: pointer to a backing array, len , and cap . append is O(1) amortized because when len

heading: Queues
text: A queue is a First In, First Out (FIFO) collection: items leave in the same order they arrived. In Go there is no queue in the standard library's slices or sort packages — you build one. The naive slice implementation (q[1:] to dequeue) leaks memory over time; a ring buffer or container/list is correct. Queues are the engine of BFS : process the front node, enqueue its unvisited neighbors, repeat. They also underpin rate limiters, work queues, and any system where fairness or ordering matters. Alright. This is where the interview separates the people who skimmed a tutorial from the people who actually understand . A queue is FIFO — First In, First Out. A line at the bank. BFS needs one. Rate limiters need one. And here's the trap: A naive slice queue is O(n) per dequeue. I've watched candidates burn ten minutes on this in whiteboard interviews, then defend their O(n) solution with confidence. Don't be that person.

heading: The Naive Slice Queue (and Why It Hurts)
text: q[1:] creates a new slice header pointing one element in — it does not copy — but the old q[0] is now unreachable through the slice. Over time, the backing array fills up with dead entries on the left side. The GC can't reclaim them because the slice header still holds a reference to the underlying array. You've got a memory leak masquerading as a queue .

heading: The Ring Buffer Queue
text: A ring buffer fixes both problems — O(1) enqueue and dequeue, O(1) space reuse — by treating a fixed-size array as a circle. Head chases tail; when either reaches the end, it wraps back to zero. Complexity: O(1) enqueue and dequeue, O(capacity) space.

heading: The Two-Stack Queue
text: Another classic interview trick: simulate a queue with two stacks. Enqueue into the "inbox" stack; when you dequeue, if the "outbox" stack is empty, reverse the inbox into the outbox (once), then pop from outbox. Complexity: O(1) amortized. Each element crosses from inbox to outbox exactly once.

heading: container/list as a Deque
text: The standard library's container/list is a doubly linked list. It's the Go stdlib's answer to a deque — O(1) push/pop at both ends. Complexity: O(1) all ops; each node is a heap allocation (pointer overhead vs. ring buffer's contiguous array). Breadth-First Search on a graph or tree processes nodes level by level . At each step it dequeues the current node, visits it, and enqueues its unvisited neighbors. The queue's FIFO order is precisely what guarantees you process shallower nodes before deeper ones — that's the whole algorithm. We'll animate this in full in the Trees & Graphs chapters. For now: whenever an interview prompt says "shortest path," "level by level," or "minimum steps," your hand should already be reaching for a queue. When you do q = q[1:], Go creates a new slice header: pointer advances by one element width, len decrements by 1, cap decrements by 1. The backing array is the same allocation. The GC sees the backing array as still live (there's a pointer to it in the slice header), so it cannot reclaim the dead prefix. After N dequeues with M enqueues, you're carrying up to N dead slots in memory — O(N) wasted space with no way to recover it short of copying the liv

heading: Linked Lists
text: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node (Next ListNode). There is no backing array — nodes are individual heap allocations connected only by pointers. This gives O(1) insert/delete at a known position (just rewire two pointers) but O(n) traversal with a cache miss at every hop, because nodes are scattered across memory. In production Go, slices almost always beat linked lists for sequences (cache locality wins). In interviews, you hand-roll them because pointer rewiring under pressure tests real understanding of references — and because the problems (reverse, cycle-detect, merge) are standard interview staples. I know what you're thinking: "We have slices. Why are we here?" You're here because every major tech interview asks you to reverse a linked list, detect a cycle, or merge two sorted lists. Not because linked lists beat slices in production Go — they don't, usually — but because pointer rewiring under pressure reveals whether you actually understand references. Buckle up.

heading: Singly Linked List
text: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next. The last node's next is nil. Build one:

heading: THE Classic: Reverse a Linked List (Iterative)
text: If an interview asks exactly one linked-list question, this is it. Three pointers: prev, curr, next. Walk the list, point curr.Next backward, advance all three. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. Variations: recursive reverse (O(n) stack space — not O(1)), reverse a sublist, reverse in groups of k.

heading: Floyd's Cycle Detection (Fast & Slow Pointers)
text: Two pointers: slow moves one step at a time; fast moves two. If there's a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow — they'll meet inside the cycle. If fast reaches nil, there's no cycle. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. Variations: find cycle start (extend with phase 2), find cycle length.

heading: Merge Two Sorted Lists
text: A classic recursion-or-iteration problem. Compare the two heads; take the smaller one; recurse (or loop). The dummy-head trick eliminates the "what's the head?" special case. Complexity: O(m+n) time, O(1) space (iterative). The dummy-head sentinel is idiomatic — use it whenever "what is the new head?" is a question.

heading: Find the Middle of a Linked List
text: Fast/slow again: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. Even-length lists: slow lands on the second middle (adjust by stopping when fast.Next == nil for the first middle). Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. A Go ListNode is a heap allocation per node: 16 bytes of ListNode struct plus the allocator header. For a list of N integers, that's N separate heap allocations, scattered across memory, each reachable only via a pointer. Traversal is a cache-miss-per-node on any real dataset, because sequential list nodes are rarely adjacent in memory. A []int of the same N values is one allocation — a contiguous array. Traversal is a sequential memory read, which hardware prefetchers and cache lines handle with ease. For N=1000, a slice traversal may be 10-50× faster than a linked list traversal on modern hardware, purely due to cache behavior. This is why production Go almost never uses container/list for sequences. Slices win. The cases where linked lists win in Go: O(1) mid-list insert/delete when you already have a pointer to the node (e.g., an LRU cache evicting an element — this is the container/list use case); or when elements are very large and copying them on reallocation i

heading: Monotonic Stacks
text: A monotonic stack is a regular slice-based stack with one extra rule: the invariant that elements stay in sorted order (strictly increasing bottom-to-top, or strictly decreasing) is maintained on every push. Before pushing a new element, pop everything that would violate the order. The pop event is not waste — it is the answer: the element being pushed is the next greater (or smaller) element for each thing it evicts. Every element is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) total work for problems that look O(n²) at first glance. Classic applications: next-greater-element, daily temperatures, largest rectangle in histogram, trapping rainwater. Here is where I separate the people who practiced from the people who merely read . The monotonic stack is a stack with an invariant: it stays sorted (either always increasing or always decreasing) by popping elements that violate the order before pushing a new one. It sounds simple. It unlocks a family of O(n) problems that look O(n²) at first glance. heading: Classic: Next Greater Element
text: Given an array, for each element find the index of the next element to its right that is strictly greater. Return -1 if none exists. Complexity: O(n) time — each element is pushed and popped at most once. O(n) space.

heading: Classic: Daily Temperatures
text: Given a list of daily temperatures, return an array where result[i] is the number of days until a warmer day. Classic monotonic stack application — same pattern as next-greater, but the answer is the index difference , not the index itself. Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space. Pattern name: "monotonic decreasing stack on indices."

heading: Classic: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
text: Given bar heights, find the largest rectangle that fits entirely within the histogram. This is the hard version — it still uses a monotonic stack (increasing), but the pop event triggers an area calculation, not just a lookup. When a shorter bar h arrives and forces popping a taller bar popped, the rectangle bounded by popped's height extends left to the new stack top's index and right to the current index. Complexity: O(n) time — each bar is pushed and popped exactly once. O(n) space. This is the canonical O(n) solution; naive O(n²) just won't cut it on large inputs. The key insight is the work-accounting argument : every element is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped at most once . The total number of push + pop operations is bounded by 2n, regardless of how many times the inner for loop fires on any given outer iteration. This is the same argument that makes append O(1) amortized. The expensive step (popping multiple elements in one outer loop iteration) is "paid for" by the cheap steps (pushes) that happened earlier. desc: Binary trees, BST invariants, DFS (pre/in/post-order) and BFS by level, recursion vs explicit stack.
text: Interview prep. That's what this track is. No microservices, no ledger invariants — just you, a whiteboard, and a binary tree that's quietly judging you. I've watched engineers who could build distributed systems freeze the moment someone asks them to invert a tree. Pathetic. Fixable. Here's what separates the ones who get the offer from the ones who get the polite rejection email: they know that every tree problem is the same problem — base case, recurse left, recurse right, combine. Once that clicks, the rest is just variations. I'll make it click for you. Personally. You're welcome. This chapter is interview prep — explicitly flagged as such. These patterns live in the DS&A Appendix Track, not in the production chapters, because grinding LeetCode trees is a different skill from building a payment service. Both matter. This is the one you need for the algorithm round. A binary tree is a linked structure where each node holds a value and has at most two children — Left and Right. A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree with a stricter rule: every value in the left subtree is less than the node's value, every value in the right subtree is greater. That invariant is what makes O

heading: Binary Trees & Recursion
text: Let's set a scene you'll actually recognize. You're two hours into an onsite loop. The interviewer slides a piece of paper across the table with a binary tree drawn on it. "Find the maximum depth," they say. Your job isn't to panic — your job is to recognize the pattern in the first five seconds and write clean Go without breaking a sweat. The pattern is this: base case, recurse on children, combine the results .

heading: The TreeNode struct
text: Every LeetCode tree problem hands you this struct. Commit it to muscle memory. No constructor needed. The zero value of a TreeNode is nil, which means "no child." That's the base case for every recursion you'll write. The Go zero value is doing real work here — a leaf node is just &TreeNode with Left and Right already nil.

heading: The recursive mindset
text: Every tree recursion has the exact same skeleton. I don't care which problem it is. The skeleton is: 1. Base case — if the current node is nil, return something sensible (often 0, true, or nil). 2. Recurse left — call yourself on node.Left. 3. Recurse right — call yourself on node.Right. 4. Combine — derive the answer for node from node.Val, the left result, and the right result. Let's animate that skeleton on the simplest useful problem: max depth (also called max height). The key insight: the work happens on the way back up . Going down, you're just asking questions. Coming back up, you're combining answers. Once you feel that rhythm, tree problems become mechanical. Here's the full runnable implementation — including a small helper to build a test tree in code:

heading: The classic four — all the same skeleton
text: Every one of these problems is the same skeleton wearing a different hat. I'll show you all four in one playground so you can see how little changes. Same tree — are two trees structurally identical with identical values? Invert tree — mirror every node's children left-to-right. Symmetric — is a tree its own mirror image? Base case = nil node. Recurse on Left and Right. Combine at the current node. That is the entire genre. O(n) for all four classics — every node is visited exactly once. You cannot do better; you must at least look at every node. O(h) where h is the height of the tree. Each recursive call adds one frame to the call stack, and the deepest path has h frames. Balanced tree: O(log n). Degenerate (linked list) tree: O(n). The isSameTree and isMirror functions check BOTH children being nil first. If you check one nil before the other without checking both, you get a nil pointer panic when you try to read .Val on a nil node. Always guard nil before accessing any field. When maxDepth(root) calls maxDepth(root.Left), the Go runtime pushes a new stack frame onto the goroutine's call stack. Each frame holds that call's local variables (left, right, the node parameter) and the

heading: DFS Traversals
text: DFS — depth-first search — means you go as deep as possible before backtracking. On a binary tree that means you commit to one subtree, recurse all the way to a leaf, then come back up and try the other side. There are three canonical orderings, and they differ only in when you visit the current node relative to its children . Pre-order : visit node → left → right ("process me before my children") In-order : left → visit node → right ("process me between my children") Post-order : left → right → visit node ("process me after my children") Here are all three traversals — recursive AND iterative — in one playground. See how the iterative versions mirror the recursive ones, but use an explicit slice as the stack instead of the call stack.

heading: Why in-order of a BST is sorted
text: This is one of those facts that seems magical until you understand it, and then it's obvious. A BST's defining property says: every node in the left subtree has a value less than the current node, and every node in the right subtree has a value greater than it. In-order traversal visits left subtree → current node → right subtree. That's exactly "everything smaller, then me, then everything larger" — sorted ascending by induction. If you need to recover a sorted sequence from a BST, in-order traversal is O(n) and requires no extra data structure. Serializing a tree (you can reconstruct it from the pre-order list + a BST invariant or structure marker). Also: copying a tree preserving shape — you write the parent before writing the children. Deleting a tree (delete children before the parent, so you never orphan a subtree). Also: evaluating expression trees (evaluate operands before the operator). BST sorted output. Validating a BST: if the in-order sequence is not strictly ascending, the invariant is violated. Iterative post-order is the trickiest of the three. A clean trick: do a "reversed pre-order" (root → right → left) and reverse the output. Or use two stacks. Don't try to do i

heading: BFS by Level
text: BFS — breadth-first search — is the other half of tree traversal. Instead of going deep first, you visit all nodes at depth 1, then all at depth 2, then depth 3, and so on. The data structure that makes this work is a queue : you enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue a node, process it, and enqueue its children. Why a queue and not a stack? Because a queue is FIFO — the first child you enqueue is the first one you process. That gives you level-by-level order. A stack would give you DFS. The "process one level at a time" insight unlocks a whole family of problems. Here's the canonical implementation plus two common variations: right-side view and level averages. The line levelSize := len(queue) is the key to all level-order problems. At the start of each outer loop iteration, len(queue) is exactly the number of nodes at the current level — because we only enqueue children of the current level's nodes. Snapshot it before the inner loop, process exactly that many nodes, and everything you enqueue during the inner loop belongs to the next level. Clean. No sentinel nodes, no two-queue dance. This asymmetry matters in interviews and in production. DFS (recursive or with an explicit s

heading: BST Invariants
text: A binary search tree is a binary tree with a strict ordering rule : for every node, all values in the left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in the right subtree are strictly greater than it. This rule applies recursively to every subtree, not just immediate children. That invariant is what makes BSTs useful: search, insert, and delete are all O(h) — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a degenerate one. Watch the invariant pay rent — searching for 43, discarding half the tree at every node: 25, so everything in 25's LEFT subtree (10) is too small. Go right. heading: Recursion vs Explicit Stack
text: Here's the thing about recursion: it IS a stack. Your call stack. The Go runtime manages it, grows it automatically, and collapses it when each frame returns. That's convenient right up until the tree has a million nodes in a straight line — then it's a million frames deep and you're leaking memory, or worse, exhausting the goroutine's stack allocation. Converting a recursive DFS to an iterative one is a one-for-one swap: replace the call stack with an explicit slice used as a stack . The algorithm is identical; only the memory manager changes. 0 return out }} / Go goroutine stacks start small (about 2 KB in current Go implementations) and grow dynamically. For typical interview-size trees, you'll never hit the limit. For a degenerate tree with 100,000+ nodes, the exact stack use depends on frame size and compiler/runtime details; it may still be fine, or it may become memory pressure. At very large depths, recursion can exhaust the goroutine stack or the process's available memory. The explicit stack approach moves that memory into a slice you control, where growth and retention are easier to reason about. In interviews: mention the stack-overflow risk when asked "what's the space

desc: container/heap in practice, top-K, merge-K, and the running median.
text: Listen carefully, because I'm about to hand you one of the most powerful weapons in the interview arsenal, and most people fumble it because they memorize the API without understanding the mechanism . A heap is not magic. It's an array that lies to you — in the best possible way. It pretends to be a tree while staying flat in memory, and it enforces one iron rule at every insertion and extraction. Learn that rule, internalize the sift-up and sift-down operations, and every "find the top-K," "merge-K," or "running median" problem becomes a pattern you recognize before the interviewer finishes the sentence. Go's container/heap package is, and I say this as someone who could write a better one in an afternoon, clunky . You will implement five methods on a slice type and hand it to the runtime. That is the deal. We are going to make it elegant anyway. This is interview prep . Every solution ships runnable, every pattern is named, and every complexity claim is justified. Let's go. This chapter is part of the Appendix Track: DS&A Interview Prep . The patterns here are idiomatic Go and correct, but the focus is problem-solving craft and pattern recognition under time pressure — not produc

heading: The Heap Property & Array Representation
text: Here's the thing, sport: every heap tutorial shows you a picture of a tree. Then they show you an array. Then they tell you the tree is the array. And somehow, most people leave still uncertain why. Let me fix that in three steps.

heading: Step 1: the heap property
text: A binary heap satisfies one invariant at every node: a parent's value compares favorably to both its children. There are two flavors: Min-heap : every parent ≤ both children. The smallest value sits at the root (index 0). heap.Pop always gives you the minimum. Max-heap : every parent ≥ both children. The largest value sits at the root. Flip the comparison in Less to turn a min-heap into a max-heap. The invariant does not say anything about ordering between siblings or cousins. That's the key: it's a local guarantee enforced at every parent-child edge, not a global sort. This is precisely why heaps are fast — maintaining a global sort takes O(n log n); maintaining the heap property on one new element takes O(log n).

heading: Step 2: the array representation
text: A complete binary tree can be stored in a flat array with zero wasted space and zero pointers. For a node at index i (0-based): The min (or max) of the entire heap. Peeking is O(1) — just read index 0. Extracting is O(log n). Given index i, left child lives at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2. No pointers needed — pure arithmetic. Integer division walks back up the tree. Sift-up uses this repeatedly to restore the property after an insert. The array representation only works for a complete binary tree (all levels filled left-to-right). Heaps maintain completeness automatically because Push appends to the end and Pop swaps the root with the last element before shrinking. A seven-element min-heap in array form:

heading: Step 3: sift-up (after insert) and sift-down (after extract)
text: These two operations are the entire mechanism. Everything else — Push, Pop, Fix — is built from them. Sift-up is used after inserting a new element at the end of the array. The new element may be smaller than its parent (in a min-heap), violating the heap property. We fix it by repeatedly swapping with the parent until the property is restored or we reach the root. Sift-down is used after removing the root. The standard trick: move the last element to the root position (to keep the array compact), then sift it down — repeatedly swap with the smaller child until neither child is smaller. Let's animate both. Sift-up travels at most that many levels upward; sift-down travels at most that many levels downward. Each level is one comparison and one potential swap — constant work per level. Total: O(log n). heading: container/heap in Practice
text: Go's container/heap is correct, efficient, and — I'll be direct — not pretty. You implement five methods. The package rewards correctness, not elegance. Let me show you exactly what it wants, then wrap it so you never have to look at the boilerplate again.

heading: The interface
text: There are five methods total: Len, Less, Swap (from sort.Interface), plus Push and Pop. The clunkiest part: Push and Pop operate on the last element of your slice, not the first. The package moves elements into position using Swap before calling Pop. You handle raw slice manipulation; the package handles the heap logic.

heading: A max-heap: flip Less
text: The only change for a max-heap is reversing the Less comparison. No other method changes. h[j] // flip: larger wins } } /

heading: A priority queue with custom priorities
text: Real interviews often demand a priority queue over structs. The pattern: embed the struct in a slice, implement Less based on the priority field. container/heap predates Go generics (it was written in 2011 for Go 1.0 and has not changed structurally since). The any in Push/Pop is the pre-generics way of saying "I don't know what type you're storing." The package avoids generics to stay in stdlib without a major API break — changing it to heap.Interface[T] would break every existing implementation. As of Go 1.24, the community idiom for a clean generic heap wrapper is to write a thin adapter yourself: This is completely valid in interviews if you explain it. In practice, copy-paste the five-method boilerplate and move on — the interviewer cares about the algorithm, not the plumbing.

heading: Top-K Problems
text: The pattern: use a heap of size k. Stream elements through it. Maintain only what you need. Pattern name: Fixed-size heap (size k) K largest from a stream of n: keep a min-heap of size k. When the heap exceeds k, pop the minimum. At the end, the heap contains the k largest. Complexity: O(n log k). Space: O(k). K smallest from a stream of n: keep a max-heap of size k. Pop the maximum when size k. Same complexity. Why a min-heap for k-largest? Because the root of the min-heap is the smallest of the k candidates. If a new element is larger than that minimum, it displaces it. You're always evicting the weakest competitor.

heading: Top-K frequent elements
text: A classic: combine a frequency map with a heap of size k. This ties directly to the hashing chapter. Size=4 k=3. 2 Complexity summary for Top-K: Approach Time Space When to use --- --- --- --- Sort then slice O(n log n) O(1) extra n is small or k ≈ n Min-heap of size k O(n log k) O(k) Streaming / large n, small k Quickselect O(n) average O(1) k-th element only, not top-k list The heap approach shines when k ≪ n — for example, finding the top-100 stocks by volume out of 50,000 tickers. Common variations: K-th largest element: same heap, just return ( h)[0] at the end (the root of the size-k min-heap) K closest points to origin: use a max-heap of size k, distance as priority Top-K frequent words: same as TopKFrequent but break ties lexicographically in Less

heading: Merge-K Sorted Lists
text: Pattern name: K-way merge with a min-heap You have K sorted arrays (or linked lists). You want one sorted output. The naïve approach — flatten and sort — is O(N log N) where N is the total number of elements. The heap approach is O(N log K). When K ≪ N, that's a massive win. The insight : maintain a min-heap containing exactly one element from each of the K lists — the front element. Each Pop gives you the globally smallest remaining element. Then push the next element from whichever list just donated the minimum.

heading: Merge-K sorted arrays
text: The pattern in four sentences: 1. Push the first element of every list into a min-heap along with a cursor (which list, which index). 2. Pop the global minimum. Append to output. 3. Advance that list's cursor by one. Push the next element from the same list into the heap (if it exists). 4. Repeat until the heap is empty. The heap never holds more than K elements — one per list. Each of the N total elements does one push and one pop: O(N log K). Common variations: Merge-K sorted linked lists (LeetCode 23): same algorithm; store ListNode in the heap instead of a cursor struct Find the smallest range covering one element from each of K lists: add a max-tracker alongside the heap External sort (sorting a file larger than RAM): split into K sorted chunks on disk, merge-K them in streaming fashion In production, merge-K shows up whenever you have multiple shards of sorted data that need to be combined: log aggregation across servers, merging sorted result sets from distributed databases, combining time-sorted event streams. The heap is your answer every time. Once you see the pattern, you can't un-see it.

heading: Running Median
text: This is the interview problem that separates the "knows heaps" engineer from the "lives heaps" engineer. It is one of the most beautiful two-heap patterns ever devised. The problem : numbers arrive one at a time in a stream. After each insertion, return the current median. Why it's hard : a median is the middle value of a sorted sequence. Maintaining a fully sorted structure is O(log n) per insert but requires sorting, and you can't just binary-search an unsorted stream. The insight — two heaps as a balanced partition: Keep two heaps that partition all seen numbers at every moment: lo : a max-heap holding the smaller half of all numbers. Its root is the largest of the small numbers. hi : a min-heap holding the larger half. Its root is the smallest of the large numbers. The invariant: lo.Len() - hi.Len() ≤ 1. When the sizes differ by at most 1, the median is: lo.root (if lo is larger) hi.root (if hi is larger) (lo.root + hi.root) / 2 (if sizes are equal) Insertion algorithm: 1. If the new number ≤ lo.root, push to lo. Otherwise push to hi. 2. Rebalance: if one heap exceeds the other by more than 1, pop from the larger and push to the smaller. lo.root(5), goes to hi. chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
desc: Adjacency lists, BFS/DFS, topological sort, union-find, and shortest paths with Dijkstra.
text: This is interview prep — say that out loud so you're not confused when things get intense. Graphs are the boss level of the algorithms round. They show up in build systems, social networks, navigation, dependency resolution, network routing — the interviewer knows this, and so now you will too. BFS, DFS, topological sort, union-find, Dijkstra: five tools. Each one is exact and non-negotiable. Learn the shape of each, know which one to reach for, and you walk out of the loop with an offer. I've guided people through far worse. Try to keep up.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Representing Graphs
text: Before you can traverse a graph, you need to hold one in memory. There are exactly two standard representations, and the choice matters. The setup. Imagine you're building the dependency resolver for a Go module system. Packages are nodes. A directed edge from package A to package B means "A imports B." You need to figure out which packages to compile first — and whether there's a circular dependency that would make compilation impossible. This graph problem is the spine of every section in this chapter. A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. An adjacency list represents it by storing, for each node, the list of nodes it connects to — in Go, either [][]int (nodes numbered 0…N-1) or map[int][]int (arbitrary node IDs). Space is O(V+E), making it the right default for any graph where edges are far fewer than V². Without a graph structure you cannot express dependency order, reachability, or routing — all of which come up constantly in distributed backend systems.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Adjacency List vs. Adjacency Matrix
text: An adjacency list stores, for each node, the list of its neighbors. In Go that's either map[int][]int (sparse graphs, arbitrary IDs) or [][]int (dense graphs, nodes numbered 0…N-1). An adjacency matrix is a 2-D boolean (or weight) array: matrix[u][v] = true if there's an edge from u to v. O(V + E). Each edge stored once (directed) or twice (undirected). The right default for sparse graphs (most real ones). O(V²). Even if there are only 10 edges in a 1000-node graph, you allocate a million cells. Wasteful when edges are sparse. List: O(degree) — scan neighbors. Matrix: O(1) — just index in. Matrix wins for dense graphs where you ask "does edge u→v exist?" millions of times. List: O(degree) — exactly as many steps as you have neighbors. Matrix: O(V) — you must scan an entire row even if only two cells are set. Add a weight: list stores []Edge where Edge has to int and weight int. Matrix stores the weight directly at matrix[u][v]. Never use adjacency matrix for graphs where V is large and edges are sparse — the O(V²) allocation alone will TLE or OOM. In interviews, state your choice and justify it. Here is how you build both representations from an edge list in idiomatic Go 1.24: In G

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: BFS and DFS
text: Before the code, watch BFS work the settlement network — level by level, never skipping ahead: Two traversals. Every graph problem is secretly one of these — or a clever hybrid. The scenario. Your module graph is loaded. You want two things: (1) the minimum number of hops from package main to any dependency (to prioritize shallow compilation), and (2) whether any connected component is an island (never reachable from main). BFS answers (1). DFS answers (2). BFS explores a graph level by level , visiting all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1. It uses a FIFO queue, and the first time a node is dequeued its recorded distance is the shortest possible. That property makes BFS the go-to algorithm for shortest paths in unweighted graphs . If you skip BFS and use DFS for shortest-path, you'll get a path — just not the shortest one, and the bug will be silent.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: BFS — Breadth-First Search
text: BFS explores the graph level by level , starting from a source. It visits all nodes at distance 1 before any at distance 2 — which is exactly why it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. The data structure driving it is a queue (FIFO). In Go, a slice used as queue[0] (dequeue front) + append (enqueue back) is the standard BFS queue. It's O(1) amortized append and O(n) overall dequeue, which is fine for interview use; container/list gives true O(1) dequeue if allocations matter. Classic BFS problems: number of islands (treat each cell as a graph node, 4-directional neighbors), clone graph, word ladder (word = node, one-letter-diff = edge), rotting oranges (multi-source BFS). DFS follows one path to its end before backtracking to try another. It runs naturally on the call stack (recursive) or an explicit stack (iterative). DFS does not guarantee shortest paths, but it excels at cycle detection , connectivity , and topological ordering — problems where you need to know whether a path exists, not how short it is. Miss a cycle in a dependency graph and you compile forever; miss it in a payment DAG and you get circular settlement references.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: DFS — Depth-First Search
text: DFS dives as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. It's naturally recursive and naturally expresses problems about connectivity , cycle detection , and ordering . Recursive DFS is cleaner and the default in interviews. Iterative DFS (explicit stack) avoids stack overflow for extremely deep graphs. Cycle detection in an undirected graph: During DFS, if you reach a neighbor that is already visited and is not the parent of the current node, you've found a back edge — a cycle. Cycle detection in a directed graph: Track three states per node: unvisited (0), in-stack (1), done (2). If you reach a node that's in-stack, the graph has a cycle. BFS works by expanding a frontier — all nodes at distance d are settled before any node at distance d+1 is enqueued. The moment you enqueue a node, you record its distance, and since it's the first time you've touched it via BFS, that distance is the minimum. No node at a shorter distance is waiting behind it in the queue — BFS's FIFO property guarantees this. DFS, by contrast, dives arbitrarily deep along one path. It might find a path of length 10 to a node before discovering a path of length 2. The traversal order has nothing to do w

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Topological Sort
text: A topological sort of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a linear ordering of all nodes such that for every directed edge u→v, u appears before v in the result. It only exists when the graph has no cycles — a cycle means "A depends on B depends on A," which has no valid ordering. In production: your build system, package manager, and database migration runner all need topological order. Get it wrong and you compile a package before its dependency compiles, or run a migration that references a table that doesn't exist yet. A topological sort of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is an ordering of nodes such that for every directed edge u→v, u comes before v. It only exists if the graph has no cycles. The scenario. Your Go module resolver needs to compile packages in dependency order. If package A imports B and C, and B imports C, then C must be compiled first, then B, then A. That ordering is a topological sort. The algorithm also doubles as cycle detection: if the graph has a cycle, no valid ordering exists and the build fails.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Kahn's Algorithm (BFS-based, in-degree method)
text: In-degree of a node is the count of edges pointing into it. Nodes with in-degree 0 have no unresolved dependencies — they can go first. The algorithm: 1. Compute in-degrees for all nodes. 2. Enqueue all nodes with in-degree 0. 3. While the queue is non-empty: dequeue a node, append it to the result, decrement the in-degree of each neighbor. If a neighbor's in-degree drops to 0, enqueue it. 4. If the result length equals V, you have a valid topological order. If not, a cycle exists. An alternative to Kahn's is DFS post-order: run DFS, and after fully exploring a node (all descendants visited), push it onto a stack. Reverse the stack at the end. Both give valid topological orderings. Kahn's is preferred in interviews because it naturally surfaces the cycle (the count check) and is easier to reason about under pressure. The DFS version is elegant but the cycle detection is subtler.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Union-Find (DSU)
text: Disjoint Set Union (also called Union-Find) answers one question with near-O(1) amortized speed: do two nodes belong to the same connected component? The scenario. You're processing Kafka events that represent new "package imports" appearing live. After each event, you need to answer: "Is package X in the same compilation unit as package Y?" Union-Find lets you answer this in effectively constant time, even after thousands of merges.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Find + Union with Path Compression + Union by Rank
text: Every node starts as its own "root." find(x) returns the root of x's component, applying path compression on the way back — every node on the path is attached directly to the root, flattening the tree. union(x, y) merges two components by rank (tree height) — always attaching the shorter tree under the taller one to keep the trees flat. Together, path compression + union by rank give amortized O(α(n)) per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant for any input size you'll ever see in practice. Without any optimization, find could traverse a chain of n nodes — O(n) worst case if every union makes a linked list. Path compression flattens that chain: every node encountered during find is re-attached directly to the root. The next find on any of those nodes is O(1). Union by rank prevents the chain from forming in the first place. The rank is an upper bound on the tree height. By always merging the shorter tree under the taller one, the maximum height grows only as log(n). With both optimizations, the amortized cost per operation is O(α(n)) — the inverse Ackermann function. For any realistic n (up to 10^80), α(n) ≤ 4. It's effectively constant. As of G

heading: Finding Boundaries

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: The scenario
text: Same order-timestamp system. Now the client asks: "Give me the first order placed at or after timestamp T, and the last order placed at or before T." That's lower-bound and upper-bound — the pair of building blocks that make every boundary query possible.

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: Lower bound: first occurrence (or insert position)
text: The lower bound answers: "What is the leftmost index where nums[i] = target?" This is also called the "search-insert position" — if target isn't present, it's where you'd insert it to keep the array sorted. Reframe: we want the leftmost position where the predicate nums[i] = target is true . The structure: the array looks like [false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true] — all the falses on the left, all the trues on the right. Binary search finds the boundary. Notice the template changed: hi = len(nums) (not len-1) and the condition is lo < hi (not lo <= hi). Why? Because the answer could be "insert at position len" — one past the end — and we need hi to be able to hold that. The invariant is now: "the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]" where both endpoints are possible, and we stop when lo == hi.

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: Upper bound: last occurrence
text: Upper bound answers: "What is the leftmost index where nums[i] target?" Then the last occurrence of target is at index upperBound - 1. A lower bound is the first index where nums[i] = target — the leftmost place the target could sit. An upper bound is the first index where nums[i] target — one past the last occurrence. Together they bracket the exact range of any value in a sorted slice, including duplicates. Go's sort.Search(n, f) is the stdlib spelling of lower bound: it finds the smallest index in [0, n) where a caller-supplied monotone predicate f first becomes true. If f is false for every index, sort.Search returns n — a past-the-end sentinel, not -1. You must always guard the result: if i == len(nums) nums[i] != target .

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: Go's stdlib: sort.Search
text: Go's standard library gives you a generic lower-bound via sort.Search(n, f). It returns the smallest index i in [0, n) for which f(i) is true, assuming f is false for indices before the answer and true after. It uses the same lo Both lowerBound and sort.Search share one mental model: the predicate partitions the index space into [false … false true … true], and you're finding the leftmost true . Once you see binary search as "find the leftmost true on a monotone predicate," every variant falls out naturally — including the answer-space searches in section 4.

The art of committing to a choice, going all the way down, and — when the universe says no — calmly stepping back and trying the next thing. Like me. Always in control. This chapter is interview prep . We are not building production systems here. We are building the pattern-recognition muscle that lets you stare at "generate all permutations" at 10am on a whiteboard and not flinch. Every solution ships runnable. heading: The scenario: generating PIN codes under a constraint
text: You're on the fraud team at a payments startup. A compromised POS terminal issued PINs following a now-known pattern: no digit appears more than once. You need to enumerate every valid 4-digit PIN from a given digit pool so your security scanner can cross-reference against transaction logs. The search space is manageable — but you need all of them, correct and fast. That's backtracking. A systematic search strategy that commits to one choice, recurses into the remaining search space, then undoes that choice before trying the next option. It is the correct algorithm whenever you need to enumerate all valid configurations (every valid PIN, every permutation, every placement of N-queens) and there is no shortcut that avoids examining each possibility. Why it matters: without the un-choose step, you cannot reuse the same path variable across branches — each branch would see the side effects of all previous branches. The conceptual tree that backtracking traverses depth-first. Each node is a partial state (a path built so far); each edge is one choice (append digit 3). Leaves are either complete solutions (record them) or dead ends (backtrack). The tree is never materialized in memory —

heading: Three moves, one recursion
text: Every backtracking algorithm is exactly three moves repeated until the answer space is drained: 1. Choose — pick one option from the available choices at the current decision point. 2. Explore — recurse deeper, making the next choice inside the reduced search space. 3. Un-choose — undo the choice after the recursion returns, restoring the state for the next option. The mental picture is a decision tree . Each node is a partial state; each edge is one choice. You walk depth-first from the root toward the leaves. When you hit a leaf (a complete solution) you record it. When you hit a dead end (constraint violated, no options left), you backtrack — climb back up one level and take the next branch. You exhaust the entire tree.

heading: The universal Go skeleton
text: The append([]int , path...) copy on the base-case line is the most important line in this entire chapter. Go slices are headers over a shared backing array. If you write result = append( result, path), every collected result ends up pointing at the same underlying array — and you'll watch your answers silently corrupt as later mutations overwrite earlier ones. We'll show this trap live in the UnderTheHood block. A Go slice is a three-word value: (pointer, length, capacity). Backtracking mutates the same underlying array in-place across every recursive call — appending to grow path, then shrinking len to un-choose. If you store the slice header without copying (result = append(result, path)), every stored result shares that same array and will be overwritten by future mutations. Fix: slices.Clone(path) or append([]int , path...) allocates a fresh array snapshot that backtracking can never touch. heading: Generate all subsets (the power set)
text: Scenario: An options-pricing engine needs to evaluate the PnL impact of every possible subset of a risk-factor set. Given n factors, that's 2^n subsets. Small n, enormous business value — enumerate them all. Pattern: At each element, make a binary choice — include it or exclude it. Use a start index to march forward through the array without revisiting earlier elements (prevents duplicates). Complexity: Time O(2^n n) — 2^n subsets, each takes O(n) to clone. Space O(n) call stack + O(2^n n) for results. Variations: Subsets with duplicates (LeetCode 90): sort first, then skip duplicates at the same recursion level with if i start && nums[i] == nums[i-1] . Subsets of a given size k : add if len(path) == k as your leaf condition.

heading: Combinations: choose k from n
text: Pattern: Same start-index trick, but only record when len(path) == k. Complexity: Time O(C(n,k) k) — number of combinations times the clone cost. Space O(k) call stack.

heading: Combination Sum: reuse allowed
text: Scenario: A cashier system needs every way to make exact change for a target amount using a given coin denominations set, with unlimited coins per denomination. Key difference from combinations: pass i (not i+1) to allow reusing the same element. Complexity: Time O(N^(T/M)) where T is target and M is the smallest candidate — roughly exponential in depth. Space O(T/M) call stack. Pass start to avoid revisiting earlier elements and generating duplicate sets. The single biggest source of confusion in this family of problems. Pass i to allow reuse (combination sum), i+1 to forbid it (combinations, subsets). One character, two entirely different problems. Sort candidates before backtracking so you can break early when the current candidate already exceeds the remaining budget. Free pruning. Subsets with duplicates (LeetCode 90): sort first, then skip at the loop level with if i start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]. The i start guard is crucial — it skips duplicates only at the same depth, not across depths. --

heading: All orderings of distinct elements
text: Scenario: A payments router needs to try every ordering of settlement channels to find which sequence has the lowest total fee. Given n channels, there are n! orderings. Pattern: Unlike subsets, permutations care about order. Use a used boolean array (indexed by position in nums) to track which elements are already on the path. Complexity: Time O(n! n) — n! permutations, O(n) to clone each. Space O(n) for the used array and call stack.

heading: Permutations with duplicates
text: When nums contains repeated elements, the naive algorithm generates duplicate permutations. The fix: sort first, then skip an unused element if it equals its predecessor (and that predecessor is unused at this level). Complexity: Time O(n! n) worst case, but pruning eliminates duplicate branches early. heading: N-Queens: the classic
text: Scenario: A hardware security module (HSM) needs to place n independent signing threads on an n x n grid of processing slots such that no two threads share a row, column, or diagonal — to prevent timing-based side-channel attacks. Model it as N-queens. Pattern: Place one queen per row. For each row, try every column; skip columns/diagonals already attacked. No need for a full board matrix — three boolean arrays (or sets) track which columns and diagonals are occupied. Complexity: Time O(n!) — at row 0 you have n choices, row 1 at most n-1, and so on. Space O(n) for the three mark arrays plus call stack.

heading: Animating N-Queens: place then backtrack on conflict
Word Search on a grid

Mark cells as visited by temporarily overwriting them (the classic Go trick to avoid an extra visited array), then restore on backtrack. Complexity: Time O(m n 4^L) where L is the word length — we start from every cell and explore 4 directions for each character. Space O(L) call stack. Three bool arrays for columns, \ diagonals, and / diagonals give O(1) conflict checks. No board scanning needed. Overwrite the cell with to mark visited inline; restore on backtrack. Avoids allocating a separate visited grid. For existence problems (word search), return true as soon as any branch succeeds — no need to explore the full tree. In the word search, after restoring board[r][c] = tmp, the OR chain bt(...) bt(...) ... short-circuits — if the first direction finds the word, the others are never called. This is implicit pruning. --

heading: The difference between TLE and AC
text: Skipping an entire subtree of the decision tree the moment you can prove no leaf in it can be valid . Example: in combination sum, once the current candidate exceeds the remaining target (and candidates are sorted), every subsequent candidate also exceeds it — break immediately rather than recurse into each one. Why it matters: pruning does not change the worst-case complexity, but it destroys the constant factor. The difference between TLE and AC on a backtracking problem is almost always a missing pruning condition. Pruning is cutting branches off the decision tree before exploring them — because you can already tell they cannot lead to a valid solution. Without pruning, backtracking is correct but often laughably slow. With it, the same skeleton goes from TLE to milliseconds on real input. The rule: any time you can prove that no leaf reachable from the current node can be valid, return immediately without recursing.

heading: Pruning techniques
text: 1. Bound-based pruning (combination sum pattern) Sort the candidates. When the current candidate already exceeds the remaining target, all further candidates (which are larger or equal) also exceed it — break immediately. 2. Count-based pruning (combinations) If (n - i + 1) + len(path)

Pruning doesn't change the algorithm — it changes which subtrees get visited. The big-O worst case is the same, but the practical constant factor drops by orders of magnitude. Always sort + break for sum-based problems. Always add the count guard for combination/subset-with-size problems. --
