desc: The hunting workflow grounded in 6,400+ real disclosed writeups: attack-surface mapping (subdomain enumeration, content/endpoint discovery, JavaScript analysis for hidden routes and keys), the hunt loop (map → probe → escalate → chain), choosing targets by bug-class ROI, triage and severity (CVSS), and writing the report that gets paid — with runnable stdlib Go recon helpers. Authorized-testing only.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Beginners think bug hunting is about exotic payloads. It isn't. It's about attack surface — finding the forgotten staging subdomain, the API endpoint that shipped in a JavaScript bundle but never in the docs, the object ID nobody thought you'd guess. The hunters who get paid aren't the ones who know the most payloads; they're the ones who see the most surface and probe it methodically. Recon is 80% of the game, and almost nobody teaches it as a system. This chapter is that system, drawn from the patterns across 6,400+ real disclosed writeups (the pentester.land corpus you'll see referenced throughout this track). We'll map an attack surface the way a pro does — subdomain enumeration, content and endpoint discovery, mining JavaScript for hidden routes and leaked keys — then run the hunt loop (map → probe → escalate → chain), pick targets by bug-class ROI (the corpus tells you exactly where the bugs are), triage findings with CVSS , and write the report that actually gets paid. Every recon helper is runnable stdlib Go — because the best way to understand a tool is to build a small one. By the end you'll have a repeatable methodology, not a bag of tricks. Ever

heading: The Attack Surface
text: A finding starts with surface. The more of a target's surface you can see, the more places a missing check can hide. Pros think in terms of expanding the surface — every subdomain, path, parameter, and endpoint is a new place to test. The attack surface is the complete set of points where an untrusted actor can interact with a system: every hostname and subdomain, every URL path and API endpoint, every request parameter, header, and input field, every third-party integration, and every piece of client-side code that reveals any of those. Recon is the disciplined expansion of your visible attack surface — turning "the main website" into a map of hundreds of hostnames and thousands of endpoints. Why it dominates: a vulnerability you can't reach can't be exploited; most high-value bugs in disclosed reports were on surface the target forgot they had (a staging host, a legacy API, an admin endpoint left in a JS bundle). --

heading: Subdomain Enumeration
text: The first multiplier. A program scoped as .example.com is really hundreds of hosts, and the interesting ones are the ones the security team forgot: staging, dev, admin, legacy, vpn, internal. Two techniques dominate: passive (query public datasets — certificate transparency logs, DNS aggregators — no packets to the target) and active (resolve candidate names from a wordlist). Subdomain enumeration discovers the hostnames under a domain. Passive enumeration mines public sources that already recorded them — most powerfully Certificate Transparency (CT) logs , the public append-only logs every TLS certificate is published to, so every host that ever got an HTTPS cert is discoverable by querying crt.sh and similar. Active enumeration (DNS brute-forcing) takes a wordlist of likely names (api, dev, staging, …), prepends each to the domain, and checks which resolve. Passive is quiet and finds real historical hosts; active finds names not in any public record but generates DNS traffic. Pros do both, then probe which hosts are alive (respond to HTTP). Here's the core of active enumeration — generate candidates and check which resolve — in runnable stdlib Go (resolving public names, no targe

heading: Content & Endpoint Discovery
text: Each live host hides paths the sitemap never mentions. Content discovery brute-forces paths from a wordlist against a host and keeps the ones that don't 404 — surfacing /admin, /api/v1, /.git/config, /backup.zip, /swagger.json. This is how forgotten admin panels and exposed config files get found. Here's content discovery against an in-process test server (so it's runnable and touches nothing real) — the exact loop a real tool runs, minus the network: A path is not one endpoint — it's one endpoint per method . The same URL can 404 on GET but accept a PUT or POST, because frameworks route (method, path) pairs and developers often guard the method they expect a browser to use while leaving the others wide open. So when you fuzz, fuzz the method too : try GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE (and OPTIONS/HEAD) on each candidate path. A GET /v1/accounts/ that returns 403 might have a PUT /v1/accounts/ that updates with no auth check at all — the broken-access-control bugs in this track hide exactly there. Two cheap habits: start path fuzzing at /v1/FUZZ (versioned API roots are where the undocumented endpoints live), and never conclude an endpoint is safe from one method's response — re-test

heading: The Recon Pipeline: anew, Liveness & the Outlier Hunt
text: Watch any experienced hunter do live recon and you'll notice it's not a tool — it's a Unix pipeline . Domains flow through a chain of small programs, each doing one thing, joined by , with results appended to flat files you grep later. And here's the part for this book: the canonical toolkit for this — assetfinder, httprobe, anew, fff, meg, gf, waybackurls, unfurl — is almost entirely written in Go (mostly by one person, tomnomnom). They're small, fast, composable Go binaries: exactly the philosophy the rest of this course teaches, pointed at recon. Let's build the mechanism of the two that change how you work.

heading: anew — the diffing pipeline
text: The workflow problem: you enumerate subdomains with several tools (assetfinder, findomain, subfinder, CT logs) because each finds things the others miss, and you re-run them over time. You don't want to re-process the thousands you already have — you want only the new ones each run, so you can pipe just those into the next stage (liveness, fetching). That's anew : it reads lines, appends only the ones not already in your file, and prints only what was new . anew reads lines from stdin and appends each one to a file only if that line isn't already in the file — and crucially, it prints to stdout only the lines that were new . It's tee -a that de-duplicates and reports the delta. This one behavior is what makes the recon pipeline incremental : assetfinder example.com anew domains.txt adds any newly-discovered domains to domains.txt and emits just those, so you can chain httprobe anew live.txt and only probe the domains you hadn't seen before . Re-run the same tool an hour later and anew emits nothing (everything's known); run a different tool and it emits only that tool's unique finds. It turns a pile of overlapping tool outputs into a clean, growing, no-duplicates dataset — and tell

heading: The outlier hunt — find the host that's different
text: Once you've fetched the root of every host, you have a pile of response headers — thousands of them. The naive move is to read them all. The expert move is to find the host that doesn't look like the others . Big organizations run configuration management, so their fleet is consistent — the same Server, the same X-Powered-By, the same custom headers everywhere. A host with a header almost nothing else has is a host built differently — maybe outside the standard build pipeline, maybe an acquisition, maybe a one-off someone stood up and forgot. That inconsistency is a strong signal: it's where the non-standard, less-reviewed, more-likely-vulnerable service lives. In a large, well-managed target, consistency is the norm and inconsistency is the lead . Configuration management and a standard SDLC make most hosts look identical — same headers, same framework fingerprints, same error pages. So instead of auditing every host, you hunt the outlier : the host with a response header (or server banner, or error format) that appears on only one host out of thousands. That singular host was probably built outside the standard process — a forgotten side project, an acquired company's infra, a qu

heading: Going back in time, and into the source
text: Two more high-yield sources the pipeline feeds: waybackurls / gau pull every URL the archive has ever seen for a domain — including historical versions of JS bundles. An old site.js from 2018 often references API endpoints that were removed from the current app but are still live on the server (and unmonitored). Filter the archive output to .js, fetch the old versions (fff, 200-only), and grep them for endpoints and keys. Removed-in-the-UI ≠ removed-on-the-server. Find repos that mention the target, clone them, and run a git dump (extract every object in .git to plain files — every file that ever existed in the history , not just the current tree). A secret or internal URL deleted in a later commit is still sitting in an old object. Grep the dumped history for in-scope URLs (filter with an inscope tool) and credentials. The current HEAD is the tip of an iceberg; the history is the rest. --

heading: Mining JavaScript
text: The richest source of hidden surface is the target's own JavaScript. Modern single-page apps ship their entire API map, route table, feature flags, and — too often — secrets in the JS bundle. Hunters download every .js, then grep it for endpoints and keys. A route that exists only in client code is surface the docs and the sitemap will never show. JS recon extracts attack surface from a target's client-side code. Single-page apps bundle their API calls (fetch('/api/internal/users/' + id)), route definitions, and config into JavaScript that ships to every visitor. Mining it with regexes surfaces: endpoints (paths and full URLs the app calls), parameters (the shape of requests), and — the jackpot — leaked secrets (API keys, tokens, internal hostnames accidentally compiled in). An internal admin endpoint referenced in JS but protected only by the UI hiding the button is a classic broken-access-control finding. The corpus is full of bugs that started "I read their JavaScript." Endpoint and secret extraction is just pattern-matching over the bundle text — runnable here over a sample bundle: A secret in a JS bundle is a real, often critical finding — but handle it carefully. If you find

heading: Search-Engine Dorking
text: The purest passive recon: let a search engine do the crawling, then ask it precise questions. A dork is a query built from advanced operators that surfaces things that are public but never meant to be found — exposed config files, login panels, indexed backups, documents whose metadata leaks PII. You touch the search engine, not the target, so it's about as low-risk as recon gets. Dorking (a.k.a. Google hacking) uses a search engine's advanced operators to filter its index down to exposed, sensitive surface. Core operators (broadly shared across Google, Bing, and Yandex, with syntax differences): site: restricts to a domain; filetype: / mime: filters by file type (Yandex uses mime:); inurl: matches a term in the URL; intitle: matches the page title (intitle:"index of" finds open directory listings); Yandex adds host: and url: . Combine them — site:target.com mime:pdf, site:target.com inurl:.env — to pull every indexed PDF or stray config file on a scope. It's passive: you query the engine, never the target, which is why it's a first-move recon source alongside Certificate Transparency. Different search engines crawl, rank, and de-index differently — so a file Google scrubbed or bur

heading: The Hunt Loop
text: Recon gives you surface; the hunt loop turns surface into findings. It's a repeatable cycle, and the best hunters run it relentlessly rather than chasing one clever idea. --

heading: Picking Targets by ROI
text: You can't test everything. The corpus tells you where the bugs are — so spend your time by bug-class ROI : frequency × impact × your skill. Across the 6,400+ disclosed reports, the classes cluster hard. --

heading: Triage & CVSS
text: You found something. Before reporting, you must say how bad it is — programs pay by severity, and an inflated severity gets your report rejected. The industry standard is CVSS . CVSS produces a 0–10 severity score from a vector of metrics. The core Base metrics: Attack Vector (Network/Adjacent/Local/Physical — how remote), Attack Complexity (Low/High), Privileges Required (None/Low/High), User Interaction (None/Required), Scope (Unchanged/Changed — does it break out of its security boundary?), and the Impact triad Confidentiality / Integrity / Availability (None/Low/High). The score maps to bands: 0.1–3.9 Low, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 7.0–8.9 High, 9.0–10.0 Critical. Why it matters for hunters: programs triage and pay by CVSS, and justifying your score honestly (an unauthenticated RCE is 9.8; a self-XSS is 2) is the difference between a fast payout and a "won't fix." Score the bug you can prove , not the worst case you can imagine. heading: Writing the Report
text: The bug doesn't pay; the report pays. A great report makes the bug trivially reproducible and its impact undeniable. The structure is universal. Title — class + location + impact in one line. Summary — two sentences a non-expert manager understands. Steps to Reproduce — numbered, exact, copy-pasteable (accounts, IDs, requests). Proof of Concept — the minimal request/screenshot that proves it; never more access than needed to demonstrate. Impact — what an attacker actually achieves. Severity — CVSS vector + score, honestly. Remediation — the concrete fix. Stay in scope — only the authorized target, only the access needed to prove the bug, and stop the moment it's proven. Reproducibility and honesty are the whole game. An LLM is a genuine time-saver for the tedious parts of a report — structuring the skeleton above, tightening prose, turning rough notes into clean reproduction steps. But it is a drafting assistant, never the author , and the failure modes are specific: LLMs hallucinate payloads and PoCs that look right but don't actually fire , write reproduction steps that don't match the real target , and pad reports with confident, unproven claims. heading: 1. Pure Go Resolver (netgo) vs. Cgo (getaddrinfo)
text: Go ships with two distinct DNS resolvers in the standard library: 1. The Cgo Resolver: Delegates resolution to the system C library's getaddrinfo(). Because getaddrinfo is a blocking C function, each concurrent DNS lookup consumes an entire OS thread ($M$). If you spawn 5,000 goroutines doing DNS lookups with cgo, the runtime attempts to spawn thousands of OS threads, hitting thread limit crashes or massive thread contention. 2. The Pure Go Resolver (netgo): Reads /etc/resolv.conf, builds raw DNS wire packets in Go, and sends UDP queries directly using asynchronous non-blocking sockets integrated into the Go netpoller (epoll/kqueue). 100,000 concurrent lookups multiplex across a handful of OS worker threads without thread-creation overhead. heading: 2. Socket Descriptor Limits & TIMEWAIT Saturation
text: Massive active enumeration rapidly exhausts system resources if network parameters are untuned: File Descriptor Limits (ulimit -n): Every open TCP connection and UDP socket consumes a file descriptor. Default limits (often 1024 or 4096 on macOS/Linux) cause immediate socket: too many open files errors under high-concurrency fuzzing. High-speed tooling scripts raise this to $65,536$ or higher (ulimit -n 65535). Ephemerals & TIME WAIT: Opening and closing thousands of TCP connections to different hosts leaves sockets in the kernel TIME WAIT state for 60 seconds (RFC 793). When scanning distinct hosts, configure http.Transport.DisableKeepAlives = true and ensure connection timeouts are aggressive (e.g., 2–3s) to prevent exhausting the local ephemeral port range (32768–60999).

heading: 3. HTTP Transport Tuning for Mass Recon
text: When transitioning from DNS enumeration to HTTP probing (httpx-style probers), the standard http.DefaultTransport bottleneck is its restrictive connection pooling (MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 2). For high-throughput recon against many endpoints on the same target host:

heading: 4. UDP Buffer Sizing for Lossless DNS Brute-Forcing
text: During active DNS brute-forcing at 20,000+ packets/sec, the OS default UDP receive buffer (SO RCVBUF) can overflow during micro-bursts, silently dropping responses and causing false negatives (missed subdomains). Tools like massdns and custom Go resolvers expand the kernel socket buffer via syscall.SetsockoptInt(fd, syscall.SOL SOCKET, syscall.SO RCVBUF, 4 1024 1024) (4 MB), preventing kernel-level packet drops. --

heading: Race Conditions
text: The bug that money systems fear most. A race condition (specifically TOCTOU — time-of-check to time-of-use) is when two operations interleave between a check and the action that depends on it, so the check passes for both. Fire enough concurrent requests and you overrun a limit that was only ever checked once per request. A TOCTOU race exists when code checks a condition (balance ≥ amount, coupon unused, withdrawal under daily limit) and then acts on it (deduct, redeem, transfer) as two separate, non-atomic steps. Between the check and the act, a concurrent request can slip in: both requests read the same "valid" state, both pass the check, both act — and the limit is overrun. On the web you trigger it by firing many identical requests simultaneously (the same race a multithreaded program has, but over HTTP). Real impact: withdraw a balance twice, redeem a one-time coupon N times, brute a "3 attempts" code by sending all guesses at once. The fix is atomicity — make check-and-act a single indivisible operation (a lock, an atomic compare-and-swap, or a database transaction with the right isolation / a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE balance = amount). The corpus is full of these. "How I

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: Account Takeover via OAuth
text: Account takeover (ATO) is the corpus's highest-value reachable class ( 532 reports). One of the most common routes is a flaw in the OAuth redirect — and it usually comes down to one weak check: redirect uri validation. In OAuth, after you authorize an app, the provider redirects back to the app's redirect uri carrying a code or token . The provider must verify that redirect uri exactly matches a pre-registered value — because whoever receives that redirect receives the credential. If the check is weak (allows arbitrary subdomains, does a prefix/substring match, permits open-redirect-style //evil.com, or ignores the path), an attacker crafts an authorization link with their redirect uri, the victim clicks it while logged in, and the code/token is delivered to the attacker — instant account takeover. The companion bug is a missing/unchecked state parameter (CSRF on the OAuth flow). The fix: exact-match redirect uri against a strict allowlist, and require a state value bound to the session. The validation logic — broken vs correct — is small, and the difference is everything: "Zero-day in Sign in with Apple" (Bhavuk Jain, $100,000 ) — Apple's OAuth-like flow let an attacker request a

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: Password Reset Flaws
text: The other main road to account takeover: the forgot-password flow. It hands out a credential (a reset token) by email — and every weakness in how that token is generated, delivered, or validated is a takeover. A password-reset flow emails a one-time token that authorizes setting a new password. The classic flaws: predictable tokens (sequential IDs, timestamps, weak PRNGs — guessable, so an attacker resets your password without the email); host-header poisoning (the reset link's domain is built from the request's Host header, so an attacker sets Host: evil.com and the victim's reset link points at the attacker's server, leaking the token when clicked); token leakage (the token returned in an API response, or sent to a redirect uri/Referer); and no expiry / reuse (an old token still works). The fixes: generate tokens with a CSPRNG (crypto/rand), never trust the Host header for link construction (use a configured base URL), single-use and short-expiry, and compare in constant time . The token-generation difference — predictable vs cryptographically secure — is the heart of it: "How I Might Have Hacked Any Microsoft Account" (thezerohack, $50,000 ) brute-forced the reset code by defeat

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: SSRF to Cloud Metadata
text: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) makes the server fetch a URL the attacker controls. On its own it's useful; pointed at a cloud provider's metadata endpoint , it becomes credential theft — the single highest-impact SSRF escalation. SSRF occurs when an app fetches a user-supplied URL without restriction (an image-from-URL feature, a webhook, a PDF renderer, a URL preview). The devastating escalation: cloud VMs expose an instance metadata service at the link-local address 169.254.169.254 , which returns the VM's configuration and its IAM credentials . If an attacker can make the server request http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, they get the server's cloud credentials — often the keys to the whole account. IMDSv1 served these to any request that reached the endpoint; IMDSv2 requires a PUT to fetch a session token first (with a TTL and a hop limit), which most SSRF can't do — so enforcing IMDSv2 is a key mitigation. The app-side fix: validate the fetch target against an allowlist , resolve the hostname and block private/link-local IP ranges (including 169.254.0.0/16, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8), and re-check after redirects. chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: Subdomain Takeover
text: A quieter but common high-value bug: subdomain takeover , where a forgotten DNS record points at a cloud resource that no longer exists — so the attacker creates that resource and becomes the subdomain. A subdomain takeover happens when a DNS record (usually a CNAME) points a subdomain at a third-party service (shop.example.com → example.myshopify.com, or an S3 bucket, Heroku app, GitHub Pages site) that has since been deprovisioned — but the DNS record was never removed. The target is now a dangling pointer : it references a name on a platform where anyone can claim that name. The attacker registers example.myshopify.com (or the S3 bucket, etc.), and now controls content served from shop.example.com — a trusted origin. That trust is the prize: serve phishing on a real subdomain, steal cookies scoped to .example.com, bypass CORS/CSP, or complete an OAuth flow against the trusted host. Detection: enumerate subdomains (recon chapter), check which CNAME to a third party, and test which of those return the platform's "no such app/bucket" fingerprint. The fix: remove DNS records as part of deprovisioning, and claim or monitor dangling ones. The detection heuristic — does a CNAME'd host

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: Supply-Chain Takeover — the abandoned artifact source
text: Subdomain takeover claimed a dangling DNS name . Apply the exact same dangling-pointer logic one layer up — to a dangling software-distribution endpoint — and the prize stops being one trusted origin and becomes code execution on every machine that fetches from it. A supply-chain takeover happens when a build or install step pulls an artifact — a binary, an install script, a package, a container layer — from a source (a cloud bucket , a registry namespace , a CDN path , a package name ) that the original owner has abandoned, but that is still referenced in thousands of Dockerfiles, CI pipelines, install scripts, and curl … sh one-liners. That reference is a dangling pointer to a name anyone can re-claim. The attacker registers the now-free bucket/namespace, serves a malicious artifact under the original name, and every pipeline that still points there fetches and executes it — frequently as root, on every build, fanned out across every consumer at once. It's subdomain takeover's blast radius squared: a dangling DNS record buys one trusted origin; a dangling artifact source buys arbitrary code on everyone who trusts that URL. Detection is empirical — claim or instrument the abandone

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: Business Logic Flaws
text: The subtlest class, and the one scanners never find: business-logic flaws . There's no malformed payload — the application does exactly what it was coded to do, and that behavior is the bug. A business-logic flaw is a vulnerability in the rules of the application, not its technical handling of input. The request is well-formed and "valid"; the logic simply permits something it shouldn't: a negative quantity that turns a purchase into a credit, a skipped step (jump straight to the order-confirmation endpoint without paying), role/state confusion (apply a one-per-customer coupon via multiple accounts, or change a price the client shouldn't control), or an integer underflow on a refund. Scanners can't find these because nothing is malformed — finding them requires understanding the intended workflow and asking "what if I do this step out of order / with a value the designer didn't expect?" That's why they're high-value and human-only. A canonical example — a refund/quantity flaw where a negative value flips the sign of the money — and its guard: "Hacking CloudKit — How I accidentally deleted your Apple Shortcuts" (Detectify, $64,000 ) was a logic/permission flaw in how CloudKit scoped

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: "Forgot to Call the Guard" — broken function-level authz, chained
text: The most embarrassing high-impact bugs aren't missing defenses — they're defenses that exist but weren't called on one route. A privileged, state-changing endpoint authenticates the caller (require auth) but skips the role check (require admin) that every other admin route has. Now any logged-in user mutates server-wide state. Chain that with a missing input guard and one forgotten line becomes a full compromise. BFLA (a.k.a. missing function-level access control, CWE-862) is when an endpoint checks that you're authenticated but not that you're authorized for this function . The classic shape: an admin action (change global config, delete a user, trigger a job) that a normal user can call because the handler never asserts the admin role. It's the function-level cousin of IDOR (which is object-level). The fix is to enforce the role check — ideally at the router/middleware layer so it can't be forgotten per-handler — and to remember that a guard that exists in the codebase but isn't invoked is no guard at all. chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: 1. The Anatomy of a Web Race Window
text: In theory, an in-memory TOCTOU condition has a microscopic window of vulnerability (a few CPU cycles between checking balance = amount and writing balance -= amount). In real-world web services, that window expands by orders of magnitude due to I/O yielding: 1. Goroutine Scheduler Yielding: When a Go handler executes a database query (db.QueryRow(...)) or an external API call, the network I/O blocks. The Go runtime scheduler immediately detaches the goroutine from the processor ($P$) and parks it in the netpoller. 2. Expansion to Milliseconds: The race window widens from nanoseconds to 5–50 milliseconds (the round-trip time to the database). During this extended window, dozens of concurrent HTTP worker goroutines can read the identical, un-updated balance. 3. HTTP/2 Single-Packet Attack: Attackers synchronize requests to hit the server within the same millisecond by multiplexing 30+ HTTP/2 streams inside a single TCP packet. All streams arrive at the server NIC in the exact same TCP window, waking up concurrent worker goroutines simultaneously.

chTitle: High-Value Bug Classes: ATO, Race, SSRF & Logic
heading: 2. Database Isolation & Atomic Countermeasures
text: A common anti-pattern is wrapping check-then-act logic in a basic database transaction: Under standard SQL READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ, both transactions see the starting balance of $100, allowing a double spend of $200. Defensive Fixes in Go: Pessimistic Row Locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): Forces concurrent transactions to block at the database engine level until the first transaction commits or rolls back. Single-Statement Atomic Decrement (Atomic CAS): Returns RowsAffected(). If RowsAffected == 0, the balance was insufficient or already consumed, guaranteeing atomicity without application-level distributed locks.

chTitle: The Case Bank: Real Disclosed Bugs by Class
heading: Exploitation Chains: From Primitive to Impact
text: Disclosed reports highlight that high-payout vulnerabilities are rarely single isolated bugs. They are exploit chains that link low-severity primitives into full system compromise. Identify neglected subdomains, unindexed staging endpoints, and client-side routes extracted from frontend JavaScript bundles. Leverage limited path traversal or overly verbose debug logs to capture internal configuration keys and tokens. Pivot the leaked credentials to authenticate to internal microservices, execute node-level RPC commands, or bypass state validation. Analyzing 6,400+ disclosed security writeups reveals fundamental engineering truths about how systems fail and how Go's design influences vulnerability lifecycles.

chTitle: The Case Bank: Real Disclosed Bugs by Class
heading: 1. The Vulnerability Chaining Graph
text: In real-world security assessments, critical vulnerabilities almost never manifest as a single, textbook exploit. Instead, attackers model targets as directed state graphs: Each intermediate finding escalates the attacker's authorization level or expands their available execution primitives. A "low severity" path traversal that only leaks .env or config.json becomes critical the moment that config contains an encryption key, database password, or inter-service cluster token.

chTitle: The Case Bank: Real Disclosed Bugs by Class
heading: 2. Memory Safety vs. Logic & State Invariants in Go
text: Go is a memory-safe language: unless code imports unsafe or calls into Cgo, buffer overflows, use-after-free (UAF), and dangling pointer exploits are eliminated by the compiler and runtime GC. Consequently, 95%+ of vulnerabilities in Go-based backends fall into state and semantic failures : Business Logic Flaws: State machines that permit invalid transitions (e.g. going from Created $\to$ Fulfilled without passing through Paid). Authorization Gaps (BFLA/IDOR): Handlers that verify that a JWT token is valid (Authentication), but fail to assert that token.Subject == resource.OwnerID (Object-Level Authorization). Concurrency TOCTOU: In-memory check-then-act operations that yield during database I/O, allowing concurrent goroutines to overrun limits.

chTitle: The Case Bank: Real Disclosed Bugs by Class
heading: 3. Parser Differentials & Grammar Discrepancies
text: When two components in a microservice pipeline parse the same payload using slightly different RFC interpretations, a parser differential vulnerability emerges. The Duplicate Key JSON Flaw Consider a request evaluated by a WAF/proxy and then processed by a Go backend: A WAF written in Python/C might validate the first key (role: user) and allow the request through. Go's standard library encoding/json.Unmarshal iterates through keys in sequence and overwrites earlier values with later values, ending with role: admin. Defense: In security-critical paths (e.g. permission or role assignments), use json.NewDecoder with token-by-token validation to reject duplicate keys explicitly before unmarshaling.

chTitle: The Case Bank: Real Disclosed Bugs by Class
heading: 4. Deterministic State Machines in Go
text: To eradicate skip-step and business logic vulnerabilities, model stateful workflows using explicit, closed transition tables rather than ad-hoc boolean flags in HTTP handlers: Enforcing state transitions through a centralized FSM turns business logic rules into deterministic, statically verifiable code invariants. --

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: Mapping a Black-Box API
text: Before any bug, you map the API. A modern API looks opaque from the outside — binary protobuf, obfuscated IDs, no docs — but it leaks its own structure if you know where to look. brutecat's "Decoding Google" is the methodology: turn a black box into a white box. API surface mapping reconstructs an undocumented API's endpoints, parameters, and types from the outside. The richest sources: discovery documents (machine-readable API specs, like Swagger/OpenAPI, that many platforms publish — sometimes staging variants leak internal endpoints and comments); embedded API keys in public web/mobile clients (which often grant access to internal APIs); error messages that name the parameter or type they rejected; and client code (JS bundles, decompiled Android apps) that reveals endpoints and request shapes. The goal is to move from "I can call this one documented endpoint" to "I know every endpoint, every field, and every type the service accepts" — because you cannot attack a parameter you don't know exists. heading: ProtoJSON Schema Fuzzing
text: The sharpest mapping technique deserves its own section, because it's a pure oracle and fully demonstrable. Many gRPC/protobuf services accept a ProtoJSON encoding where fields can be sent positionally (by field number, as a JSON array). Send [1, 2, 3, ...] and the server's error messages leak each field's name and type — one request at a time, the whole schema falls out. Protobuf messages number their fields (field 1, field 2, …). Some services accept a JSON-encoded protobuf (application/json+protobuf) where a message is an array indexed by field number . If you send a value of the wrong type at position N , the server replies with an error like field 'browse id' (2): expected string, got number — leaking the field's name and expected type . Iterate position by position and the error oracle reconstructs the entire message schema, including nested types — no source access, no docs. brutecat used exactly this against YouTube's InnerTube API to extract field names like browse id and continuation. The fix: generic error messages that never echo internal field names or types. Verbose error messages are a vulnerability, not a convenience. Every error that echoes an internal field name,

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: ID → PII Over-Disclosure
text: The YouTube-emails hunt is a perfect, simple lesson: an endpoint that converts an obfuscated identifier into personal data without checking whether the caller should be allowed to. The obfuscation felt like security; it wasn't. Systems use obfuscated/opaque IDs (a Gaia ID, a UUID, a hashed token) to refer to users internally, on the assumption that an attacker can't link them to a real person. The vulnerability: some other endpoint accepts that opaque ID and returns PII (an email, phone, name) without verifying the caller is authorized to learn it. If the attacker can obtain the opaque ID through one feature (YouTube live-chat leaked Gaia IDs) and resolve it to PII through another (Pixel Recorder's share endpoint returned the email for a Gaia ID), the obfuscation is defeated end to end. The root cause is missing authorization on the resolution endpoint — an opaque ID is not an access-control boundary. The fix: every endpoint that returns PII must check that this caller is allowed to see this subject's data, regardless of how the ID was obtained. brutecat's "Leaking the email of any YouTube user" chained exactly this: YouTube's live-chat Internal People API leaked any channel's obfu

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: Rate Limits at Scale
text: To brute-force anything against a giant, you must defeat the rate limit. The phone-number hunt shows the two ways attackers do it: token reuse (a token meant for a hard path accepted on an easy one) and — the big one — IP rotation via IPv6 . An IP-based limiter assumes IPs are scarce. With IPv6, they aren't. Rate limiters often key their counters on the client IP address — N requests per IP per window. This assumes addresses are scarce, which is true for IPv4. But an attacker with an IPv6 allocation typically controls an entire /64 subnet — that's 2⁶⁴ (over 18 quintillion) addresses, all theirs. If the limiter keys on the full 128-bit address, the attacker simply uses a fresh source address for every request , and every request looks like a brand-new client — the limit never triggers. The fix: for IPv6, rate-limit by the /64 (or shorter) prefix , not the full address, because a /64 is the smallest unit normally assigned to a single customer. Keying on the prefix collapses the attacker's 18 quintillion addresses back into one bucket. The fix is a one-line change to what you key the counter on — runnable: When executing high-throughput reconnaissance or distributed API fuzzing at sca

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: 1. The http.Transport Pooling Architecture (Go 1.22+)
text: In Go's net/http, http.Transport manages a pool of idle network connections via an internal idleConn cache (keyed by connectMethodKey, which encapsulates proxy, scheme, and target address): Default Limits: The default http.DefaultTransport sets MaxIdleConns = 100 globally, but MaxIdleConnsPerHost = 2 . Under 10,000 concurrent goroutines hitting the same host, 9,998 connections are aggressively closed (TIME WAIT socket explosion on the OS). Custom Tuned Transport: High-scale tooling sets MaxIdleConns = 0 (unlimited), MaxIdleConnsPerHost = 10000, and tunes IdleConnTimeout = 90 time.Second. Dialer Context & Socket Binding: For IPv6 rotation, custom net.Dialer.Control or DialContext functions invoke syscall.Bind before connect() to cycle source IPv6 addresses within a /64 prefix per TCP handshake without allocating new transport instances.

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: 2. HTTP/2 Multiplexing & Frame Processing
text: When http2.Transport upgrades a connection via ALPN (h2): Single TCP Connection, Multiple Streams: Instead of opening 1,000 TCP sockets, Go opens a single TLS connection and multiplexes requests using 31-bit stream IDs. The server's SETTINGS MAX CONCURRENT STREAMS (typically 100–250) determines the concurrency ceiling. Stream State Machine & Flow Control: Each HTTP/2 stream maintains independent WINDOW UPDATE credit counters. If the client floods the server without consuming response bodies, Go's stream buffer fills, stalling subsequent frame writes until backpressure clears. HPACK Header Table Compression: Go allocates dynamic ring buffers (hpack.Decoder and hpack.Encoder) per connection to deduplicate repeated headers (e.g., :authority, User-Agent), saving significant CPU and egress bandwidth during large-scale fuzzing campaigns.

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: 3. Memory & GC Footprint Under Load
text: Buffer Pooling with sync.Pool: Go's runtime uses internal sync.Pool instances for bufio.Reader and bufio.Writer allocations (typically 4KB–32KB chunks). Failing to drain and close resp.Body via io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body) and resp.Body.Close() leaks underlying buffers back to the garbage collector rather than recycling them to the pool. Goroutine Worker Pools: Spawning an unbounded goroutine per request (2 KB × 100,000 ≈ 200 MB just for stack frames) causes GC latency spikes. High-performance fuzzers use fixed worker pools paired with persistent http.Client instances to keep allocations near zero. --

heading: The Masked-Value Oracle
text: Rate limit defeated, you still need to shrink the search space . Recovery flows helpfully show a masked version of the secret (•• ••••••03), and a separate endpoint acts as an oracle telling you hit-or-miss. Together they make brute force tractable. A masked-value oracle combines two leaks. First, a UI shows a partial secret to help a legitimate user recognize it — a masked phone (•• ••••••03), masked email (a••••@gmail.com), or last-4 of a card. This reveals some digits and the length , collapsing the search space (a 9-digit number with 2 known digits is 10⁷, not 10⁹). Second, a separate endpoint behaves as a boolean oracle : it responds differently for a correct vs incorrect guess (a 302 to …/challenge vs …/noaccountsfound), so the attacker can test candidates. Mask shrinks the space; oracle searches it. The fix: don't reveal mask details to unauthenticated callers, and make the oracle indistinguishable (identical response + timing whether or not the account/value exists). brutecat's "Leaking the phone number of any Google account" combined all of it: a Looker Studio ownership-transfer leaked the target's display name (needed to validate guesses), the password-recovery flow showe

chTitle: API Recon & Abuse at Scale: Lessons from the Google Hunts
heading: Notification Suppression
text: A small but devastating trick from the YouTube hunt: the email-resolution would have emailed the victim ("X shared a recording with you"), tipping them off. brutecat suppressed it by making a different field — the recording title — 2.5 million characters , which broke the notification path while the resolution still succeeded silently. Many sensitive actions fire a notification (email/SMS) so the victim notices ("a new device signed in", "X shared with you"). An attacker who can make that notification fail gets to act silently . A common way: find an unbounded input field the notification depends on (a title, a display name) and supply a value so large it breaks the notification pipeline (a template that can't render, a downstream size limit that throws) after the core action has already committed. The action succeeds; the alert never sends. Root causes: no length validation on the field, and a notification path that fails open (silently) instead of closed . The fixes: bound every input field, and treat a failed security notification as a failed operation (roll back or alert), never a silent no-op. --

text: None of these bugs is "RCE" alone. The Google Cloud hunt's lesson is composition : information disclosure → IDOR → privilege escalation → arbitrary RPC execution, each step a separate medium-severity bug, the chain a P0. brutecat's two-part Google Cloud hunt (CVE-2026-2031 and a follow-up) chained: proto-definition disclosure (verbose debug endpoints) → cross-tenant IDOR (the UUID binary-search above, plus GetIntegrationVersion) → ACL bypass (a second admin account approving the attacker's own workflow, defeating two-person review) → arbitrary Stubby RPC via the over-permissioned GenericStubbyTypedTaskV2, executing as the platform's production service identity . First RCE $60,000 , second $88,337 . The meta-lesson the report drives home: an internal task system that can call arbitrary RPCs under a production identity is a loaded weapon the moment any authorization gap reaches it — defense in depth means every link, and least privilege on the task system itself. --

chTitle: CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, From Zero
heading: The Same-Origin Policy
text: You cannot understand CORS until you understand the rule it bends. That rule is the same-origin policy (SOP) , and it is the single most important security boundary in your browser. An origin is the triple of scheme + host + port — for example, the scheme https, host app.example.com, and port 443. Two URLs have the same origin only if all three match exactly. https://app.example.com/login and https://app.example.com/account are same-origin (only the path differs, and the path is not part of the origin). But http://app.example.com (different scheme), https://api.example.com (different host), and https://app.example.com:8443 (different port) are each a different origin. The common mistake is thinking "same domain = same origin"; the scheme and port count too, and a subdomain is a different host. The same-origin policy is a browser rule: JavaScript running on one origin may send a request to another origin, but it generally may not read the response unless that other origin explicitly permits it. Without SOP, any website you visited could quietly make requests to mail.yourbank.com using the cookies already in your browser and read your inbox or balance. SOP is what stops evil.com's Ja

chTitle: CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, From Zero
heading: What CORS Actually Is
text: Strip away the mystique: CORS is a set of HTTP response headers your server sends, plus a handshake the browser runs on its own. There is no magic, no library requirement, no framework. CORS is your server answering one question for the browser: "Is the origin that made this request allowed to read my response, and if it's a risky request, is it even allowed to send it?" CORS is a W3C/Fetch standard that lets a server selectively relax the same-origin policy for chosen origins, using HTTP headers. When a browser makes a cross-origin request, it adds an Origin request header naming the page's origin. The server's response includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and friends) saying which origin(s) may read the response. The browser compares the two: if the response permits the requesting origin, JavaScript gets to read it; if not, the browser throws the famous CORS error and hides the response. CORS is opt-in by the server and enforced by the browser — a server with no CORS headers simply can't be read cross-origin (the safe default), and a server can open up to specific partners by echoing their origin. --

chTitle: CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, From Zero
heading: Simple vs Preflight
text: Not all cross-origin requests are treated the same. The browser splits them into two kinds, and the second one sends a second, hidden request first — the thing that confuses everyone the first time they open the Network tab and see an OPTIONS they never wrote. A simple request is one the browser considers low-risk enough to send directly (and only then check the response's CORS headers). Only if the server's preflight response approves does the browser send the real request. heading: Credentials & Cookies
text: This is where CORS gets dangerous, and where the worst misconfigurations live. By default, cross-origin fetch does not send cookies. But the moment credentials enter the picture, the rules tighten — and getting them wrong is how a CORS header becomes an account takeover. By default a cross-origin fetch sends no cookies, no HTTP auth, no client certs — so even a wide-open Access-Control-Allow-Origin: only exposes public data. Credentials are sent only when the client opts in (fetch(url, )) and the server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true . Critically, when credentials are allowed, the spec forbids the wildcard : Access-Control-Allow-Origin must be a specific echoed origin , never . The reason is exactly the danger — credentialed cross-origin reads expose authenticated data (the user's inbox, balance, tokens), so the browser refuses to let "any origin" ( ) read them; the server must name the one origin it trusts. The lethal bug is a server that reflects the request's Origin into Allow-Origin and sends Allow-Credentials: true — that's "any origin, with the user's cookies," the wildcard the spec forbids, achieved by hand. heading: 1. The Preflight Decision Tree in Web Engines (Chromium & WebKit)
text: A browser determines whether to trigger an OPTIONS preflight before dispatching a cross-origin network request based on the Fetch Specification: Simple Request Criteria: A request bypasses preflight only if the HTTP method is GET, HEAD, or POST, and all custom headers belong to the CORS-safelisted set (Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type), with Content-Type restricted to application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain. Preflight Cache Partitioning (Access-Control-Max-Age): Browsers maintain a preflight cache keyed on (origin, url, method, request-headers). Chromium caps Max-Age at 7,200 seconds (2 hours), while Firefox allows up to 86,400 seconds (24 hours). The Critical Vary: Origin Header: When a Go server dynamically inspects r.Header.Get("Origin") against an allowlist and responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://trusted.example.com, it must attach Vary: Origin. Without Vary: Origin, reverse proxies (Cloudflare, Fastly, Nginx) or browser disk caches will cache the response for Origin A and serve it to Origin B, causing CORS failures or leaking authenticated JSON responses across origins.

heading: When CORS Won't Save You
text: The most dangerous misconceptions about CORS are about what it doesn't do. Internalize these or you'll trust it for protection it never provides. CORS is enforced by the browser . A non-browser client — curl, a Go program, a script — ignores it completely and reads your response regardless of any Allow-Origin header. CORS controls what other websites can do in a victim's browser . It is not authentication or authorization. Your real access control (auth tokens, ownership checks) still has to be there. CORS governs reads ; CSRF is about unwanted writes . A simple cross-origin POST still reaches your server with the user's cookies even with no CORS headers — the attacker just can't read the response. If that POST has a side effect, you have CSRF. Defend it separately (SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, CrossOriginProtection). Allow-Origin: on a public, unauthenticated endpoint is fine. The same on an endpoint that returns user data with credentials is a serious vulnerability. The bug isn't the wildcard itself — it's the combination with credentials/sensitive data. desc: The producer side of real-time Go, built end to end: the WebSocket Hub pattern (one goroutine owning the client set; register/unregister/broadcast over channels; per-client send buffers and slow-client drop so one stalled connection can't block the fan-out; ping/pong keepalives) for pushing live events to many clients; and outbound webhooks (signing the payload with HMAC-SHA256, delivering with retries + exponential backoff + jitter, dead-lettering after exhaustion, and at-least-once delivery that forces the receiver to dedup). text: Here's the thing, sport. Your server knows something — a payment cleared, a price moved, a job finished — and someone else needs to know now . Not on their next poll. Now. There are two ways a Go server pushes an event out into the world, and this chapter builds both , properly. The first is the WebSocket Hub : a long-lived, full-duplex pipe to many connected clients — a live dashboard, a trading feed, a chat room — where your server fans one event out to thousands of browsers at once. You've seen a single WebSocket connection (the HTTP-servers chapter). That's not a real-time app; that's an echo. The real thing is the Hub pattern — one goroutine owning the whole client set, broadcasting over channels, and (the part everyone gets wrong) surviving the one slow client that would otherwise freeze the fan-out for everybody. The second is the outbound webhook : instead of holding a connection open, you POST the event to a URL the other system gave you — how Stripe tells your backend a charge succeeded, how GitHub tells your CI a push happened. chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: Two Ways to Push
text: Both patterns solve the same problem — get an event from my server to someone else, promptly — but they make opposite trade-offs, and picking the wrong one is a design smell you'll feel for months. A server has two fundamental ways to push an event outward. A WebSocket holds a single TCP connection open between your server and a connected client (typically a browser) and sends frames over it in both directions, for as long as the connection lives — ideal when the client is online now and wants a stream of low-latency updates (a live feed, a chat, a dashboard). An outbound webhook keeps no connection: when an event happens, your server makes a brand-new HTTP POST to a URL another server registered in advance, then hangs up — ideal for server-to-server notifications where the recipient may be offline, behind a queue, or processing asynchronously (a payment processor telling your backend a charge cleared). The rule of thumb: WebSocket when a user's screen needs live updates; webhook when another system needs to be notified of an event. One is a held-open pipe to a present client; the other is a fire-and-retry message to an absent server. Full-duplex, low-latency, client usually a brow

chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: The WebSocket Hub
text: A single WebSocket connection is easy. The app is the hard part: when an event fires, every connected client must get it — and clients connect and disconnect constantly. The answer is the Hub : one goroutine that owns the entire set of clients, so the set is mutated from exactly one place and needs no lock. The Hub pattern is the canonical Go design for broadcasting to many WebSocket clients. A single hub goroutine owns a map of connected clients and selects over three channels: register (a new client joined), unregister (a client left), and broadcast (an event to send to everyone). Because only the hub goroutine ever touches the client map, there is no mutex — concurrency is handled by communication , not shared memory (the Go proverb). Each client gets its own buffered send channel ; the hub writes a broadcast into every client's send channel, and a per-client writer goroutine drains that channel to the socket. This cleanly separates who is connected (the hub's job) from writing bytes to one socket (each client's job), and it's the structure under essentially every Go chat/live-feed/dashboard server. heading: Slow Clients
text: That non-blocking send is not a detail — it's the entire reason a hub survives production. Get it wrong and a single phone on a flaky connection takes down your broadcast for every user. A blocking broadcast lets one slow client freeze everyone. The naive hub writes c.send --

chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: Ping/Pong & Lifecycle
text: A WebSocket can sit open for hours. Two things will bite you: connections that die silently (no FIN packet — the client's laptop just slept), and writes that block forever on a stuck socket. Keepalives and deadlines handle both. The server periodically sends a ping frame; a healthy client auto-replies pong . No pong within a deadline → the connection is dead (silently dropped, asleep, gone), so you close it and unregister. Without this, dead connections accumulate as zombie goroutines forever. coder/websocket and gorilla/websocket both expose this. After the HTTP upgrade, net/http's WriteTimeout no longer applies — the connection was hijacked out of its control (you saw this in ch19). So you set a deadline on every write (a context timeout, e.g. 5–10s). A slow client that can't accept a write is closed instead of pinning its writer goroutine until the TCP stack gives up minutes later. Every exit path — read error, failed ping, write deadline, server shutdown — must funnel to hub.unregister, which deletes the client and closes its send channel. That close is what ends the writer goroutine (a range over a closed channel returns). Miss it and you leak a goroutine per dead connection.

chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: Outbound Webhooks
text: Switch models. The recipient isn't a browser holding a connection — it's another company's server, and it gave you a URL. When your event fires, you POST to that URL. Simple in the happy path; the entire engineering is in the failure path, because their server will be down sometimes and you must not lose the event. An outbound webhook is your server notifying another server of an event by making an HTTP POST to a URL that server registered with you in advance , carrying the event as a JSON body. Unlike a WebSocket there is no persistent connection: each event is a fresh, independent request. Because the receiver is an external system you don't control — it may be deploying, overloaded, or briefly offline — reliable delivery is not "send and forget." It requires four things: signing the payload (so the receiver can verify it really came from you and wasn't tampered with), retrying on failure with backoff (their 503 is usually transient), dead-lettering after you exhaust retries (so a permanently-down receiver doesn't block or lose everything), and accepting at-least-once semantics (a retry after a network timeout may deliver twice, so the receiver must dedup). chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: Signing
text: The receiver needs to know the POST really came from you and wasn't forged or modified in transit. You don't share a password on every request — you sign the payload with a shared secret, and they recompute the signature to check it. (This is the exact mechanism you verified on the inbound side in the payments chapter — now you're the one producing it.) HMAC signing proves a webhook's authenticity and integrity without sending the secret. You and the receiver share a secret out of band (when they register the webhook). For each delivery you compute HMAC-SHA256(secret, rawBody) and send it in a header (e.g. X-Signature: sha256=…). The receiver recomputes the same HMAC over the exact raw bytes it received and compares — using a constant-time comparison (hmac.Equal) to avoid timing attacks. If they match, the body is authentic (only someone with the secret could produce that MAC) and untampered (any change to the body changes the MAC). Two non-negotiables: sign the raw bytes , not a re-serialized struct (re-marshaling can reorder keys and break the signature), and compare in constant time. chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: Retries & Dead-Letters
text: Now the delivery engine itself — the part that turns "POST once and hope" into reliable delivery. We send the signed payload, retry transient failures with backoff, and give up into a dead-letter queue after a bounded number of attempts. The retry loop above just says "sleep backoff(attempt)". Get that backoff wrong and you build a self-inflicted outage: if every sender retries on the same exponential schedule, a receiver that blips comes back to a synchronized thundering herd — every pending webhook from every sender hitting it at the identical instant, knocking it back down. The fix is exponential backoff plus jitter (randomize each delay) so retries spread out instead of resonating. This is exactly the time/backoff/jitter material — reuse it here; a webhook sender is one of its highest-value applications. --

chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: At-Least-Once
text: The last truth about webhooks, and the one that surprises people: you cannot guarantee exactly-once delivery, so you guarantee at-least-once and make the receiver dedup. This is the same lesson as idempotency in distributed systems, applied to your delivery engine. At-least-once means every event is delivered one or more times — never zero, possibly twice. It's unavoidable: if your POST times out, you don't know whether the receiver processed it before the network dropped the response, so you must retry — and if it had succeeded, that retry is a duplicate. You can't tell the two cases apart, so you choose at-least-once (retry, risk a dupe) over at-most-once (don't retry, risk a loss) — losing a "payment succeeded" event is far worse than processing it twice. The contract that makes this safe is a stable event id (e.g. X-Webhook-Id: evt 123) sent identically on every retry of the same event. The receiver records processed ids and ignores any it has already seen, so a duplicate delivery is a no-op. You provide the stable id and the retries; the receiver provides the dedup. heading: 1. The HTTP Connection Hijack (http.Hijacker)
text: Standard net/http handlers manage the request-response lifecycle and automatically close connections on return. Upgrading to a persistent WebSocket requires seizing direct ownership of the underlying TCP socket: Calling Hijack() detaches the connection from http.Server. Go returns a bufio.ReadWriter (bufrw) holding any bytes already buffered from the client handshake. Any subsequent writes bypass net/http's response formatting.

chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: 2. RFC 6455 Framing & The Client Masking Invariant
text: A WebSocket message is split into one or more binary frames on the wire: Byte 0: FIN (1 bit indicating final frame), RSV1-3 (3 extension bits, usually 0), Opcode (4 bits: 0x1 Text, 0x2 Binary, 0x8 Close, 0x9 Ping, 0xA Pong). Byte 1: MASK bit (1 bit) + 7-bit Payload Length. If length $\le 125$, the 7-bit value is the exact length. If length $= 126$, the next 2 bytes encode an unsigned 16-bit integer length. If length $= 127$, the next 8 bytes encode an unsigned 64-bit integer length. Masking Key (4 bytes): Mandated by RFC 6455 for all client-to-server frames (and strictly forbidden for server-to-client frames). Why? To prevent cache poisoning attacks against intermediary transparent proxies: if an attacker's script in a browser could send unmasked predictable raw HTTP request bytes inside a WebSocket payload, an unsuspecting intermediate proxy might misinterpret the stream as pipelined HTTP requests.

chTitle: Real-Time Go: WebSocket Hubs & Outbound Webhooks
heading: 3. TCP Buffer Bloat, SOSNDBUF, and Netpoll Semantics
text: When a Go server writes to a WebSocket (conn.Write(b)): Bytes enter the OS kernel socket send buffer (SO SNDBUF, typically 64KB–256KB). If a slow client stops acknowledging TCP packets (window size collapses to 0), the kernel buffer fills. When SO SNDBUF is full, conn.Write would block the calling goroutine. In Go's runtime, net.Conn delegates to the runtime network poller (netpoll via epoll/kqueue), parking the goroutine until the socket is writable. If the Hub sends directly to slow sockets without buffered channels and select with default, every active sender goroutine parks in netpoll, stalling the entire broadcast system. Per-client buffered channels decouple the Hub's broadcast loop from kernel socket backpressure. --

heading: 1. Ephemeral Container Isolation & Linux Cgroups
text: To run untrusted user-submitted Go code safely and instantly, sandbox runners employ a hardened execution environment: Linux Cgroups v2 Resource Constraints: Every execution is isolated within a lightweight container bounded by strict kernel cgroups — typically capped at cpu.max = 100000 100000 (1 vCPU core), memory.max = 64MB, and pids.max = 64 to prevent fork bombs and memory exhaustion. Seccomp Syscall Filtering: The runner drops Linux capabilities (CAP NET RAW, CAP SYS ADMIN) and restricts syscalls via a custom BPF filter. Raw socket creation (AF INET, AF PACKET) and arbitrary disk I/O are blocked; file writes are restricted to an ephemeral, in-memory tmpfs volume that is wiped upon process exit. Strict Execution Timeouts: A hard timeout (usually 3.0 to 5.0 seconds) is enforced at the kernel level via SIGKILL if code encounters an infinite loop or deadlock.

heading: 2. Fast Compilation Semantics & Pre-Warmed Toolchains
text: Compiling Go code in sub-100ms response windows requires bypassing standard go build cold-start penalties: Pre-Compiled Standard Library Cache: The standard library (fmt, net/http, sync, os, crypto/...) is pre-compiled into Go's build cache (GOCACHE and pkg/linux amd64). When the runner compiles main.go, the compiler only tokenizes and generates machine code for your single file, linking against the pre-warmed archive objects (.a files). In-Memory Compilation: The source file is written directly to a tmpfs RAM disk (/tmp/sandbox/main.go), eliminating disk controller latency. The compiler emits an in-memory ELF executable that is directly invoked with syscall.Exec.

heading: 3. Runtime Determinism & Output Capture (Go 1.22+)
text: Buffered Standard Stream Interleaving: Output from os.Stdout and os.Stderr is buffered through non-blocking Linux pipes. The runner captures stdout and stderr concurrently, returning a unified JSON payload containing the exit code, execution duration, and combined output string. Deterministic Scheduling: Under sandboxed single-core execution (GOMAXPROCS=1), goroutine preemption occurs primarily at function prologues and runtime scheduler checkpoints, making concurrent test assertions reliable and deterministic. --

desc: The PortSwigger-class attacks that exploit how proxies, caches, and origin servers DISAGREE about a single HTTP request — explained from the bytes up, Go-grounded. HTTP request smuggling (CL.TE / TE.CL desync, and an empirical look at how strictly Go's net/http parses ambiguous Content-Length / Transfer-Encoding so a Go origin doesn't disagree with itself); Host header attacks (password-reset poisoning, routing and cache off a forgeable r.Host, with the allowlist/configured-base-URL fix); and web cache poisoning (reflecting an unkeyed input like X-Forwarded-Host into a cached response that's then served to every victim). Every server-side behavior runnable and verified.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Most vulnerabilities live inside a request — a bad parameter, a missing check. This chapter is about a stranger class: bugs that live in the request itself , in how the machines along its path disagree about what it even is. A modern web request passes through a chain — CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy, your Go server — and each one re-parses it. When two of them read the same bytes differently , an attacker slips into the gap. That's the whole family: request smuggling (the front-end and back-end disagree where one request ends and the next begins), Host header attacks (your server trusts a header the client controls to decide who it is ), and web cache poisoning (a shared cache stores one attacker's poisoned response and serves it to everyone ) — plus its mirror image, web cache deception (the attacker reads a victim's cached, authenticated page back out). These are PortSwigger Web Security Academy signature topics, and they reward understanding HTTP at the byte level — which is exactly where Go is interesting. We'll empirically test how strictly Go's net/http parses ambiguous Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding (the answer is reassuring, and precise), then

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: The Disagreement
text: Every attack in this chapter has the same shape: two machines parse one request differently. Name that shape and the whole family clicks into place. A request travels through a chain of HTTP intermediaries — CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy, application server — and each one re-parses the raw bytes . They're supposed to agree, because they all implement the same HTTP spec. A request-level attack exploits a case where two of them disagree : they read the same bytes and reach different conclusions about where a request ends ( smuggling ), which site it's for ( Host header ), or what may be cached and reused ( cache poisoning ). The attacker crafts bytes that are ambiguous — valid to read one way by the front-end and another way by the back-end — and lives in the gap. The defense theme is equally consistent: eliminate the ambiguity (strict, identical parsing everywhere) and never trust a request-controlled value (framing headers, Host, forwarded headers) for a security decision without validating it. --

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: Request Smuggling
text: The canonical disagreement is over a request's length . HTTP/1.1 gives two ways to say how long a body is — Content-Length (a byte count) and Transfer-Encoding: chunked (length-prefixed chunks). Send both , contradictorily, and you've handed the front-end and back-end a choice to disagree on. HTTP request smuggling desynchronizes a front-end proxy and a back-end server by making them disagree about where one request ends and the next begins. The body length of an HTTP/1.1 request can be declared by Content-Length (CL) or Transfer-Encoding: chunked (TE). If a request includes both , the two servers may resolve the conflict differently: in CL.TE , the front-end uses Content-Length while the back-end uses Transfer-Encoding; in TE.CL , the reverse. Either way, one server thinks the request ended where the other thinks it's still going — so bytes the attacker placed after the "end" get prepended to the next request on that shared connection. That smuggled prefix can poison another user's request: stealing their session, bypassing front-end security rules, or routing them to attacker content. The root cause is ambiguous framing tolerated by at least one parser ; the cure is for every hop

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: Why Go Resists It
text: So where does a Go server sit in this? The reassuring, precise answer: Go's net/http is strict and deterministic about ambiguous framing — which means a Go origin doesn't disagree with itself, and is a hard back-end to desync. Don't take my word for it — let's send raw ambiguous requests down a TCP socket to a real Go server and watch how it responds. A strict Go origin is not the same as a safe deployment. Go follows TE-over-CL, rejects duplicate Content-Length (400), and rejects unknown Transfer-Encoding (501) — so it parses ambiguity consistently , which is exactly what a back-end needs to resist smuggling. But smuggling lives in the disagreement between hops, so your safety also depends on the front-end. If a CDN/proxy ahead of Go is less strict — say it honors Content-Length while Go honors Transfer-Encoding — the two disagree and the desync happens regardless of how clean Go is. The robust fixes are architectural: prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end (its length framing is unambiguous, killing the CL/TE class), ensure every hop parses identically and rejects ambiguity , and avoid reusing a single back-end connection across different users where you can. Go gives you a strong back-end; th

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: 1. The Parsing Pipeline in Go's net/http (Go 1.22+)
text: Inside net/http/request.go, Go invokes readRequest(b bufio.Reader) to parse incoming wire bytes into structured http.Request instances: Strict Header Field Line Grammar: Go uses net/textproto.Reader.ReadLineBytes. It strictly enforces \r\n line delimiters and rejects obsolete line folding (multiline headers starting with whitespace/tab), returning 400 Bad Request. Precedence Rule Enforcement (RFC 7230 §3.3.3 / RFC 9112 §6.3): If an incoming request contains both Transfer-Encoding: chunked and Content-Length: , Go removes the Content-Length header from req.Header and sets req.TransferEncoding = []string . The body is wrapped in an internal chunkedReader. Duplicate & Malformed Header Handling: Multiple Content-Length headers with mismatched values immediately trigger a bad Content-Length header error and a 400 Bad Request response. Any unknown Transfer-Encoding token (e.g. Transfer-Encoding: chunked, identity or obfuscated Transfer-Encoding: xchunked) causes Go to return 501 Not Implemented, refusing to guess or fall back to Content-Length.

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: 2. Front-End vs. Back-End Desync Vectors
text: While Go's origin server behaves deterministically, request smuggling occurs when upstream proxies (Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB, Cloudflare) parse headers differently: CL.TE Desync: The front-end proxy reads Content-Length, forwarding $X$ bytes across a persistent backend connection. Go's backend reads Transfer-Encoding: chunked, reading the terminal chunk 0\r\n\r\n and interpreting the trailing bytes as the prefix of the next HTTP request in the TCP stream. TE.CL Desync: The front-end proxy processes Transfer-Encoding: chunked and forwards the entire stream. If an obfuscation (e.g. Transfer-Encoding: [\t]chunked) causes the front-end to recognize chunked encoding but causes an intermediary to ignore it and fall back to Content-Length, remaining chunk payloads leak into subsequent user requests. H2.CL / H2.TE Request Downgrading: Modern front-ends receive HTTP/2 from clients (where stream length is framed explicitly) but downgrade connections to HTTP/1.1 keep-alive pools when talking to backend Go origins. If the front-end translates HTTP/2 pseudo-headers into conflicting HTTP/1.1 content-length and transfer-encoding headers, request smuggling can occur across downgraded pools.

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: 3. Connection Reuse & Boundary Isolation
text: Smuggling relies on persistent TCP connection reuse across multiple distinct users. Enforcing http.Transport.DisableKeepAlives = true on sensitive internal proxies, or running end-to-end HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 (where binary frame stream multiplexing eliminates text-based framing ambiguity), completely neutralizes the attack surface. --

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: Host Header Attacks
text: Next disagreement: not about length , but about identity . Your server often needs to know "what host am I serving right now?" to build absolute URLs or route. The only source for that is the Host header — which the client sends and can set to anything. The HTTP Host header tells a server which virtual host a request is for; in Go it surfaces as r.Host (from the Host header, or the :authority pseudo-header on HTTP/2). It is client-controlled — an attacker can send any value. A Host header attack exploits code that trusts r.Host for a security-relevant decision. The classic is password-reset poisoning : the reset email builds its link from r.Host, so an attacker triggering a reset for a victim — with Host: evil.attacker.com — causes the victim's email to contain a link to the attacker's domain carrying the real reset token ; when the victim clicks, the token leaks. The same trust enables cache-key confusion, routing bypasses, and SSRF-via-routing. The fix is to never derive security-relevant values from r.Host unchecked : validate it against an allowlist of expected hosts, or build absolute URLs from a configured base URL held in server config, not from the request. --

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: Web Cache Poisoning
text: The third disagreement is about reuse . A shared cache stores a response under a key (usually method + path + a few headers) and serves it to everyone who asks for that key. If the response depends on an input the cache doesn't include in its key, an attacker can save a poisoned response once and have it served to every later visitor. A web cache speeds things up by storing a response under a cache key — typically the request method and URL path, plus a small set of headers — and replaying it for every subsequent request with the same key. A keyed input is part of that key (different value → different cache entry); an unkeyed input is not (the cache ignores it). Web cache poisoning happens when a response reflects an unkeyed input into its body: the attacker sends a request whose unkeyed header (say X-Forwarded-Host: evil.attacker.com) gets reflected into, e.g., a , the cache stores that poisoned response under the normal key, and every later victim requesting that path is served the attacker's version — a stored, cache-amplified XSS/redirect affecting everyone. The defenses: don't reflect request inputs into cacheable responses at all; if a response legitimately varies by a header

chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: Web Cache Deception
text: Poisoning and its mirror image share one machine — the shared cache — but run in opposite directions . Poisoning has the attacker write a bad response into the cache so it's served to everyone. Web cache deception (WCD) has the attacker read a response the cache should never have stored in the first place: a victim's own authenticated page , sitting in a shared cache, fetched back out by the attacker. No injection, no XSS — just a sensitive response that got cached under a key the attacker can also request. Web cache deception tricks a shared cache (CDN/proxy) into storing a user-specific, authenticated response, which the attacker then retrieves . The mechanism is a disagreement between the cache and the origin about whether a response is cacheable . Two ingredients are required: the response must contain sensitive per-user data (a profile page with PII, or — as in real reports — an auth token embedded in the HTML/JS ), and the cache must decide to store it (the origin didn't mark it Cache-Control: no-store/private, so the CDN's default — cache a 200 GET — wins). chTitle: Request-Level Attacks: Smuggling, Host Header & Cache Poisoning
heading: Defenses
text: The three attacks share one cure and a few specifics. Internalize the pattern and you defend the whole class. Prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end (unambiguous length framing eliminates the CL/TE class). Ensure every hop parses identically and rejects ambiguity — Go's origin already 400s duplicate Content-Length and 501s unknown Transfer-Encoding; demand the same strictness from your CDN/proxy. Avoid sharing one back-end connection across different users where feasible. Build absolute URLs (reset links, redirects, canonical links) from a configured base URL in server config, not from r.Host. Where you must use the request's host, validate it against an allowlist of expected hosts and reject the rest. Treat X-Forwarded-Host/X-Forwarded-For as untrusted unless set by a proxy you control. Never reflect a request input into a cacheable response. If a response legitimately varies by a header, include that header in the cache key and announce it with Vary . Strip forwarded headers your app doesn't use so a cache can't be tricked into keying (or not keying) on them. Every one is a request-controlled value trusted too far across a parser boundary. text: Here's the thing, sport. Every web hacker you've ever read a writeup from used the same tool, and it isn't magic — it's a proxy . Burp Suite sits between your browser and the target, and every request your browser makes flows through Burp first. That one fact — that Burp is a man-in-the-middle you point at yourself — is the whole foundation. Once a request is paused in Burp, you can read it, change it, replay it a thousand times with different values, and watch what comes back. That's how you find an IDOR (change the id), test an auth bypass (drop the token), or fuzz a parameter (Intruder). The browser is just where the request starts ; Burp is where you attack it. This chapter explains Burp from the mechanism up , the way the rest of the Bible does — not a button tour, but why it works. We'll prove the interception model with a runnable Go proxy that does exactly what Burp does at its core (intercept a request and modify it in flight), explain the TLS story (why you install Burp's CA certificate and what that actually means), then walk each tool — Proxy , Repeater , Intruder , Decoder , Comparer , Sequencer , Scanner — and when you reach for it.
