chTitle: Burp Suite: How It Works & How to Use It
heading: What Burp Is
text: Strip the marketing and Burp Suite is two things glued together: a proxy that captures your traffic, and a toolkit that operates on captured requests. Burp Suite is an integrated platform for testing web application security, built around an intercepting proxy . You configure your browser to send all its traffic through Burp; Burp records every request and response (building a sitemap of the target), and lets you pause, inspect, modify, and replay any of them. Around that proxy sit specialized tools: Repeater (resend and tweak a single request by hand), Intruder (resend a request many times with automated payloads — for fuzzing, brute-forcing, enumeration), Decoder/Inspector (encode/decode data), Comparer (diff two responses), Sequencer (analyze the randomness of tokens), and — in the paid Professional edition — an automated Scanner . The free Community edition includes the proxy, Repeater, Decoder, and a rate-limited Intruder, which is enough to learn every technique in this course. Burp is not an exploit; it's a precision instrument for seeing and manipulating HTTP, which is where almost every web vulnerability lives. Everything starts here: your browser → Burp → the target. chTitle: Burp Suite: How It Works & How to Use It
heading: How Interception Works
text: The one concept to truly understand: Burp is a man-in-the-middle proxy you deliberately insert into your own connection. Your request doesn't go to the target — it goes to Burp, which can read and change it, then forwards it on. Don't take it on faith; here's that exact mechanism in runnable Go. An intercepting proxy sits between a client and a server so that all traffic passes through it: the client sends its request to the proxy, the proxy may read and modify it, then forwards it to the real server — and does the same to the response on the way back. Burp is such a proxy, pointed at your own browser. For plain HTTP this is trivial (the bytes are right there). For HTTPS , the traffic is encrypted end-to-end, so to read it Burp performs a deliberate man-in-the-middle: it terminates TLS itself , generating an on-the-fly certificate for the target's domain signed by Burp's own Certificate Authority . Your browser would normally reject that cert (it isn't from a real CA) — which is why you install Burp's CA certificate into your browser's trust store as a one-time setup. After that, the browser trusts Burp's generated certs, Burp decrypts the traffic, and you can read and edit HTTPS l

heading: 1. The HTTP CONNECT Tunneling Lifecycle
text: When a browser configured with an explicit proxy attempts to navigate to https://target.example.com, the connection handshake proceeds as follows: 1. The Plaintext Handshake (CONNECT): The browser establishes a plain TCP connection to Burp (e.g. 127.0.0.1:8080) and issues: 2. Proxy Hijacking & 200 Connection Established: The proxy calls http.Hijacker.Hijack(), detaches the raw TCP socket from net/http, and sends: 3. Downstream TLS Termination: The proxy now treats the client socket as a TLS server connection (tls.Server(conn, tlsConfig)), expecting a TLS ClientHello with SNI target.example.com.

chTitle: Burp Suite: How It Works & How to Use It
heading: 2. On-the-Fly X.509 Leaf Certificate Minting (crypto/x509)
text: To satisfy the client's TLS handshake without triggering a certificate validation error: The Root CA Pair: Burp generates a long-lived RSA-2048/ECDSA CA private key and self-signed root certificate (PortSwigger CA), installed in the user's OS/browser trust store (/Library/Keychains on macOS or cert9.db in Firefox). Dynamic SAN Generation: When the client sends ClientHello with SNI target.example.com, the proxy's GetCertificate callback dynamically creates an x509.Certificate template: Leaf Key Caching: To avoid burning CPU generating new asymmetric keypairs for every TCP connection, the proxy reuses a single shared ephemeral leaf private key across all minted host certs, caching signed DER certificates in an in-memory LRU map.

heading: 3. Upstream Dialing & Hop-by-Hop Header Stripping (Go 1.22+)
text: Independent Upstream TLS Handshake: Simultaneously, the proxy dials target.example.com:443 using a standard tls.Dialer, performing authentic public certificate validation against Mozilla's root store. Hop-by-Hop Header Sanitization: RFC 7230 requires proxies to strip hop-by-hop headers (Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Authenticate, Proxy-Authorization, TE, Trailers, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade) before forwarding the sanitized request to the upstream target. Most hunting is done with intercept off , sending interesting requests to Repeater. Every request the proxy sees is recorded in HTTP history and organized into a sitemap (a tree of the target's paths). heading: Repeater
text: Repeater is the manual workhorse — and the tool that maps most directly onto the attack classes in this course. One request, edited and resent by hand, response shown side by side. Repeater holds a single HTTP request that you can edit and resend as many times as you like, showing the response each time. It's the manual-testing core of Burp: you send an interesting request here from the proxy, then change one thing and observe the effect — change an object id to test IDOR/BOLA , remove or swap the session cookie/Authorization header to test broken authentication/authorization , alter a role or price field to test business-logic flaws, inject a ' or SLEEP(5) to probe SQL injection , change the Host header to test host-header attacks, add ../ to test path traversal . Repeater is deliberately one-request-at-a-time and human-driven — it's for understanding a single endpoint deeply, forming and testing one hypothesis at a time. When you want to test many values automatically, you graduate the request to Intruder. Method, path, any header (cookie, Authorization, Host, X-Forwarded-For), query params, and the body. chTitle: Burp Suite: How It Works & How to Use It
heading: Intruder
text: When you've found what to change in Repeater and now want to try many values , you hand the request to Intruder. It marks positions in the request and substitutes payloads automatically. Intruder automates sending a request many times with payloads substituted into marked positions . You pick the spots to vary (a parameter, a header value), supply a payload list (a wordlist, a number range, a charset), and Intruder fires the request once per payload, tabulating status/length/timing so anomalies stand out. Its four attack types differ in how payloads map to positions: Sniper (one position at a time, one payload set — the default, for fuzzing a single field); Battering ram (the same payload in all positions at once); Pitchfork (multiple positions, each with its own payload list, advanced in lockstep — e.g. matched username/password pairs); and Cluster bomb (every combination of multiple payload lists — e.g. all usernames × all passwords). Intruder is how you do enumeration (user IDs, endpoints), fuzzing (parameter values, injection payloads), and brute-forcing — at scale, with the results sortable to spot the one response that's different. chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
desc: The response envelope, from zero. A single Go HTTP response is a body wrapped in instructions to the browser and every cache between you and it. Assumes no prior knowledge: what an HTTP header is and how net/http reads/writes them (Set vs Add, canonicalization, the set-after-WriteHeader gotcha, default headers, content sniffing); the caching family (the full Cache-Control vocabulary, ETag/If-None-Match 304 revalidation, Vary); the cookie family (the http.Cookie struct and every attribute, the __Host- prefix, the unset-SameSite-is-Lax gotcha); and the security headers Go sets NONE of by default (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy). Ends with a reusable secureHeaders middleware. Every header behavior measured against go1.24.
text: Here's the thing, sport. When your Go handler calls fmt.Fprint(w, "..."), you think you sent a page . You didn't. You sent a page wrapped in instructions — a stack of Name: value lines that tell the browser and every cache between you and the user what to do with that page: how long to keep it, who's allowed to see the copy, whether scripts may run, whether the cookie rides along on the next request. Get the page right and the instructions wrong, and you leak a user's data into a shared cache, you hand an XSS payload a place to run, you let another site frame your bank page. The body is the easy part. The envelope is where the security lives. This chapter teaches the envelope from zero — no assumed knowledge of any of these headers. We'll start at "what even is a header" and how Go's net/http reads and writes them, then build the three families that matter most: caching (the Cache-Control vocabulary, revalidation, Vary), cookies (Set-Cookie and every attribute), and the security headers Go ships none of by default. Every single behavior here was measured against go1.24 — printed off a real connection, not recalled from memory — because the whole point of headers is that the machine

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: What a Header Is
text: Forget Go for one paragraph. An HTTP response is text on a wire , in a fixed shape: a status line, then a block of headers, then a blank line, then the body. An HTTP header is a single Name: value line of metadata attached to a request or response, sitting before the body. The response from a server looks literally like this on the wire: The body is the content (the HTML, the JSON). The headers are instructions about that content — its type, how long it may be cached, what cookies to store, what security rules apply. A request header (sent by the browser) and a response header (sent by the server) are the same shape; this chapter is about the response headers your Go server emits, because those are the ones that carry your security decisions. Header names are case-insensitive (Content-Type and content-type are the same header); a single header name can carry multiple values (you can send two Set-Cookie lines, or one Vary with several entries).

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: How Go reads and writes headers
text: In Go, the response headers live in w.Header(), which is an http.Header — and an http.Header is just a map[string][]string (a map from a header name to a list of values, because a header can repeat). Three methods do almost everything: Set replaces, Add appends another value, Get reads the first value, Values reads them all. And Go canonicalizes the name for you — content-type is stored and sent as Content-Type.

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: The one ordering rule: headers before the body
text: Here's the rule that trips up everyone once: you must set every header before you write the status line or any body byte. The moment you call w.WriteHeader(code) — or the first w.Write/fmt.Fprint, which calls WriteHeader(200) for you — Go serializes the header block onto the wire . Anything you set after that is too late: the bytes are already gone. httptest.ResponseRecorder will lie to you about this. Run the exact same handler against a ResponseRecorder instead of a real connection and X-After shows up as "lost" — present — because the Recorder is an in-memory fake that keeps a live reference to the header map and never actually serializes at WriteHeader. So a unit test using a Recorder can pass while the real server drops the header. When a header's timing matters, test it against httptest.NewServer (a real connection over loopback), not a bare Recorder. This is the same lesson as the rest of the Bible's testing material: a fake that's too forgiving hides the bug you're testing for.

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: What a bare handler already sends
text: You're never starting from nothing. Even a handler that sets no headers ships three, because Go fills them in: The headline to carry into the rest of the chapter: Go has no secure defaults for the response envelope. It hands you Content-Type, Content-Length, Date, and stops. Every caching rule, every cookie attribute, every security header in this chapter is something you must put on the response or it isn't there. --

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: The Caching Family
text: A cache is any box between your server and the user that keeps a copy of a response so the next request can be answered without bothering your server. There are two kinds, and the difference is the whole security story. A private cache belongs to one user — the browser's own on-disk cache. A copy stored there is only ever served back to that same person, so caching their account page there is harmless. A shared cache sits in front of many users — a CDN edge node, a reverse proxy, a corporate proxy — and serves one stored copy to whoever asks for that URL next. Caching a user-specific page in a shared cache is the dangerous case: the next visitor gets the previous user's data (that's web cache deception, ch32). The caching headers exist to tell each kind of cache, precisely, whether it may store a response and for how long — and several directives target the shared cache specifically.

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: The Cache-Control vocabulary
text: Cache-Control is the master switch, and it's a comma-separated list of directives . Here's the full working vocabulary — read it as "what each word tells a cache to do": directive what it tells caches --- --- no-store Never store this, anywhere. The strongest. Use on every authenticated/sensitive response. private Browsers may cache it; shared caches (CDN/proxy) must NOT. The targeted fix for cache deception. no-cache May be stored, but must revalidate with the origin before each reuse (a 304 check). A misnomer — it means "always re-check," not "don't cache." public Explicitly cacheable by shared caches, even for responses they'd normally skip (e.g. ones with Authorization). max-age=N Fresh for N seconds ; after that it's stale and must be revalidated or refetched. s-maxage=N Like max-age but for shared caches only , and it overrides max-age there. must-revalidate Once stale, a cache may not serve the stale copy on a whim (e.g. during an origin outage) — it must revalidate. stale-while-revalidate=N May serve a stale copy for up to N seconds while fetching a fresh one in the background. Hides latency. immutable This won't change during its freshness lifetime, so the browser won't ev

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: Revalidation: ETag / If-None-Match and the 304
text: "Stale" doesn't mean "throw it away" — it means "check if it's still good." That check is a conditional request , and it's how a cache avoids re-downloading something that hasn't changed. An ETag ("entity tag") is a short fingerprint the server attaches to a response — change the content, change the ETag. When a cache holds a copy and wants to know if it's still current, it sends the fingerprint back in an If-None-Match request header: "I have the version tagged "v1" — is that still right?" If it is, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body — a tiny response that says "your copy is fine, keep it." If it's changed, the server sends 200 with the new body and a new ETag. The sibling pair is Last-Modified (a timestamp) and If-Modified-Since . Either way, revalidation turns "this is stale" into a cheap round-trip instead of a full re-download. In Go, http.ServeContent and http.ServeFile implement the whole conditional dance for you.

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: Vary: telling caches what changes the response
text: A cache stores a response under a key — by default just the method and URL. But what if the same URL returns different bytes depending on a request header (gzip vs plain, English vs French, logged-in vs not)? Then a single key isn't enough, and Vary is how you say so. The Vary response header lists the request headers that change this response , so a cache adds them to its key instead of serving one variant to everyone. Vary: Accept-Encoding says "the gzipped and plain versions are different — key on the client's Accept-Encoding." Vary: Cookie says "this response depends on the cookie, so don't share it across users." Omitting Vary when a response does depend on a request header is precisely the mistake behind web cache poisoning (an unkeyed header gets reflected and cached for everyone) and contributes to deception (a per-user page shared across users). The rule: if a request header changes the bytes, either name it in Vary or don't let it change a cacheable response at all. chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: The Cookie Family
text: A cookie is a small named value the server tells the browser to store and send back automatically on every subsequent request to that site. It's how a stateless protocol remembers who you are between requests — and because the browser attaches it automatically , every one of its attributes is a security decision. A server sets a cookie with a Set-Cookie response header (Set-Cookie: session=abc; HttpOnly; Secure); the browser stores session=abc and, from then on, automatically includes Cookie: session=abc on requests back to that site. That automatic attachment is the cookie's superpower (seamless sessions) and its danger (the browser sends it even on requests another site triggered — the root of CSRF, and the cookie ride-along behind web cache deception). The attributes after the value are the controls: who may read it (HttpOnly), over what transport (Secure), on which cross-site requests it rides (SameSite), its scope (Path, Domain), and its lifetime (Max-Age/Expires). In Go a cookie is the http.Cookie struct, written with http.SetCookie(w, c) and read with r.Cookie("name").

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: The attribute vocabulary
text: attribute what it controls --- --- Secure The cookie is only sent over HTTPS — never plaintext HTTP. Mandatory for anything sensitive. HttpOnly JavaScript cannot read it (document.cookie won't show it) — so an XSS payload can't steal the session. SameSite=Strict Never sent on a cross-site request, even a top-level link click. The strongest anti-CSRF / anti-deception value. SameSite=Lax Sent on top-level GET navigations but not cross-site POST/fetch/subresources. The browser's default when no SameSite is given. SameSite=None Sent on all cross-site requests — requires Secure . Only for cookies that truly must work third-party. Path=/x Only sent for request paths under /x. A scope limiter, not a security boundary. Domain=... Which host(s) the cookie is sent to. Omit it to scope to the exact host (the safer default). Max-Age=N / Expires=date Lifetime. Max-Age is seconds-from-now (modern); Expires is an absolute date (legacy). Max-Age wins if both are set. The hardened session cookie that the auth chapter (ch20) builds is just these turned to their safe positions: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict. chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: Security Headers
text: Now the family with the bluntest rule of all: Go sets none of these for you. There is no middleware on by default, no secure baseline — if you don't emit a Content-Security-Policy, your response simply doesn't have one. Each of these headers is a one-line instruction that switches on a specific browser protection. An allowlist of where scripts/styles/images may load from. default-src 'self' says "only load resources from my own origin." This is the strongest defense against XSS : even if an attacker injects a , the browser refuses to run inline or off-origin code the policy doesn't permit. The single most valuable header here. max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains tells the browser "for the next year, only ever reach me over HTTPS — never plaintext, no exceptions." Defeats SSL-stripping (an attacker downgrading the first request to HTTP). Only emit it once HTTPS is solid everywhere; it's sticky. Tells the browser stop guessing the content type — trust my Content-Type exactly. Without it, a browser may "sniff" a response that says text/plain but looks like HTML and run it as HTML — turning a file upload or a JSON endpoint into stored XSS. One value, always: nosniff. text: Because Go won't, you set these once, centrally, with a middleware that wraps every handler. This is the practical payoff of the whole chapter — and it doubles as the cache fix: the authenticated handler marks itself no-store while the middleware supplies the security baseline. --

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: How They Interlock
text: None of these families is the whole defense for any one attack — the attacks live in the gaps between them. This is the chapter's payoff: read an attack as "which header was missing." A per-user page leaks because it was cacheable (no Cache-Control: no-store/private) and its cookie was sendable cross-site (SameSite=Lax, the default). Two missing instructions from two different families. Fix either: no-store on the response, or SameSite=Strict on the cookie. (ch32) An unkeyed request header gets reflected into a cacheable response and served to everyone. The missing instruction is Vary (key on it) — or better, don't reflect request input into a cacheable response at all. (ch32) A forged cross-site request rides the browser's automatic cookie attachment. The defending instruction is SameSite=Strict/Lax on the session cookie (plus Go 1.25+ CrossOriginProtection). Header-based Authorization: Bearer auth has no ambient cookie, so it's largely immune. (ch20) Two layers: HttpOnly stops an injected script reading the session cookie, and CSP stops the injected script running in the first place. Defense in depth across the cookie and security-header families. (ch14 / ch20) Your page gets fra

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: Defaults & Gotchas
text: The catalog — the things that bite precisely because Go is quiet about them. Go emits Content-Type, Content-Length, Date — and nothing else. No Cache-Control, no security headers, not even a Server header. Every protective instruction is opt-in. Centralize them in middleware so "on" is the default. WriteHeader (or the first Write) commits the header block. Anything Set after that is silently dropped on a real connection. Set all headers first; in middleware, set then call next. A ResponseRecorder keeps a live header-map reference and never serializes, so a header set after WriteHeader still shows up in a Recorder test — masking a bug a real connection would expose. Test header timing against httptest.NewServer. Don't set Content-Type and Go guesses it with http.DetectContentType. Convenient, but a guess — set it explicitly and pair it with nosniff so the browser doesn't guess either. ServeContent/ServeFile/FileServer give you ETag/304 revalidation but never Cache-Control. Add public, max-age=... for assets you want cached — and no-store for anything sensitive you serve through them. The zero-value SameSite (and SameSiteDefaultMode) emit no attribute, so the browser uses its own def

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: 1. Key Canonicalization in net/textproto (Go 1.22+)
text: When you invoke w.Header().Set("x-custom-key", "value"), Go converts the header key using textproto.CanonicalMIMEHeaderKey: The Canonicalization Algorithm: The algorithm capitalizes the first letter and any letter following a hyphen (-), converting all other ASCII characters to lowercase (e.g. content-security-policy $\to$ Content-Security-Policy). Direct Map Access Hazard: Because http.Header is defined as type Header map[string][]string, indexing the map directly via h["content-type"] fails if the key was stored under its canonicalized form h["Content-Type"]. Always use h.Get(), h.Set(), or h.Values(), which normalize keys through CanonicalMIMEHeaderKey automatically.

chTitle: HTTP Response Headers You Must Get Right: Caching, Cookies & Security Headers
heading: 3. Dynamic CSP Nonce Generation & HSTS Preloading
text: Cryptographic CSP Nonces: Static CSP policies often struggle with inline analytics or hydration scripts. Secure Go servers mint dynamic single-use 128-bit cryptographic nonces per request via crypto/rand, inject them into the response context, and attach Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce- ' 'strict-dynamic'. HSTS Preload Standards: Strict-Transport-Security requires max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload (2 years) to qualify for Chrome and Mozilla's hardcoded browser HSTS preload list, ensuring clients never attempt an initial unencrypted HTTP connection. --

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
desc: Delegated auth the way the developer who built it sees it. Builds on the sessions/JWT/cookie foundations (ch20) and goes deep on the OAuth/OIDC half: authentication vs authorization; OAuth's four roles and two tokens; refresh-token rotation with reuse detection; the six-step Authorization Code Flow and its back-channel client_secret; exact redirect_uri matching vs the loose-match bug; PKCE (verifier->challenge, S256 vs plain, the downgrade); the four other flows and which are deprecated; OAuth 2.1's hardening; JWT validation and the alg-confusion seam (alg:none); OIDC id_token vs access_token and the email_verified account-takeover (capped by the $100,000 Sign in with Apple zero-day); and the Protection Map. Every mechanism is a runnable, go1.24-verified stdlib Go demo.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Most hunters open a proxy, see state, code challenge, redirect uri scroll past, and look away — not because they can't read them, but because nobody ever told them why each one exists . Every guide opens with "RFC this, specification that," and by the end you still can't say what redirect uri actually protects. So we do it the other way around: we learn auth the way the developer who built it sees it — why each piece exists, what attack it stops, and what assumption it's quietly making about you. Do that, and you stop reading auth flows and start hunting them: you open any flow on any target and instantly see the seams — the places a developer trusted something they shouldn't have. This chapter is the delegated-auth half of the story. The sessions, cookies, password-hashing, and JWT foundations live in the auth & API design chapter (ch20) — skim it first if HttpOnly/SameSite/the session-ID-is-the-account model isn't already reflex. Here we go deep on OAuth 2.0/2.1 (four roles, two tokens, the six-step code flow, PKCE ), OpenID Connect (the id token, and the email verified account-takeover most apps ship), and the payoff — the Protection Map : eleven protect

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: Authn vs Authz
text: Every system on the internet answers two questions about every request — and conflating them is where most auth bugs are born. Authentication answers who are you? — the login, the password check, the session cookie, the token in the header. Anything that proves you're not a stranger off the street. Authorization answers what are you allowed to do? — the permission check, the ownership check, the scope enforcement that decides whether this user may perform this action on this resource. They're two separate decisions, and most companies get the first right and the second wrong — because authentication is a solved, reusable problem (use a library, hash the password, issue a session) while authorization is custom code on every endpoint , written by hand, easy to forget. That's why the bugs live there. Every broken-access-control bug you've read — the IDOR where you swap a user ID, the privilege escalation where a regular user hits an admin route, the OAuth scope bypass where a read token writes — is the same shape : authentication passed, authorization failed. The bug is never in the login; it's in the gap between knowing who you are and knowing what you can do. Why is this hard at all

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: OAuth's Roles & Tokens
text: Sessions and JWTs answer how does one app remember me? OAuth answers something different: how do two apps work together on my behalf, without me handing one the keys to the other? Before OAuth, if Calendly needed your Google Calendar, you gave Calendly your Google password — the "password anti-pattern": a third party holding your master credential, able to read your email, change your password, impossible to revoke without breaking everything. OAuth 2.0 (2010) fixed exactly this: it lets you delegate a specific capability without delegating your identity . Calendly gets calendar read access , scoped to what it needs, revocable in one click — never your password. The single biggest misconception: OAuth is not an authentication protocol. It answers what is this app allowed to do with my data (authorization), not who is this user (identity). "Sign in with Google" feels like authentication, but that's OAuth plus a second layer — OIDC — bolted on. Apps that treat raw OAuth as login get taken over, because the protocol was never designed to tell the app who the user is. chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: Refresh-token rotation turns a backdoor into a tripwire
text: The refresh token is now the long-lived secret — steal it and you mint access tokens for months. So modern OAuth makes refresh tokens single-use with rotation : every redemption issues a new refresh token and kills the old one. The payoff is reuse detection — if a token that was already redeemed is presented again, that's the fingerprint of theft, and the server revokes the entire token family . Here's that model, runnable and verified — the reuse of a spent token revokes the family: Finally, scopes : a scope is a string (calendar:read) bound to the token at consent time. The catch is in the word supposed to — the resource server is supposed to check the scope on every call. That check is custom logic on every endpoint, so it's exactly what gets forgotten. And any scope check done client-side (a hidden button) is decorative — the attacker calls the API directly. The only check that matters is the one on the server. --

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: The Code Flow
text: OAuth defines several flows; one dominates the modern web. The Authorization Code Flow is what every "Sign in with X" button fires. It has six steps , and each is a place a developer can get something subtly wrong. (1) The redirect. The client sends the browser to the auth server's /authorize with five parameters: response type=code, client id, redirect uri (where to come back), scope, and state (a random value bound to the user's session). (2) Login + consent. The user authenticates and approves the consent screen — entirely on the auth server's domain; the client never sees the password. (3) Redirect back with a code. The auth server redirects to redirect uri with code (a short-lived, single-use ticket — not a token) and the same state echoed back. (4) The back-channel exchange. The client's backend POSTs code + client id + redirect uri + client secret to the token endpoint — server-to-server, the browser never sees it. (5) Tokens returned. The auth server returns the access token, refresh token, and granted scopes, as JSON. (6) Call the API. The client uses the access token (Authorization: Bearer) at the resource server. The genius is step 4: the browser only ever holds the code

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: PKCE
text: The client secret works for apps with a backend. But OAuth is also used by public clients — mobile apps and single-page apps that have no backend and can't keep a secret (anyone can unzip the APK or open DevTools and read it). For them the client secret protection evaporates, and on mobile there's a real way to steal the code: a malicious app registers the same custom URI scheme (legitapp://callback) and the OS may hand it the redirect. PKCE ("pixie") was built to make that theft useless. PKCE adds a per-flow secret the attacker can't intercept . (1) Before starting, the client generates a high-entropy random code verifier (43–128 chars). (2) It hashes it: code challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)) — a one-way derivation. (3) It sends the challenge (and code challenge method=S256) in the authorization request. (4) The auth server stores the challenge next to the code it issues. (5–6) At the token exchange, the client sends the original verifier — the raw string that has been sitting in its memory the whole time, never on the wire . (7) The server hashes the presented verifier and compares it to the stored challenge; match → tokens, mismatch → rejected. A malicious app that interc

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: The other four flows — recognition, not memorization
text: You don't need to exploit each from memory; you need to recognize it in a proxy and know whether it's modern, situational, or shouldn't-exist: Flow Recognize it by Status --- --- --- Authorization Code (+ PKCE) response type=code, then a token-exchange POST with a code verifier The modern default — what you want to see Implicit response type=token; token returned in the URL fragment ( access token=…), no exchange POST Deprecated (removed in 2.1) — token-in-URL leaks via history/Referer/JS Client Credentials POST to /token with grant type=client credentials, no user/redirect Legit for machine-to-machine; leaked client creds = mintable tokens Device a short user code + a /activate URL on one device, polling the token endpoint Legit for TVs/CLIs; watch for code-phishing and weak rate limits ROPC POST to /token with grant type=password + username/password in the body Shouldn't exist — the client sees the password; undoes OAuth's whole point

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: OAuth 2.1 — a decade of bug reports, baked into the spec
text: OAuth 2.1 is what you get when fifteen years of real-world takeovers are fed back into the protocol. Treat it as your safety baseline — anything in the wild that violates one of these is potentially reportable: Mandatory for all clients, public and confidential — closes the code-interception class across every code-using flow. Neither is a valid grant type anymore. A server that still supports response type=token or grant type=password is running 2.0, not 2.1 — a sign of an older implementation. For public clients, the single-use + reuse-detection model is mandatory, not optional. Tokens go in the Authorization header (not query strings — they leak to logs/Referer), and redirect uri must match the registered value character for character . The redirect change is the most important hardening — loose matching was behind countless account takeovers. --

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: JWTs & OIDC
text: OAuth carries permission . To carry identity , you need one more layer. But first the token format both lean on — the JWT — and its single most important seam. (The JWT structure — three base64url parts: header, payload, signature; payload is readable, not encrypted — is covered in ch20; here we focus on the validation chain and where it breaks.) When a JWT arrives, the server is supposed to: decode the header , verify the signature with the correct key , check exp (expiry), check iss/aud/nbf (right issuer, right audience, valid yet), and only then trust the payload . That last step is the power and the danger: once the chain passes, the role/scope/identity in the payload is ground truth. One weak link and the server is trusting whatever the attacker wrote. The signing algorithm is named in the header ( ) — and the header is part of the token, which comes from the client . So the algorithm the server verifies with is, technically, a value the attacker controls . That's the whole bug class. Its most famous form is alg:none , where an old library sees "alg":"none", concludes "no signature to check," and accepts the token. There's also RS256→HS256 confusion (the server uses the public

heading: Lab: pin the algorithm
text: The naive verifier above reads alg from the token. Here's a verifier that trusts any well-formed token — so an alg:none forgery (and even a token with a garbage signature) sails through. A test harness checks three things: a correctly signed token verifies, an alg:none forgery is rejected, and a wrong-signature token is rejected. Fix verify so it pins HS256 server-side — never reading alg from the token — recomputes the HMAC, and compares with hmac.Equal. Self-contained — stdlib only, no network. The forgery works only because the verifier trusts the token to declare its own algorithm. Pin HS256 server-side, recompute the HMAC, and hmac.Equal it against the signature — now alg:none (and any tampered payload) fails the signature check, regardless of what the header claims. Get the flag.

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: OpenID Connect: the identity layer OAuth was missing
text: Apps hacked identity on top of OAuth for years (call the /userinfo endpoint and guess ) until OpenID Connect (OIDC) , 2014, standardized it. OIDC is a layer on top of OAuth — same redirects, same code exchange — that adds one thing: the id token . The access token says "this app may do X" — it's a key to an API, validated by the resource server . The id token says "this user is who they say they are" — a statement of identity, a JWT validated by the client . You turn an OAuth flow into OIDC by adding the openid scope (usually openid email profile); the auth server then returns an id token alongside the access token. Its standardized claims: iss (which provider minted it — must match what you expect), sub (the permanent, opaque, unique user id within that issuer — not the email), aud (the client id it was minted for — must match yours, or it's a token-confusion attack), exp/iat (expiry/issued-at), nonce (echoes the client's random value, replay protection), and profile claims like email and email verified . The client must verify the signature (via the provider's JWKS endpoint), iss, aud, exp, and nonce — and only then trust the claims. The single most under-checked claim — and the

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: When the issuer itself is the bug — the $100,000 Sign in with Apple zero-day
text: The email verified gate in loginSafe quietly assumes one thing: that when a provider asserts email verified: true, it actually checked ownership . In April 2020 that assumption broke at the very top of the trust chain. Bhavuk Jain found that Apple's own authorization server would mint a fully valid id token for any email an attacker named in the request — signed by Apple's real key, carrying the trusted issuer (https://appleid.apple.com), every claim looking exactly as legitimate as a genuine login. The server never confirmed the requester owned the address. Any app that offered "Sign in with Apple" and then linked the session to its local account by the email claim was exposed to full account takeover from a single forged token, zero victim interaction — and major consumers like Dropbox, Spotify, and Airbnb integrate Sign in with Apple. Apple paid $100,000 and, on investigation, reported no evidence the flaw had been abused in the wild. This is the hard case the section has been building toward. A sloppy provider sending email verified: false is the easy one — the gate above already rejects it. Here a top-tier provider sent email verified: true for an email the real user never own

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: The canonicalization seam: normalize before you decide
text: A real $6,000 finding: an app with enforced SAML SSO let a hunter authenticate with a password instead, by appending a single encoded trailing space (%20) to the email. The mechanism is pure order-of-operations — and it generalizes far past SSO. Software constantly canonicalizes input — trims whitespace, lowercases, URL-decodes, Unicode-normalizes — so that Alice@Example.com , alice@example.com, and alice@example.com%20 all resolve to one account. The bug appears when a security decision is made on one form of the input and the action is taken on a different , later-normalized form. In the SSO case: the server checks "is this email's account SSO-enforced?" against the raw request value, then a downstream lookup trims the email. Append a trailing space and the two forms disagree — the raw victim@example.com%20 (decoded: a trailing space) misses the SSO-enforced set, so the server skips SSO and offers the legacy password path, while the account lookup trims back to the real victim. The enforcement check and the resolved identity refer to different strings . chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: 1. PKCE Mathematical Construction & Invariants (RFC 7636)
text: The Proof Key for Code Exchange protocol defends against authorization code interception in public clients (mobile applications, SPAs) where client secrets cannot be securely stored: Entropy & Character Set: The code verifier is a high-entropy cryptographically random string generated using crypto/rand containing between 43 and 128 characters from the unreserved URI character set [A-Za-z0-9-. ]: The S256 Transformation: code challenge = BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code verifier))) Constant-Time Verification: When the authorization server receives the code verifier at the token endpoint, it recomputes the SHA-256 digest and validates it against the stored code challenge using crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare (or hmac.Equal) to eliminate timing side-channel leaks. Why OAuth 2.1 Forbids plain: Under the legacy plain method, code challenge = code verifier. Any passive eavesdropper on the authorization request obtains the raw verifier, defeating the entire protection.

chTitle: OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect from the Ground Up: Flows, PKCE, and the Protection Map
heading: 2. Token Introspection (RFC 7662) vs. Local JWT Cryptographic Verification
text: Resource servers must validate incoming Bearer access tokens using one of two models: Opaque Reference Tokens (RFC 7662): The resource server issues an authenticated back-channel HTTP POST to the authorization server's /introspect endpoint. While this guarantees instant revocation awareness, it incurs network latency on every API call. Self-Contained JSON Web Tokens (RFC 7519 / RFC 7515): The resource server fetches the public key set (/.well-known/jwks.json) and verifies signatures locally. Key ID (kid) Routing: The JWT header specifies which key in the JWKS signed the token. Keys must be cached with an in-memory TTL and rotated gracefully. Algorithm Pinning: The verification engine must ignore the algorithm declared in the JWT header (alg) when selecting verification algorithms. Hardcoding the expected algorithm (e.g. jwt.WithValidMethods([]string ) or checking alg == "RS256" before calling rsa.VerifyPKCS1v15) blocks both alg:none and RSA-to-HMAC public key confusion attacks.

chTitle: The Bug Bounty Income Playbook: From Zero to a Steady $300+/Month
heading: Master One Class: IDOR
text: The single highest-return decision a beginner makes: pick one bug class and hunt it exclusively for three to six months. The unanimous recommendation across every honest 2026 source — and the right one for a developer — is IDOR / broken access control. Insecure Direct Object Reference is a broken-access-control bug: the app uses a user-supplied identifier to fetch a resource without checking that this user owns it. It is the best starting class for four reasons. (1) It's the most-rewarded — broken access control has held 1 on the OWASP Top 10 since 2021, and platform data consistently shows it as the top-paid category. (2) The barrier is almost nothing — you need two accounts and Burp Repeater, no exploit chains, no payload craft. (3) The attack surface is enormous — it exists anywhere a developer forgot an ownership check: every API endpoint, every file download, every admin panel, every multi-tenant query. (4) It's about logic, not tricks — exactly the authorization reasoning a developer already understands. The access-control check a developer forgot is as present in a $100M fintech as in a weekend project. That's the whole job: find the missing check, prove the impact, write it

text: The same endpoint can be worth $100 or $5,000 depending on what you can do with the IDOR. Always push from read toward write toward vertical escalation: Rung What it is Typical severity / range --- --- --- Read IDOR View another user's data (GET /invoice/124) Low-Medium, ≈$100-500 Write IDOR Change another user's data — email, password, address, order (PUT/POST/PATCH/DELETE) P1, ≈$1,500-5,000 Vertical IDOR A regular user hits an admin-only endpoint (/api/admin/ ) Critical — the program's nightmare Blind IDOR The action fires but the response is generic (200 OK); verify out-of-band Same impact as the action it performs UUID IDOR IDs are UUIDs (not guessable) — but they leak in other endpoints Often overlooked = often unduplicated The two mindset shifts that move you up the ladder: don't stop at read — if you can read user B's data, test whether you can PUT to it (write IDORs turn Low into P1); and UUIDs are not safe — a GET /api/team-members that lists UUIDs hands you the keys to GET /api/user/ /salary. Always cross-reference IDs leaked in one response against object endpoints elsewhere.

heading: The detection mechanic, in Go
text: The Burp extensions Autorize and Authz automate IDOR hunting with one idea: replay every request under a second, lower-privileged identity and diff the response against the owner's baseline. Same status and same body under the attacker's session means the ownership check is missing — a mechanical green/red signal instead of eyeballing. Here's that core logic, runnable and verified: Manual ID swapping — your first move on any object reference. Change 124 to 125, resend, read the response. Numeric enumeration — fuzz IDs 1000-2000 and grep responses for email/address/total. A 200 with someone else's data is your finding (and proves mass exposure = higher severity). The IDOR machine — log in as the low-priv user, browse as the high-priv user, and the extension replays every request with the low-priv session, flagging bypasses red. This is the classify() logic above, applied to your whole session automatically.

heading: 1. The Unix Pipe & JSONL Stream Architecture
text: Modern Go security tools (subfinder, httpx, katana, nuclei) communicate over stdin/stdout using line-delimited streams (\n) or structured JSON Lines (jsonl). Stream Decoupling: Instead of buffering millions of discovered hostnames in memory, Go tools stream results directly through buffered channels (chan string). Bounded Worker Pool Concurrency: DNS Resolver Sharding: High-speed subdomain probing quickly triggers DNS query rate limits on default upstream resolvers. Production recon engines shard queries across a pool of hundreds of public recursive resolvers using miekg/dns, randomizing nameservers per query to prevent socket packet loss.

heading: 2. Differential Response Triaging (Autorize Engine Internals)
text: Automated IDOR detection requires eliminating false positives caused by dynamic page elements (session tokens, timestamps, nonces): Status Code Heuristics: Owner = 200, Attacker = 401/403 $\to$ Access Control Enforced. Owner = 200, Attacker = 200 $\to$ Potential Access Control Bypass (requires payload similarity check). Owner = 200, Attacker = 404 $\to$ Ownership filter active (or hidden endpoint). Body Similarity Ratio (Levenshtein / SimHash): If both owner and attacker receive 200 OK, the engine strips transient fields (e.g. timestamp, csrf token) and computes text similarity. If similarity $ 95\%$ while body lengths match within $\pm 2\%$, the finding is flagged as high-confidence IDOR.

heading: Is This Still Worth It? The 2026 AI Reckoning
text: The honest question, before you spend eight weeks on this: aren't bug bounties cooked by AI? Point a frontier model at a program, say find bugs in this , and it will — a huge chunk of submissions are now AI-found. So is there still a $300/month in it for a human? The answer is yes — but the game transformed, and you have to play the transformed game. The useful analogy (from hakluke's Are bug bounties cooked? ) is Swiss watchmaking and quartz: cheap quartz didn't kill watchmaking, it killed one tier of it . Seiko and Swatch adapted; mechanical watches became a premium craft . Same shape here. What collapsed is the floor . Bugs that were genuinely hard to find five years ago are now findable by almost anyone — and by automation — so the supply of commodity findings exploded while demand stayed flat, and the value of a commodity bug plummeted. Running the same nuclei templates and parameter scanners as everyone else (and every AI) lands you in a sea of duplicates and low-floor info-disclosure — fine for learning, not a durable income. chTitle: Inside PocketBase: How a One-Binary Backend Is Engineered
desc: The engineering of PocketBase from the source up: how one Go binary embeds SQLite (modernc, no CGO) and a bundled dashboard (embed.FS); why it runs two connection pools against one SQLite file (concurrent readers + a single serialized writer) with WAL and a database-is-locked retry loop; the generic hook.Hook[T] chain built as reversed continuation closures; the net/http 1.22 ServeMux router wrapper that replaced echo; how user-defined collections compile to real SQL tables via a Field interface and CREATE/ALTER TABLE DDL; the fexpr filter DSL that compiles API-rule strings into parameterized dbx WHERE clauses (and why it's injection-safe); the SSE realtime broker that access-checks every record against each subscriber's rule; the goja JS VM pool behind pb_hooks; and the origin story (Gani Georgiev, Presentator, the v0.23 framework rewrite). Every mechanism is a runnable, Go 1.26 stdlib re-implementation.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Most "backends" are a sprawling mess — a Postgres box, a Redis box, an API container, a websocket service, a migration runner, three YAML files, and a Kubernetes cluster to babysit the whole circus. PocketBase is one file . You download a single binary, run it, and you have a REST API, a realtime subscription server, an admin dashboard, file storage, auth with OAuth2, a migration system, and an embedded database — all inside one process, no dependencies to install. That's not magic. That's engineering , and unusually good engineering at that. One person — Gani Georgiev — built the core, and the whole thing is small enough that you and I can read it end to end and understand every decision. So that's what we're doing. Not "how to use PocketBase" (the docs do that). chTitle: Inside PocketBase: How a One-Binary Backend Is Engineered
heading: Why One Binary
text: Before a single line of code, understand the thesis . PocketBase makes one bet that shapes every internal decision: most applications do not need a distributed system, and the complexity of running one is pure cost. The FAQ says it plainly — "Most of the time, you may not need the complexity of managing a fleet of machines and services." So PocketBase scales vertically (a bigger single box), not horizontally (more boxes), and it commits to that so hard that it uses an embedded database and refuses to support networked ones. Vertical scaling means making one machine more powerful (more CPU, RAM, faster disk) and running your whole app on it. Horizontal scaling means running many machines behind a load balancer and coordinating state between them (a shared Postgres, a Redis cache, sticky sessions, distributed locks). Horizontal scaling is how you survive beyond one big machine — but it introduces network partitions, consistency problems, and a mountain of operational work (covered in Part 2's replication/sharding/consensus chapters). PocketBase's bet is that a surprising number of real apps fit comfortably on one box, so paying the horizontal-scaling tax up front is a mistake. Is the

chTitle: Inside PocketBase: How a One-Binary Backend Is Engineered
heading: Embedding SQLite & the UI
text: Two things make PocketBase "one file": the database engine is compiled into the binary (there's no separate DB server to connect to), and the admin dashboard is compiled into the binary (there's no separate static-file server or CDN). Both use a Go feature that's central to the whole design.

chTitle: Inside PocketBase: How a One-Binary Backend Is Engineered
heading: SQLite with no C compiler
text: The classic Go SQLite driver, mattn/go-sqlite3, wraps the C SQLite library via cgo — which means you need a C toolchain to build, and cross-compilation becomes painful. PocketBase's default is modernc.org/sqlite : SQLite's C source transpiled to pure Go . No cgo, no C compiler, trivial cross-compilation (GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build just works, which is how a Mac laptop produces the ARM binary that runs on that Hetzner box). cgo is Go's foreign-function interface for calling C code. It's powerful but costly: you need a C compiler present at build time, cross-compilation requires a cross C toolchain, builds are slower, and each Go↔C call has overhead and sits outside the Go scheduler's view. modernc.org/sqlite sidesteps all of it by being actual Go — SQLite's amalgamation mechanically translated to Go source — so CGO ENABLED=0 builds produce one static binary with zero external .so/.dll dependencies. The connection setup is where the real engineering shows. PocketBase doesn't just open the file — it opens it with a carefully chosen set of PRAGMAs passed as query parameters. Here's the actual core/db connect.go: Every one of those PRAGMAs is a deliberate decision. Let's name them

chTitle: Inside PocketBase: How a One-Binary Backend Is Engineered
heading: The dashboard, baked into the binary
text: The second half of "one file": the admin UI. PocketBase's dashboard is a client-side app (historically Svelte; as of v0.37 rebuilt on the author's own tiny "Shablon" library, still bundled with Vite into static files under ui/dist). Those static files are pulled into the Go binary at compile time with //go:embed: //go:embed is a compiler directive that reads files from disk at build time and stores their bytes inside the compiled binary, exposed as a string, []byte, or an embed.FS (a read-only in-memory filesystem implementing fs.FS). all:dist means "embed everything under dist, including files starting with . or ." At runtime you serve it with http.FileServerFS(ui.DistDirFS) — no files on disk, no separate web server. This is the feature that lets a Go program ship its own frontend. Notice the build tags : //go:build !no ui on the embed file and !no default driver on the SQLite connect. If you build with -tags no ui the dashboard bytes are excluded (smaller binary, headless deployment); with -tags no default driver you can plug in a different SQLite driver (libsql/Turso, sqlcipher, or the cgo mattn driver) via a custom DBConnect. So "one binary" is the default, but the seams to sl

chTitle: Inside PocketBase: How a One-Binary Backend Is Engineered
heading: Two Pools, One File
text: Here's the cleverest piece of the whole DB layer, and it falls straight out of the WAL fact from earlier: WAL gives you many concurrent readers but only ever one writer. So PocketBase opens the same SQLite file twice , with two connection pools tuned for the two roles. Look at the real core/base.go initialization: The defaults are declared right there in base.go: DefaultDataMaxOpenConns = 120, DefaultDataMaxIdleConns = 15. So one pool can open up to 120 parallel read connections , and the other is capped at exactly one write connection. Go's database/sql.DB is not a single connection — it's a pool of them. SetMaxOpenConns(n) caps how many physical connections can be open at once; when all are busy, further queries block until one frees up. So SetMaxOpenConns(1) turns a pool into a serialization gate : only one operation touches the DB through that pool at a time, and the rest queue. PocketBase uses that intentionally as an application-level write lock. Why does capping writes at one connection help ? Because SQLite already only allows one writer — if you let 120 connections all try to write, 119 of them collide on the SQLite write lock and get SQLITE BUSY errors that you then have

heading: The Hook Chain
text: Everything extensible in PocketBase — "run my code before a record is created," "after a user logs in," "when the app boots" — flows through one generic type: hook.Hook[T]. Understanding it unlocks the entire event model, and it's a genuinely elegant use of Go generics + closures. A hook is a list of handlers, and each handler must call e.Next() to pass control down the chain (exactly like net/http middleware). The surprising part is how Trigger builds that chain. Here's the real tools/hook/hook.go: A continuation is "the rest of the work, captured as something callable." Here, event.Next() is the continuation: calling it runs the next handler in the chain. Each handler decides whether to call Next() (proceed), skip it (short-circuit — e.g. an auth guard that rejects), or wrap it (do work, call Next(), then do more after — e.g. start a transaction, Next(), commit). This is the same shape as net/http middleware (next.ServeHTTP) and the router chain we'll see next — one idea reused everywhere in the codebase. Read the loop carefully, because it's doing something subtle. It walks the handlers back to front . At each step it captures the current next function as old, then installs a ne

heading: The Router
text: PocketBase used to embed the echo framework. In the v0.23 rewrite it dropped that dependency and built a thin router on top of the standard library's net/http.ServeMux , using the pattern-matching enhancements that landed in Go 1.22 (method-aware patterns like "GET /api/collections/ " with path wildcards). This is a great case study in "how much router do you actually need." ServeMux is Go's built-in HTTP request multiplexer. Since Go 1.22 its patterns understand methods ("POST /users"), path wildcards ("/users/ ", readable via r.PathValue("id")), and precedence (more specific patterns win). Before 1.22 you needed a third-party router (gorilla/mux, chi, echo) for any of that; now the stdlib covers the common cases, which is exactly why PocketBase could delete echo. PocketBase's Router[T] is generic over an event type and adds three things ServeMux lacks: route groups (shared path prefixes), middleware (the same hook-chain idea), and a per-request event object . Its BuildMux() flattens all the groups into a plain http.ServeMux. heading: Collections Are Real Tables
text: A backend-as-a-service lets users invent data models at runtime — a posts collection today, a comments collection tomorrow, each with fields they define in the dashboard. The lazy way to implement that is to store everything as generic key-value rows or a JSON blob per record. PocketBase does something braver and far better: every collection is a real SQL table, and every field is a real column. Edit the schema in the dashboard and PocketBase runs actual ALTER TABLE DDL. EAV stores dynamic data as rows of (entity id, attribute name, value) in one giant generic table — the classic trick for faking a dynamic schema. It queries terribly (every field read is a self-join), types nothing, and can't use real indexes. The "one JSON data column per record" variant is EAV's lazier cousin with the same costs. PocketBase rejects both: if users define structure, hand the database that structure — real columns, real types, real indexes — so the full SQL toolbox (WHERE title LIKE …, real ORDER BY, true pagination and counts) keeps working at native speed. That single decision is why the filter DSL in the next section can compile to a real WHERE clause instead of scanning in Go. The machinery has

heading: The Filter DSL
text: Here's a hard problem PocketBase solves beautifully. The API lets clients send filter strings like ?filter=(status='active' && created '2026-01-01'), and collection access rules are stored as strings like @request.auth.id != "" && author = @request.auth.id. Both must become SQL WHERE clauses — safely , without SQL injection. How do you turn arbitrary user-supplied filter text into a parameterized query? The answer is a proper little compiler. PocketBase uses fexpr (also by Gani Georgiev) to parse the filter string into an expression tree, then walks that tree to build a dbx expression with placeholder parameters — never string-concatenating user values into SQL. A parameterized query sends the SQL structure and the values to the database separately: WHERE status = plus a bound value . The value is never parsed as SQL — it can contain quotes, OR 1=1, DROP TABLE, anything, and it's still treated as an opaque string literal. SQL injection happens only when you build SQL by string concatenation ("WHERE status = '" + userInput + "'"), letting the input escape the quotes and become code. PocketBase's filter compiler only ever emits placeholders for values, which is what makes accepting r

heading: Realtime Broadcast
text:
PocketBase's realtime is Server-Sent Events (SSE) , not WebSockets. That's a deliberate simplicity choice: SSE is just a long-lived HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream that the server keeps writing to — no upgrade handshake, no separate protocol, works through every proxy, and it's one-directional (server→client), which is all a "your data changed" feed needs. The client subscribes/unsubscribes over normal HTTP requests. SSE is a browser standard (EventSource) for server→client streaming over a single kept-open HTTP response. The server sets Content-Type: text/event-stream, then writes messages formatted as id: ...
data: ...

 and flushes after each one. The connection stays open; the browser auto-reconnects if it drops. Compared to WebSockets it's simpler (plain HTTP, no upgrade), text-only, and one-way — a perfect fit for "notify subscribers that a record changed." The realtime chapter (appendix ch30) contrasts SSE, WebSockets, and webhooks in depth. The connection handler (apis/realtime.go) is a clean piece of long-lived-connection engineering. heading: The JS VM Pool
text: Not everyone extending PocketBase writes Go. The jsvm plugin lets you drop .pb.js files into a pb hooks/ directory and write hooks in JavaScript — onRecordCreate((e) = ). Under the hood that's goja , a pure-Go JavaScript interpreter (no V8, no cgo — consistent with the whole no-cgo philosophy). But JS interpreters have a problem: a goja.Runtime is not safe for concurrent use , and creating one per request is expensive. PocketBase solves this the classic way — a pool of pre-warmed runtimes . An object pool keeps a set of expensive-to-create objects alive and hands them out on demand, returning them for reuse instead of allocating fresh each time. It's the right pattern when (a) creating the object is costly (a JS runtime must parse and load all its bindings) and (b) the object can't be shared concurrently (so each in-flight request needs its own). PocketBase pre-warms HooksPoolSize goja runtimes at startup; a hook execution borrows one, runs, and returns it — so a burst of requests reuses warm runtimes instead of paying construction cost each time. The real plugins/jsvm/jsvm.go builds this pool. HooksPoolSize controls how many runtimes are pre-created; each gets the full set of Pock

heading: The Whole Picture

text: Write a route(sql string) string function that returns "WRITE" if the trimmed, upper-cased SQL starts with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, ALTER, or DROP, and "READ" otherwise (e.g. SELECT). This is the essence of how PocketBase picks the write pool vs. the read pool. PocketBase's real dualDBBuilder doesn't parse SQL text — it routes at the builder method level (Select → read pool, Insert/Update/Delete → write pool), which is cleaner because the operation is known before any SQL string exists. This exercise is the same decision made one layer lower. Implement Chain(handlers ...func(next func())) that runs handlers in order, where each handler receives a next function it must call to continue. Build the chain so that calling the returned function runs handler 0, whose next runs handler 1, and so on. Prove that a handler which doesn't call next stops the chain. Handler C omits next(), so D never runs — exactly the "forgot e.Next()" bug from the chapter. desc: How LuanRT's YouTube stack actually works, rebuilt from the wire up in Go, demystified for total beginners. Why YouTube has no public streaming API and third-party clients must speak its internal one (InnerTube): the JSON /youtubei/v1/player call, the client context that impersonates a real app, and the streamingData it returns. Why stream URLs are locked behind two ciphers extracted from YouTube's obfuscated base.js — the signature transform and the n throttle param. BotGuard attestation demystified step by step: the Create -> run-interpreter -> GenerateIT -> mint handshake that produces content-bound PoTokens, and why it's the same JS-engine seam as deciphering. The proprietary UMP wire format (a custom varint plus typed length-delimited parts) and a from-scratch Go reader for it. The SABR streaming protocol: a protobuf VideoPlaybackAbrRequest POST, a streamed UMP response of MEDIA_HEADER/MEDIA/MEDIA_END parts, and the adaptive control loop. The Onesie instant-playback optimization: an encrypted single round-trip that folds the /player call into the media server (ONESIE_HEADER/ONESIE_DATA, gzip). Why ytc-bridge (the CORS-bypass extension) exists only because browsers are sandboxed — and why a Go backend deletes that layer. How real clients consume it: MSE, kira's Shaka networking-scheme adapter, and SimpMusic's StreamRepository interface seam. Every mechanism is a runnable, stdlib-only Go re-implementation.
text: Here's the thing, sport. You open a YouTube video, bytes arrive, a picture appears. Looks simple. It is not simple. There is no public API that hands you a video file — none. Every third-party client you've ever admired (FreeTube, NewPipe, GrayJay, SimpMusic ) gets its video the same way: by pretending to be the YouTube app, talking to YouTube's private internal API, and then decoding a proprietary streaming protocol that no off-the-shelf video player understands. One person mapped most of that maze in public: LuanRT . His YouTube.js speaks the internal API; his googlevideo library implements the streaming protocol (UMP/SABR); ytc-bridge is the browser-sandbox escape hatch; and kira is a reference player that stitches it all together. maxrave-dev's SimpMusic is the real, shipping app that consumes this whole world. We're not going to use those libraries. We're going to open them up , understand every load-bearing decision, and rebuild the core in Go — the language you'd actually pick for a headless streaming backend, because it has no browser sandbox to fight and it eats concurrent byte streams for breakfast. heading: The Problem: No Public API
text: Start with the thing nobody tells you. YouTube's official "Data API" can list videos, read titles, and manage playlists — but it will never give you a playable media URL. The bytes that make up the actual video are served by a separate fleet of servers ( .googlevideo.com) and gated by a private protocol that YouTube's own web player and mobile apps use internally. That internal system is nicknamed InnerTube . An API a company builds for its own apps to talk to its servers, never published or documented for outsiders. There's no contract, no versioning promise, and no permission — it can change any day. Reverse-engineering one means watching what the official app sends and replaying it faithfully. YouTube's internal API is called InnerTube ; the media servers behind it are googlevideo.com. So every alternative client faces the same four-part obstacle course, and each part is a distinct engineering problem we'll solve in Go: LuanRT's libraries are TypeScript because they must run in a browser (and Node/Deno). heading: InnerTube: The Hidden API
text: Door one. Everything starts with a single POST to InnerTube's player endpoint. It's plain HTTPS with a JSON body — no gRPC, no exotic transport. The trick isn't the transport; it's convincing the server you're a real client by sending the exact context its own apps send. A block of identity fields every InnerTube request carries: which app you claim to be (clientName like WEB or WEB REMIX), its clientVersion, language/region (hl/gl), and a visitorData blob that ties requests together. YouTube branches its behavior on these — different clients get different formats, different ciphers, sometimes no cipher at all. Choosing the client is a strategic decision, not boilerplate. Here is the shape YouTube.js sends (src/core/Session.ts builds context.client; src/utils/Constants.ts holds the versions — WEB was 2.20260623.01.00, YouTube Music's WEB REMIX was 1.20250219.01.00 in July 2026). Let's build the exact request body in Go and marshal it, so you can see every field that matters. That JSON body and those headers are the impersonation. heading: Deciphering the Player
text: Door two, and the one that trips up most newcomers. Many stream URLs don't arrive ready to use. They arrive locked by two separate mechanisms, both implemented in a giant obfuscated JavaScript file YouTube ships called base.js. Buried inside it are two functions YouTube changes frequently: one that unscrambles the stream signature and one that transforms the n parameter . To play a WEB stream you must find those functions in the script and run them. This is the anti-scraping front line — the code is deliberately obfuscated and rotated. Two locks, two jobs: Some formats come as a signatureCipher string: s= &sp=sig&url= . The s value is a scrambled signature. You run it through the player's signature function (a fixed sequence of reverse/swap/splice steps), then attach the result to the URL as the sp parameter (usually sig). Wrong signature → HTTP 403. Every stream URL has an n= query param. If you send it unchanged, YouTube throttles you to a crawl (think dial-up). The player's nsig function transforms n into a new value that unlocks full speed. heading: Attestation: Proving You're Human
text: Door three, and the meanest one. Even with a perfect InnerTube request and correctly deciphered URLs, YouTube can still stop you cold with one question: "Prove you're a real app and not a script." The proof it wants is a PoToken (proof-of-origin token). No valid token when one is demanded → the stream server refuses you (you'll see a STREAM PROTECTION STATUS telling you you're blocked). This is the part that makes YouTube clients genuinely hard, so let's take it slowly and demystify it completely. The general idea of a server making your client prove something about itself before it's trusted — that it's a genuine app on a real device, not an automated script. The server sends a challenge; your client answers in a way only a "real" environment can; the server issues a token that says "this one checked out." Bank apps, DRM, and anti-cheat all do this. YouTube's flavor is called BotGuard , and the token it issues is the PoToken . Any non-human, automated client — a script, a scraper, a headless downloader. heading: UMP: The Wire Format
text: Door four is where LuanRT's googlevideo earns its reputation, and where Go shines. Once you have a deciphered streaming URL, the bytes don't come back as a plain MP4. They come back as UMP — a custom binary container YouTube invented, which no standard video player understands. Before we can talk about the SABR protocol , we have to parse the UMP format it rides on. This is the most self-contained, rebuildable piece of the whole stack, so we'll do it properly in Go. YouTube's proprietary framing for media responses. A UMP body is a flat sequence of parts , each one [part-type][part-size][payload], where type and size are written with a custom variable-length integer (not protobuf's varint — a different scheme). Part types are a fixed enum: MEDIA HEADER (20), MEDIA (21), MEDIA END (22), plus control parts. googlevideo's UmpReader decodes this stream; we'll rebuild it. First, the atom everything is built from: UMP's variable-length integer. The first byte's high bits tell you how many bytes the number occupies — a self-describing length prefix. heading: SABR: The Streaming Loop
text: Now the protocol that rides on UMP. SABR (Server-side Adaptive Bitrate) inverts classic streaming. In DASH/HLS the client decides which quality to fetch next and asks for specific byte ranges. In SABR the client tells the server its state — where playback is, what's buffered, its bandwidth estimate — and the server decides which segments to send back. It's a conversation, not a shopping list. YouTube's streaming protocol where the server picks the next media segments based on client-reported state (player time, buffered ranges, bandwidth). The client POSTs a protobuf VideoPlaybackAbrRequest describing its situation; the server replies with a UMP stream of segments and control parts. The client updates its state and POSTs again. Repeat until the video is fully buffered. Implemented in googlevideo's SabrStream. Google's compact binary serialization format (deep-dived in the gRPC chapter). heading: Onesie: Instant Playback
text: kira's README brags about "nearly instant playback load times." That's not marketing — it's a specific optimization called Onesie , and once you see it you'll want the trick for your own APIs. It's optional (you can stream fine without it), but it's the difference between "click, wait, play" and "click, play." Let's demystify it, because on the surface the code in kira/src/services/onesie.ts looks intimidating and underneath it's one clean idea. Start with the problem it solves. Normally, getting a video playing takes two sequential network round-trips : A round-trip is one full request→response cycle to a server. Latency is how long that cycle takes — dominated not by bandwidth but by distance and setup (often 50–300 ms each). The killer detail: if step B needs the result of step A, the two round-trips add up — you wait for both, back to back. Cutting two sequential round-trips down to one can halve your startup delay. The one idea: send your InnerTube player request inside the request to the media server, and let the media server run it for you. heading: The Browser Tax
text: Here's my favorite part, and the one that most clearly justifies choosing Go. There's a whole repo in this stack — ytc-bridge — whose entire reason for existing is that browsers are sandboxed . Study it and you'll see a component that, in a Go backend, simply vanishes . A browser security rule (covered in the CORS appendix chapter): JavaScript on site-a.com can't freely read responses from site-b.com unless site-b opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. It's enforced by the browser , for web pages — not by servers, and not for non-browser clients. A Go program has no origin and no CORS. The problem ytc-bridge solves: a web app (like kira) running on localhost wants to POST to googlevideo.com. Two browser-only walls block it: YouTube's servers expect Origin/Referer to say youtube.com. But browsers forbid JavaScript from setting Origin or Referer — they're on the "forbidden header" list precisely so pages can't lie about who they are. Your JS literally cannot send the headers the server wants. A .mp4 file you can double-click, sure — but SABR gives you a stream of segments , not a file. Two real clients answer this two different ways, and both lessons point straight at your Go backend. A browser API that lets JavaScript feed video bytes to a element piece by piece , instead of pointing it at a finished file URL. You create a buffer, append segment after segment as they arrive, and the player decodes and shows them. Every in-browser adaptive player (YouTube, Netflix) uses MSE. It's the mechanism that turns "a stream of segments" into "a moving picture." Google's open-source JavaScript video player, built for adaptive streaming (DASH/HLS) on top of MSE. Shaka thinks it's doing ordinary DASH; in reality every segment request is hijacked, routed through the SabrUmpProcessor you met earlier, and answered with bytes pulled from the SABR stream. Shaka never learns the truth. That's the essence of an adapter: make a weird thing wear the costume of a familiar thing , so existing tools work unchanged. kira adapts SABR to a player, inside the browser . Your Go backend does the mirror image: it adapts SABR to a standard format, at the server edge . Instead of hijacking a player's requests, your service consumes SABR itself and re-exposes the result as something every client already speaks — a plain progressive .mp4 download, or an HLS/DASH manifest with normal segment URLs. Each settlement requires a TLS-encrypted TCP handshake, an XML payload validation, a database transaction, and a confirmation callback. Under standard conditions, user-space APM tools report an average latency of 4.2ms. But during market opening, the 99.9th percentile latency explodes to 850ms. When you rely exclusively on user-space telemetry: 1. You cannot see kernel queue delays : If a packet waits 300ms in the socket receive buffer (SO RCVBUF) before Go's runtime netpoll calls read(), your application timer only measures from the moment read() returns. Application crashes kill your visibility : If a microservice panics or deadlocks, its internal metrics server dies with it. Kernel-level probes continue running unaffected.
